Hon Dame Margaret Kerslake Shields

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I regret to inform the House of the death on
29 May 2013 of the Hon Dame Margaret Kerslake Shields DNZM, QSO, who
represented the Kapiti el ectorate from 1981 to 1990. From 1984 to 1990 she held a
number of portfolios, includi ng Minister of Customs, Mini ster of Consumer Affairs,
Minister of Statistics, and Minister of Women’s Affairs. I desire on behalf of this House
to express our sense of the loss we have su stained and our sympat hy with the relatives
of the late former member. I now ask members to stand with me and observe a period of
silence as a mark of respect for her memory.
Honourable members stood as a mark of respect.
Prime Minister—Decision Making and Constitutional Safeguards
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements regarding Government policy?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that the Auditor-General’s
report into the Skycity deal vindicates his Government, given that the Auditor-General’s
response to his claim was not to agree with  him, but rather to state: “we have
established deficiencies on the part of both officials and Ministers.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Absolutely, and the reason for that, as the member will be
aware, is that the Auditor-General’s report was divided into three parts. The first part of
it was focused on my involvement, and I was totally and utterly cl eared and vindicated
in that. That was my only involvement.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to ta ble a legal opinion by constitutional lawyer
Stephen Franks, principal at Fr anks and Ogilvie, outlining se rious legal deficiencies in
the Government’s Skycity deal. The opinion is dated 16 May 2013.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that le gal opinion. Is there any objection?
There appears to be none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he agree with Mr Franks’ view that the agreement with
Skycity is “arguably unlawful ” and “skirts important constitutional safeguards”; if he
does not understand this constitutional princi ple, will he read the central case on the
issue, the case of Fitzgerald v Muldoon?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, but I am sure what Mr Franks would find unlawful is
someone coming in and telling the Ne w Zealand public that they have 100,000
signatures—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he agree with Mr Franks ’ view that “The ability to
‘purchase’ a dispensation from regulation sits uncomfortably with the rule of law.”?
10626 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and no more than Labour would agree with that, given it
did exactly the same deal back in 2001.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he agree with Mr Franks that “Case law discourages
anything … to fetter Parliament’s … power to legislate on future matters,”; if so, will he
reconsider the aspects of the Skycity deal that do exactly this, such as the 35-year
clause?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is this backroom deal with  Skycity—along with the cancelling
of democracy in Canterbury, taking away the ri ghts of carers to have  their day in court,
giving Bathurst Resources the keys to our conservation estate, stopping free speech at
sea, granting the Government Communications Security Bureau the power to spy on us,
and failing to act in good faith to reform MMP—not indicative of a Government that
will not let our democracy stand in the wa y of special favours for its friends and
donors?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: If the Government was doing that  I might be inclined to agree
with him, but it is ac tually not correct. If one looks at, for instance, the changes to
people’s ability to protest at sea, the ability is very much there. There is a safety area
that actually makes sense to all partie s. When it comes to the Government
Communications Security Bureau, the member  sits on the Intelligence and Security
Committee and is well and truly aware that, in fact, the Government Communications
Security Bureau has been carrying out activ ities under an agency relationship for a long
period of time. In fact, all we are doing is clarifying the law, so there is no change in
position there. There is no backroom deal with  Skycity; it has been totally transparent.
And even though the member does not like to hear it, my role in that was totally cleared
by the Auditor-General.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Yeah, right!

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member just ask his supplementary question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he listen to Otago University law professor Andrew
Geddis, Canterbury University law professo r Philip Joseph, former Prime Minister and
Law Commission head Sir Geoffrey Palmer, cu rrent New Zealander of the Year Anne
Salmond—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am having trouble hearing the question. Would the member
please start the question again.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he listen to Otago University law professor Andrew
Geddis, Canterbury University law professo r Philip Joseph, former Prime Minister and
Law Commission head Sir Geoffrey Palmer, cu rrent New Zealander of the Year Anne
Salmond, and many, many other New Zealanders, who have raised concerns about the
Government riding roughshod over New Zeala nders’ democratic rights and over our
constitution?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I would not agree with the point that they are making. I would
have to look at all the different contexts. They may not be in exactly the same place. But
the bottom line is th at the Government was elected  under a mandate it took to the
people. It has absolutely stuck to that mandate. When it comes to these issues, the
Government has presented them to the pe ople of New Zeala nd. The people who are
riding roughshod over the rest of New Zeal and are the Greens, who have played
economic sabotage with the country and do not seem to care about that.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that answer, can the Prime Minister point to exactly
where in his election platform he promised th at he would remove from family carers of
disabled people the right to go to court to  challenge the lawful ness of Government
actions?
4 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 10627

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I would have to go back and look at al l of the particular
details, but, from memory, the Government made it clear we would look at the matter.
Let us understand exactly what the Government did in that legislation, which is that it
said, rightfully so, that it would address the issues raised in the Atkinson case. It also
gave the right to pay family caregivers when they were looking after an adult disabled
child. But the Government also said that there has been a very longstanding position—a
very longstanding position—where there was,  arguably, a line dr awn about where the
State’s responsibilities start and finish and where family responsibilities start and finish.
This Government is actually moving the country to a place that only two other countries
in the world are in, and we happen to be doing something that Labour never did in
office.
Income Gap, Parity with Australia—Minimum Wage
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that his Government has a “100
percent record” on the minimum wage; if s o, how does he explain the now $6-plus an
hour gap between Australia and New Zealand, after Australia raised its minimum wage
to NZ$19.80 an hour?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. The Government has been raising the minimum wage
within the bounds of what we think is possible to  ensure that we preserve people’s
work. If we look at the minimum wage in New Zealand, it is $13.75. That is half the
average adult working wage. Th at puts us at the highest av erage in the OECD. We also
have the significant payments, which we have maintained throughout the difficult times,
of Working for Families. As I pointed out in the House last week, if somebody earns

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: The widest gap between rich and poor ever.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, you may not want to hear it, but if you want to let me
give the answer, I am more than happy to do so. OK, so if you go and have a look at
someone who earned the minimum wage of  $13.75 an hour for 40 hours per week and
who was bringing up three children, that person would earn just a touch under $29,000 a
year. They would pay $4,500 in tax, and by the time they got their Working for Families
payments and accommodation supplements, they would receive over another $20,000-
odd in the hand. That makes New Zealand, in the relative scheme of  things, reasonably
generous for at-risk and low-income New Zealanders.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Why does he think a minimum wage worker deserves $3 in
Australia for every $2 they would earn in  New Zealand for doing exactly the same
work?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, there are different i ssues in each country. There are
different costs—the inflation rates being si gnificantly higher in Australia. For a period
of time, they have had higher levels of inte rest rates. But one of the most important
points is that there is a balancing act here between making sure that people get pay rises
and making sure that people do not lose their jobs. If the member be lieves there is no
correlation between the two, he  is not only demonstrating that he does not understand
economics but he is equally free to go and tell New Zealanders on the campaign trail
that he wants to put them in the dole queue, because that is the simple message you will
be sending them.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he aware that Australia’s unemployment rate is lower than New
Zealand’s, despite a higher minimum wage; if  so, does not that confirm the Department
10628 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013
of Labour’s finding in 2004 of “positive em ployment responses” to minimum wage
increases under the last Government?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. I am surprised that the member is spending so much time
wanting to quote Australia, because if one look s at a few things that have happened in
Australia recently—let us just look at thos e. Firstly, its unemployment rate is on the
way up. Our unemployment rate has been on a track lower. This Government is going to
get New Zealand back into surplus by 2014-15;  the Australian Government is likely to
get back into surplus by onl y 2016-17. The BNZ believes that  this country will grow
faster than Australia in the next few years. And I notice that the member does not get on
his feet any more and ask about people leavi ng for Australia, and the reason is that they
are not leaving in droves any more; they ar e responding to New Zealand. In fact, maybe
the member should—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is a sufficiently long answer.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that he said in 2008 of Ne w Zealanders leaving for Australia
that it was a vote of no c onfidence in Helen Clark’s Gove rnment, what does he say to
people now, given that the number is 43 percent higher today?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, yes, some people have left for Australia—a lot more—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I am glad they are cheer ing, because a lot more of them
left under a Labour Gove rnment numerically. [ Interruption] Yes, they did—yes, they
did. By the way, if it is such a bad place to live—[Interruption] Well, if it is such a—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is a very unsatisfactory interjection coming from over
on that side.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Supplementary question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Supplementary—

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I have not fini shed—no, I have not fini shed. And if it is
such a bad place to live, under such a bad Government, then maybe someone with
Australian citizenship will want to go back to Australia, rather than live under this
Government in New Zealand.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he aware that McDonald’s, KFC, Starbucks, Pizza Hut, The
Warehouse, Farmers, Kmart, Bunnings, and Countdown are not implementing his youth
minimum wage rates; if so, does that mean that major corporates actually care more
about New Zealanders’ cost of living than the Government does?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I am aware of that. I think the important point to note
here is that this is the minimum wage. You are not actually required to pay that wage,
and the vast bulk of New Zealand workers are paid well and trul y above the minimum
wage. But here is a very si mple point: if you are 16 or 17,  under this Government, the
message is that an employer may give you a chance to get a job. You see, these people
on the other side of the House, they do not want to give employers any incentives—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The Prime Minister answered
the question in the first sentence. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! If the member is happy with the answer, then we will
proceed to further supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We have got into the habit
of having long speeches from Ministers in an swers, and it always requires a point of
order from us to bring the answer to an end—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No. [Interruption] Order! That is not right, and if the member wants
to have another look at the recording earli er, he will see that I brought the Prime
Minister to heel only about two questions ago, when I felt the an swer was quite long
enough.
4 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 10629
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus, Reduction in Debt, and
Superannuation
3. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What progress is
the Government making in reaching its fiscal targets of returning to surplus in 2014/15
and reducing net government debt to 20 percent of GDP by 2020?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is on track to
meeting both of those targets. Budget for ecasts show a surplus of $75 million in 2014-
15 and net debt peaking at 28.7 percent of GDP  in the same year before falling to 17.6
percent of GDP in 2021. Taking on more de bt over the past few years has been
appropriate to support our future economic gr owth and to cushion New Zealanders and
their families from the worst effects of recessi on. But, at the same time as taking on the
debt, the Government has laid out a path back  to surplus and, furthermore, a path back
to reducing Government debt to levels that we believe are prudent.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: Why is it important that the Gove rnment gets back to surplus and
starts repaying debt?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Although the level of Government debt is well below that of
many other Governments that we compare ourse lves with, it is important that we keep
Government debt low in order to offset very  high household debt and to ensure that we
can manage through another r ecession. Net Government debt  is still rising today by
around $130 million a week and will reach $70 billion in 2016-17, up from around $10
billion just 5 years ago. Th at is the equivalent of around $15,000 for each and every
New Zealander. We simply believe that it w ould be prudent to return Government debt
to lower levels so that we are better able to reduce the pressure on interest rates rising
sooner than they otherwise would, and reduce pressure on an exchange rate that is
already higher than is comfortable for us.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What recent reports has the Minister received on Government
finances?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Treasury today issued the Government Financial Statements
for the 10 months to 30 April. They show that a stronger economy and the tax reforms
of 2010 are underpinning more tax revenue.  Combined with the Government’s
responsible control over expenditure, this has restricted the deficit to less than $4 billion
for the 10 months, which is $600 million less th an was forecast in the Budget just a few
weeks ago. Tax revenue is around $3.1 billion higher than the corresponding period last
year. This is one of a number of indicators that New Zealanders have some well-earned
confidence and optimism about the future.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What are some of the risks to the Government’s improving
finances and the brighter outlook for the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There are some risks in the global economy. Europe still has
deep-seated and long-term debt problems and productivity problems. The US economy
looks to be recovering, but it is unclear just how robust that is. China faces risks of both
lower growth and problems with excessive cr edit. In Australia there seems to be a
sharper than expected downturn in mining investment, which could lead to Australia
having lower growth rates over the next couple of years th an in New Zealand. So there
are global risks and also dom estic risks if the Government does not stay on track with
this moderate, consistent, and long-term economic policy.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he agree that his claims  to fiscal responsibility are
undermined by his refusal to address the superannuation entitleme nt age well in
advance, so that people have time to prep are, given that costs of superannuation have
increased by $3 billion, from $7 billion to $10 billion per annum, in the last 5 years, and
that in just 2 years’ time the cost of New Zealand superannuation to the taxpayer will be
more than the entire cost of preschool, primary, intermediate, and secondary education?
10630 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not agree.  Of course, no one is proposing changes
in the age of eligibility in a way that w ould affect the costs of superannuation over the
next 2 years. The Government has been so busy dealing with the large and rising costs
of law and order and welfare, which got out of control under the previous Government.
Fortunately, we are having some success in  bringing those long- term costs under
control.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Well, then, if the Minister does not agree with the Labour Party,
does he agree with Gareth Kiernan of Info metrics, who said: “If Key is genuinely
interested in what’s good for the future of  the country … [and his] decision-making is
not dominated by his own ego, he would recognise his mistake about the retirement age
and stand down.”; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I do disagree with him. The Government made some
very clear undertakings. I know that it is no t the style of the Oppos ition parties, but we
have said that we would not change the age and we will not. At the same time, as I
pointed out to the member before, there are other long-term costs where the failures of
the previous Government meant that they ha ve got out of control, particularly for
welfare and law and order. The Government is implementing a range of innovative and,
in some cases, world-leading policies to bring those costs under control. That, of course,
will help our ability to meet superannuation obligations in the future.
Ministers—Confidence and Security of Government Information
4. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Prime Minister: Has
he recently had reason to have lost confidence in any of his Ministers; if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Did he or his office question th e Minister of Revenue as to
how a Dominion Post journalist received inside inform ation, leading that journalist to
write on 5 February this year: “A ministry briefing leaked last night”—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: When?

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: —last night—“suggests N ovopay needs a fundamental
redesign.”, and outlining that the Inland Revenue Department—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Will the member please continue with his question.
[Interruption] Order! Will the member please continue with his question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Down here we can hardly hear a thing because of the
noise.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: There were interjections, I acknowledge that to the member, but
they were not that loud. Th ey are often substantially lo uder than that. Would the
member please start his question again.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Did he or his office question th e Minister of Revenue as to
how a Dominion Post journalist received inside inform ation, leading that journalist to
write on 5 February this year: “A ministry briefing leaked last night suggests Novopay
needs a fundamental redesign.”, and outlining that the Inla nd Revenue Department had
installed a senior manager and small teams of payroll experts at the Ministry of
Education to sort out the Novopay mess?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I certainly have not. I am  not aware of my office doing
such a thing. From what the member seems to  be saying—I have not read the article; I
presume I may have read it at the time, but I do not have it in front of me—it does
sound like it is quite possible that a journa list could have information on that, simply
because it was in the public domain anyway that Novopay was going to be substantially
reworked.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: As Prime Minister and Minister responsible for the GCSB,
did he or his office investig ate the leaking of an intern al survey on the Government
4 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 10631
Communications Security Bureau to a Dominion Post journalist, outlining how low the
morale at the bureau was, as reported in the Dominion Post on 16 October 2012?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, not to the best of my knowledge.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Has he directed his staff to  investigate how a journalist
from the Dominion Post obtained the information that led to a report that Parliament’s
Intelligence and Security Committee members were being muzzled from asking detailed
questions on the Dotcom saga, as reported in the Dominion Post on 13 December 2012?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: As Prime Minister and ch air of the parliamentary
Intelligence and Security Committee, does he be lieve there is a leak in that committee
and, if so, who does he believe is that l eak—Mr Shearer, Mr Norman, Mr Banks, the
Prime Minister himself, or the remaining member of that five-member committee who
wrote of the Government Communications Secu rity Bureau on 24 October last year: “I
am starting to feel very uncomfortable.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I do not think there is a le ak. It is possible that someone
has made an indiscreet comment, and if they have, I am sure that they would regret that.
Crown Revenue—Accident Compensation Levies and Carbon Taxes
5. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by
his statement that the proposed reductions in ACC levies is a “stealth tax cut”; if so,
does he agree that by keeping levies higher th an they need to be, ACC is operating as a
stealth tax; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I stand by my statement in the
context that it was made, where the member labelled ACC levies as  a stealth tax. I do
not agree with the member’s second point. La st month the Budget signalled ACC levies
will fall by $300 million in 2014-15 and by around a billion dollars in 2015-16. This is a
direct result of a much-improved performance by ACC. The Government has been keen
to ensure that its much-impr oved performance on rehabilitation, which is the core of its
activities, is well bedded-in before we have considered passing some of the benefits of
that back to households and businesses.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is it correct that if he implemented the reduction of $700 million
in ACC levies for this year and next, as recommended by ACC, an operating balance
before gains and losses surplu s would not have been foreca st for 2014-15 in his most
recent Budget?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, not necessarily, because, as  I pointed out to the member
before, there is no single decision that mean s the Government achieves surpluses, and it
makes its Budget decisions as a package—for instance, you could argue that if we had
not given schools up to $80 million in increased  operational grants, we would not have
posted a surplus. But, of course, that is not how the Government approaches the issue.
The Government has had a different view from ACC about the future funding track,
because we wanted to ensure that its better performance was well embedded and that we
could reduce the number of changes in the le vy—for instance, not have levies go down
and then have to put them up again.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Well, then, if other revenue and other expense items were
unchanged but he implemented the reduction of ACC levies, as recommended by ACC,
is it correct that an opera ting balance before gains and losses surplus would not have
been forecast for 2014-15 in his most recent Budget?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, because we could say that about every single decision,
as I have explained to the member. What we do know for sure is that if ACC had
continued to be run as it was by the Labour Party, as a political tool, we would be
nowhere near surpluses today, because it was losing hundreds of millions of dollars.
10632 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question could not have
been more specific—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! And I invite the member to ask his question again.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: If all other revenue and expense items were left unchanged and
if he had implemented the reduction of ACC levies, as recommended by ACC, is it
correct that an operating balance before ga ins and losses surplus would not have been
forecast for 2014-15 in his most recent Budget?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, for exactly the reasons I st ated in the previous answer,
when I also said no. That is because that is not the way the Government makes Budget
decisions—either this Government or the prev ious Government. What I can also repeat
is that if we had left A CC running as it was under the previous Labour Government,
losing billions of dollars a year, we would certainly not have surpluses.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Again my question has not
been addressed. My question said: “All other th ings being equal, if you changed this, if
you had accepted the ACC advi ce, would you not have reache d surplus?”. The Minister
does not want to admit it, but that question is  directed specifically, and I would like the
Minister to be required to answer that question, not what he wanted the question to be.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept that the answer is not according to the design or the wishes
of the member, but the Minister when he st arted his answer disput ed that. He simply
said no and then gave some reasons.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: What reports has he seen on proposed stealth taxes?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have seen a proposal to in crease taxes under the emissions
trading system by up to $500 per household. This report has puzzled me, because the
same people who are proposing to put up taxes on electricity by $500 per household
have told the public they are going to reduce the cost of electricity by $300 per
household. Both of those policies cannot be right.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the Minister aware that if the system of pricing electricity
moved to a basis of production cost plus retu rn on capital, the cost of carbon would not
flow through to all electricity , and the total cost of carbon and electricity prices would
decrease?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I am not sure what the member meant, and I was not
aware of it. I was not aware of it. What I can say is that it is puzzling that the same two
parties are promising to put up electricity  prices by $500 a year with one policy, and
reduce it by $300 a year with another policy.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Why did he ignore official minist ry advice in the regulatory impact
statement that keeping ACC levies artifi cially high would “negatively impact on …
economic growth and reducing costs for business.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government considered that advice but did not agree
that the levies were artific ially high. What it did agree on is that ACC had done a good
job of turning round the fact that under the previous Government rehabilitation rates for
injured workers got significantly worse, and that meant that ACC was making large
losses. It has over the last few years significantly improved the rehabilitation rates. Now
that we believe that the damage done by Labour  has largely been fixed, we can start to
reduce the levies.
Canterbury, Recovery—Housing New Zealand Properties
6. NICKY WAGNER (National—Christchurch Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Housing
items.text: What progress has the Government made  in repairing or replacing the over
5,000 Housing New Zealand homes damaged or “munted” by the 2010 and 2011
earthquakes?
4 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 10633

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The repair and replacement job
from the Christchurch eart hquakes is a massive undert aking involving hundreds of
millions of dollars. The first phase, which started on 4 September 2010, involved 27,000
emergency repairs to make pr operties safe and functional in the immediate term. The
second phase involves the substantial l ong-term repairs on 5,000 homes so they are
brought up to full standard. That work is well under way and will be completed by the
end of 2015. The third phase, announced on Fr iday with the earthquake recovery
Minister, Gerry Brownlee, was the construc tion of 700 new houses to be built on sites
where home are uneconomic to repair or are m unted, as I think Cantabrians call it. This
programme will involve a new house being built—a new house being built—every
single working day from now until the end of 2015, and it is the largest and fastest
Government house-building programme ever in Christchurch’s history.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: How has the settlement of the Housing New Zealand’s $320 million
insurance claim helped to advance this work and get a better outcome for Christchurch’s
highest-need citizens?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The insurance settlement has made an enormous difference
to both the pace and the quality of the re build. Previously, each house had to be
individually assessed, quotes checked with the insurer,  and work done to repair the
house to its pre-earthquake status. This wa s both slow and cumbersome. Housing New
Zealand now has the flexibility with the insu rance money in the bank to reconfigure its
housing stock for today’s needs. That mean s more one, two, and four-bedroom homes,
rather than just rebuilding the old three-be droom ones. It means moving to a mixed and
denser housing model, and it means that we in vest simultaneously in safer, drier, and
warmer homes. It means that by the end of 2015 not only will we have the same number
of houses as we did pre-earthquake but they  will be better in terms of being safer,
warmer, and drier.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: Will all the 700 new houses be retained by Housing New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No. We are taking the opportunity to rebuild a lot more
houses on the land where older homes are be ing demolished, and we want to take the
opportunity to move to mixed housing a nd to expand community social housing. I
notice members opposite interjec ting. It shows how lit tle they care for the poor people
of Christchurch whose homes have been affected by the earthquakes. Some of the
houses will be onsold to low-income families as affordable houses, and others will be
sold to community social housing providers  as part of the Government’s broader
programme of expanding community social housing.
Child Protection—Methamphetamine Labs in Homes
7. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour)  to the Minister for Social Development : What
advice has she received about the number of  methamphetamine labs that have been
found by Police to have children present, a nd how many of these children have been
subsequently removed by Child, Youth and Family Services?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.role: Associate Mi nister for Social Development
items.text: on
behalf of the Minister for Social Development : I can advise that, as per the written
response to her written question, these numbe rs are not gathered centrally on a crime-
specific basis. The interventions that are made on a house by house, case by case basis
are done according to a protoc ol signed up to by pol ice, and child safety is at the
forefront of those decisions.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does Child, Youth and Family Serv ices have a formal protocol for
children found living in homes with methamphe tamine labs; if not, why not, and when
can we expect to see one?
10634 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: Interventions that are made with the police as a result
of crimes committed are conducted in respect of  a protocol that was drafted in 2010. It
is currently being re viewed at the moment, and ongoi ng discussion between police and
Child, Youth and Family Services specifically  in respect of methamphetamine labs is
part of those discussions.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I asked specifically about the
Child, Youth and Family Services protocol. The police protocol I am aware of—it has
been around since 2009—but there is no Child, Youth and Family Services protocol—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Would the member, please, just re peat the question. It might not
have been heard correctly.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does Child, Youth and Family Serv ices have a formal protocol for
children found living in homes with methamphe tamine labs; if not, why not, and when
can we expect to see one?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: My understanding is that there are discussions going
on currently between the police and Child, Youth and Family Services as to a
memorandum of understanding that would form the basis of that protocol. Currently,
they are in discussion. The protocol that is being operated on at the moment is a generic
criminal memorandum of understanding protoc ol that operates between the police and
Child, Youth and Family Services but is not crime-specific.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: How long will it take for her depart ment to settle on a protocol to
protect these children, when more than 480 children have been found in meth labs
already, the police have had a protocol for several years, and Child, Youth and Family
Services has said that it has been working on one for more than 12 months now?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: As I understand it, there have been 384 children who
were found in 199 methamphetamine labs. In the same time frame of those offences, the
police have referred 250,000 children to Child, Youth and Family Se rvices for dealing
with and for consideration of intervention, not including those young children on the
premises where family violence has occurred. In terms of what the time frame would be
for the completion of that protocol, I do not ha ve that information in front of me, except
that it is urgent for the department. It is working with the police currently. That is the
way that it should be, bearing in mind that when we are dealing with these sorts of
matters, the police has one role and Child, Youth and Family Services has another role.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. One could not be other
than concerned to have a Mini ster answering questions in a way that denies Parliament
information on the basis that there is some so rt of protocol, and then giving a figure for
the number of children who are found to be present at a methamphetamine lab
discovery—right? [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am trying to understand what the point of order is.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: It is that he knows how many children were found when
there was a meth lab discovery, but he cannot say how many we re removed. We are
being deliberately denied knowledge essentia l for parliamentarians to make a decision
here.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Minister at all times, in my  mind, has addressed the questions
adequately. He said right at the start, from the first question, that the information as
requested was not gathered. We have moved on from that question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does she think it is acceptable—

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. To clarify in
terms of the point of order made by the pr evious speaker, Winston Peters, the numbers
that the member Jacinda Ardern, in asking her question, referred to were not referring to
the same period as the numbers of children I was referring to. I was talking about the
execution of search warrants, the discove ry of 199 methamphetamine labs, and 384
4 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 10635
children found in those labs. It was not part of the same ques tion, but it did relate to the
number I later gave her—250,000.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! And that is now becoming another answer to the question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Why do the police collect inform ation on how many children are
found in homes with methamphetamine labs , but Child, Youth and Family Services,
which is charged with the children’s ca re and protection, doe s not collect that
information?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: It is not true to say that Child, Youth and Family
Services does not collect that information. Th at information is collected on a region by
region basis, as matters are intervened in on a case by case basis. If that information
were collected nationally, it would not cha nge the protocol, it would not change the

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That is the precise
point of my original point of order. Now we are being told that the information is
available region by region. The Minister ha s had 3½ hours for his department to find
out, region by region, the total number. Why is  Parliament being denied this important
information?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Does the member want to speak to the point of order?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: That was not the subject of the original question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Just for further clarification for the Speaker, I asked that question
on notice. I have asked it in written form before and been denied that information by the
Minister.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: At the end of the time, it is now for Parliament, the House here, and
the public to judge the quality of the answer s that have been gi ven. I have become
increasingly confused by the answers that ha ve been given, but that  being the case, the
Minister started by saying that  information was not available—it was not gathered in
that form. He has then proceeded to give  further information, but maybe that was
sourced from police rather than Child, Yout h and Family Services. So if the member
wishes to ask further supplementary questions—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am sorry, but the fact
is that this is a very particular, specific  question on notice, and, apparently, has been
asked before in writing, and it is about how  many of these children have been removed
by Child, Youth and Family Services as a re sult of methamphetamine lab discovery by
the police. We started off with “Well, you can ’t have the information, because that is
subject to a protocol.”, and then we got to “Well, yes, the information is available
region by region.” If that is the case, surely  the Minister can tell  us, after 3½ hours of
time to prepare, what, region by region, that all adds up to.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is not my job here to desi gn the answer for the Minister. The
Minister started a question, a nd at that stage the House ac tually accepted his answer:
that such information as requested was not gathered. Subsequent supplementary
questions have gleaned some information. I can do no more today with the particular
answer that has been given by the honourable Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I think you were right at
the beginning, and you were right in the first part of your—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Well, credit when it is due.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Would the member please come to his point of order.
10636 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I am now getting to the second point, and that is that in the
past, Speakers have advised Ministers to get their offi ces to use old-fashioned
technology, like a phone, and get on the phone to the regions to get the answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We are moving forward now. If th ere are no further supplementary
questions, we are going—[Interruption] Further supplementary questions?

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does she think it is acceptable that there are reports of children
being found in meth labs and being removed by Child, Youth and Family Services, only
to be returned to caregivers who, after bei ng bailed, have continue d to cook meth with

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I am not aware of such a ca se specifically. If it was
drawn to the Minister’s attention, then she would certainly have that investigated. My
understanding is that when a clan-lab has b een searched and children are located, they
are taken into care. They may be put back, they may be given to other members of the

situation.
Schools, Partnership—Use of Closed State School Sites

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Tēnā koutou e te Whare. My question is
to the Minister of Education and asks—[Interruption] Thank you, Mr Mallard.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe. The Public Works Act,
not the Education Amendment Bill, continues to govern the process for the disposal of
any surplus—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speake r. Sorry, with all the chatter from

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! There was substantial noise from many parts of the House. I

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: T ēnā koe. The Public Works Act, not the Education

items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. My question had nothing to do

items.text: Can the Minister confirm that she told Cabinet earlier this year that
“The most practical options for the first partnership sc hools are renting premises,
4 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 10637
including existing educational buildings such as a closed State school or by a private

items.text: No, I cannot confirm that. I wo uld have to investigate the

items.text: That is sufficient information. Leave is sought to table that

items.text: To be clear, the Education Amendment Bill is focused on

as. The Education Amendment Bill is about partnership schools. Partnership schools are

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was twofold—

items.text: Order! I suspect that the Minister did not hear your question clearly.

items.text: How many of the schools closed in Christchurch were done so
purposely, so that private businesses could ta ke them over as charter schools; if none,
will she rule out the use of any closed school s in Christchurch for private profit charter

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, none.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: No.

items.text: Will she give the people of Christchurch a guarantee that she will
not approve the opening of a partnership school on a school site where she has closed a

items.text: No, I will not give guarantees of that nature, because they

Budget 2013—Tertiary Training in Science and Engineering
9. SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki) to the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment : What investment has the Government made in
new funding for science and engineering in Budget 2013?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): As part of the $130 million in new funding initiatives for tertiary
education announced in Budget 2013, the Gove rnment is investing an additional $17.9
million in science tuition and $9.3 million in  engineering tuition, an increase of 2
percent funding per full-time equivalent. Science and engineering degrees have been the
10638 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013
subject of under-investment in the past, and industry demand for skilled engineers and
scientists remains high. The G overnment has made investment in these areas a priority
in the last 2 years, recognising that scientists and engineers are key drivers of innovation
and productivity, and are crucial for growth in our economy.
Simon O’Connor : How is this part of the Government’s wider commitment to
science and engineering?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The increased funding as part of Budget 2013 builds on
recent announcements committing the Government to providing an additional 1,000
engineering places at universities and polytech nics. This puts us on track to achieve our
goal of producing an extra 500 engineering graduates per year by 2017. The increase in
funding is also on top of the $159 million committed to engineering, science, and
research - led learning in our tertiary institutions announced in last year’s Budget, which
demonstrates this Government’s ongoing co mmitment to investing in areas that will
help grow our economy and retain our international competitiveness.
Simon O’Connor : Why is the Government focusing on increasing science and
engineering funding?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: New Zealand has historica lly had an undersupply of
engineers. In fact, we have  been training only about ha lf the number we  require and
about half the OECD average for many, many years. We have also recognised the need
to increase our investment in training scient ists to help fuel the innovation required to
grow our economy. Compared with Australia , we subsidise engineering, science, and
other degrees with high capital costs much less than those with lower capital costs, like
arts and humanities degrees. The Business Growth Agenda outlines the actions the
Government is taking to build a more productive and innovative workforce, giving
Kiwis the skills they need to compete in a complex and dynamic global environment.
Employment Relations—Legislative Reform and Effect on Wages
10. DARIEN FENTON (Labour)  to the Minister of Labour : What advice has he
received about the effect on wages of changes to collective bargaining in the
Employment Relations Amendment Bill?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I have not received any advice on
the member’s specific point. The change s are fundamentally about improving the
efficiency and fairness of the bargaini ng process not pushing wages one way or the
other. I would not expect these changes to have a significant impact on wages.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: How will his changes in the Employment Relations Amendment Bill
improve wages, given his department advise d that removing the 30-day rule will allow
employers to pay less to new workers performing the same work?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: If the member had listened to my answer, I made it clear
that I do not think it will pa rticularly push wages one way or the other. Actually, you
can make a very strong argument that th rough improved efficien cies and productivity,
that leaves more money in an employer’s pocket to pay higher wages.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: How will wages be improved when his bill will enable employers to
fine workers 10 percent of their pay for ta king partial action and reduce pay below the
minimum wage, regardless of how much time is actually lost?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I do not accept that at all. I think, actually, what these
changes do is level the playing field so that, actually, employers have the same sorts of

Fenton’s Arthur Scargill - like  world that is not right, but , actually, on this side, we

JONES (Labour) to the Minister of M āori Affairs: Does he stand by his statement

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question was about

items.text: I invite the member to ask the question again.

business exports, and when you do that th e money trickles back to the hap ū and the
iwi—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Oh no!

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Oh yes! Take the honey c ontract that has gone to
China. It is produced by the people along the river, along the villages, and they get the
benefits of that when it comes in—[Interruption] No, this is the reality. You have got to

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My point of order is
simply this: first of all, we have had a long explanation of why things are not
happening; then he started to blame you.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The answer was certainly l ong enough. The Minister was asked
what initiatives have supported whānau, etc., and he gave adequate examples.

items.speaker: Rino Tirikatene
items.text: Does he support the target of his Government colleague Steven
Joyce to raise median incomes for Māori to that of the overall population by 2040; if so,
does he think that 200 years since the signing of te Tiriti is an acceptable time frame for
Māori to achieve parity in this country?

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Absolutely, and that is why we have created He Toki ki
te Rika, as well as He Kai Kei Aku Ringa—both of those. The first person to start things
down in Christchurch was from the M āori Party, where we gathered all the builders
together, and Ng āi Tahu, Te Puni K ōkiri, and all those for He Toki ki te Rika. In
addition to that, now we have He Kai Kei Aku Ringa, and that is a joint venture
between Māori and the Crown to develop initiati ves based on education and everything
else to increase M āori productivity. If you do not do th at, you ain’t going to succeed.
You cannot just pick out one thing. And so education becomes a very important arm of
that development.
Spring Hill Corrections Facility—Riot

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from David Clendon seeking to debate under
Standing Order 386 the riot that occurred on Saturday, 1 June at Spring Hill Corrections
Facility. The occasion of the riot is a part icular case of recent occurrence involving
ministerial responsibility. The test for whether a particular matter requires the
immediate attention of the House is a very high one, and the fact that the Budget debate
is before the House means that there is another means by which the House can discuss
the matter. The purpose of an urgent debate is to hold the Government accountable for
its decisions. Working through the riot’s underlying causes will take time. Resolution of
the wider matters the member raises in an application is important for public confidence
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates Declined 10641
in the prison system, but I am not convinced that I would be justified in setting aside the
business of the House today. The application is, therefore, declined.
Teachers and Support Staff, Payroll—Ministerial Inquiry into Novopay System

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have also received letters from Metiria Turei and Chris Hipkins
seeking to debate under Standing Order 386 the findings of the minist erial inquiry into
the Novopay school payroll system. The release of the inquiry report is a particular case
of recent occurrence involving ministerial responsibility. Although the Budget debate is
ongoing, the significance of the fi ndings and the urgent need to  restore public trust and
confidence in the education sector are suffici ent reasons to warrant the attention of the
House today by way of an urgent debate. As  Metiria Turei’s application was received
first, I call on Metiria Turei to move that the House take note of an urgent matter of
public importance.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I move, That the House take note of a
matter of urgent public importance. This Government has a habit of making its officials
take the knocks for its decisions. We saw that  when it apparently vindicated itself over
Skycity, blaming the officials for not givi ng it enough information, and we are seeing
exactly the same here: a Minister who has no idea what is going on in her own ministry,
who is prepared to re ly on advice without qu estioning any of it reasonably when she
makes her decisions, and who is then found to have managed it so appallingly that she
had to give it over to another Minister, who also cannot hand le it. And this is a deal—
this Novopay deal—worth tens of millions of dollars.
What do we find in this report, the Report of the Ministerial Inquiry into the Novopay
Project, from Maarten Wevers? Well, I can cert ainly say that the public are tired of
Ministers pretending that they have no respons ibility for asking the right questions over
these enormous projects that not only co st millions and millions of New Zealand
taxpayers’ dollars but have significant implications for families and for teachers and
schools, and that is what we have seen. It  has been teachers and schools who have paid
the cost of the failure of Minister Hekia Parata and the roll-out of Novopay. Although, it
has to be said, the Novopay i nquiry does highlight some of the failures from officials, it
certainly does not vindicate Ministers, as they would like to say. If it did, why, then, did
Maarten Wevers find that the “creation of a dedicated ministerial portfolio for Novopay,
and the appointment of a new Acting Secretar y gave the sharper fo cus for addressing
the issues and improved the key relationships.” ? He said that because the fact is that
when Novopay was in the hands of Hekia Parata, there was no sharp focus on the
issues, there was no interest in improving th e key relationships, and there certainly was
not any commitment to making sure that when Novopay was brought in, it would be a
system that would work for families, for schools, and for teachers.
When this fiasco was in full boil, Hekia Parata was in charge, along with a woman
with whom we now know Hekia Parata had a pathological problem communicating, and
that was Lesley Longstone. Is it any w onder that Wevers found that key questions
around the finance were not asked by the Minist er, by other Minister s related in that
portfolio, or by their officials, and that the decisions were rushed through without
proper oversight, without listening to all th e warnings from teach ers and from payroll
workers who said that they did not trust the system to work, because they were having
to deal with the consequences  of it? The context was a mi nistry overseen by a Minister
who we now know is incapable of listening. We know that this report shows how that
kind of attitude can infect a whole workplace,  and how information just will not flow
freely when you simply cannot trust a Minister to deal with that information effectively.
10642 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
Ministers can blame official s for not giving them good advice in the crucial 5 June
report to Parata, English, and Foss, but the inquiry found that there were concerns in
that 5 June report that were so obvious that most of us are now left wondering why they
were not picked up on by Ministers. Did they  not bother to read th at report? Although
the officials reported that they were ready to  go live and they did not think that there
were any outstanding issues, in that 5 June report they also pointed to two criteria that
were not being met, and they described elsewh ere in the report that some criteria were
only “close to being met.” With the stability of the entire education system at risk and
with the fortnightly pay of hundreds of thous ands of New Zealande rs at risk, why did
these Ministers Parata, English, and Foss not  just ask a few ke y questions? Why did
they not say to officials: “Go and get thes e uncertain elements checked out first. Find
out why the criteria have not been properly met.”? Wevers found that Ministers at the
time were not even sure who was in charge  of the project and that Ministers were
having meetings with these great teams of people but were completely unclear as to who
had responsibility for a multimillion-dollar IT project that affected thousands and
thousands of New Zealanders and their fort nightly pay. How is that even possible?
What kind of mickey mouse operation was Hekia Parata, Bill English, and Craig Foss—
and effectively this entire National-ACT G overnment—running that they did not even
know who was responsible for a multimillion- dollar IT project? It was like Novopay
just did not exist. It was not on their rada r, even though it affected thousands of New
Zealanders.
Ministers were told back in July of 2009 of significant risks with the system, and
they should have been on heightened alert. We have to ask ourselves why they were so
obsessed with pushing go before the system was ready to handle the problems. What
kind of culture had infected the ministry that officials did not feel free to give Ministers
good and honest information? What kind of culture did these Ministers create? The 5
June report—5 June was a key date according to Wevers. There was no turning back
from the decisions that were made then. It was crucial that Minist ers got that decision
right. Ministers either did not read that 5 J une report or did not r ead it properly. On one
page the report stated that go-live was ready and there were no issues; on another page it
said that there were a couple of criteria th at had not been met, and not a single question
was asked about those criteria or about whether that advice was really accurate.
We cannot blame Ministers for everything; I think that has to be said. But they do not
work in a critical vacuum. They exist in this House to be account able to the public.
They exist to ask the questions of officials, and to make sure when they make the final
decisions they are making them with full information, and with the concerns of the New
Zealand public at heart, particularly wh en you are talking about a multimillion-dollar
project that affects thousands and thousands of New Zealand families. That was clearly
not the case. These Ministers took their hands off the reins and left a vacuum of
leadership. That is what we have seen here with Minister Hekia Parata.
This project was given the go-ahead by this  Government at a time when there were
very serious concerns about its ability to go live. As a resu lt, we have had more than 12
months now of families not being paid and people being overpaid and chased by debt
collectors. Schools have had to fork out th eir own money to make  sure that their
teachers and employees were being paid. We  have had schools having to use the money
that would otherwise be used for the educa tion of our kids to fix up, to patch up, the
mistakes made by this Government and by Ministers who did not bother to care enough
to make sure that they looked at the papers properly. The families in this country are the
ones who have borne the price of the negl ect by these Ministers Parata, English, and
Foss. They owe it to them.
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10643
In fact, even the money that  this Government has alloca ted to schools to help cover
the costs, we know, does not cover the costs.  We know that schools have lost workers,
particularly payroll workers, who were extremely important and long-time employees of
those schools, because of the harm that was caused by Parata, English, and Foss. Those
Ministers led those schools to be existing in  extreme stress for months and months on
end, just for the basics, just because they wa nted to make sure that their teachers and
their workers were being paid their wages.
This Government clearly has a problem w ith workers or it would not have put New
Zealand workers at such risk with such negl ect and such complete lack of consideration
for the people who are being affected by their decision, so much so that they did not
even bother to read the papers and make su re that they had the right information to
make the right decision.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: They don’t like teachers.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: They do not like teachers. I think that is right. I think we have
seen that in the way this whole education portfolio has played out. The effect of that has
been that for many, many families, many, many teachers, and their kids, they have had
real difficulty paying their bills and have bo rne real financial costs because of this
debacle. These Ministers owe the country an  explicit and very clear apology for their
consistent and persistent failures over this  issue. The Government has tried to make
things easier and has been trying to improve the system, but there is still no certainty for
schools and for teachers as to when the system  will work effectively and properly as it
is supposed to. We know that more and more millions are being poured into the
Novopay system to try to patch it up. That is millions of dollars that are not going to the
education of our kids, because it is going to  patch up the IT mistakes that Novopay and
Talent2 made in their process, and that the Ministers allowed them to proceed with.
This apology needs to be made explicitly and immediately to the teachers, to the
students, and to the schools for the hugely destabilising effect that these decisions have
had on them. They need to admit that it was a fiasco, that prudent ministerial oversight
could have been avoided, and heads need to roll. We have previously called for the
Minister Hekia Parata to be sacked for both this debacle over Novopay and the
Christchurch schools debacle, and the persis tent failures in her management of her
portfolio. This report is a clear example, th is report from Maarten Wevers and others,
that she can be held responsible for the decision to go live, for the failure to get proper
advice from officials, to ask the important questions, and to make the right decisions.
The only genuinely respectable action that Hekia Parata can now make is to step down
as Minister as part of her apology to schools,  to teachers, and to families for the debacle
that she has created. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Today was the day
the Report of the Ministerial Inqu iry into the Novopay Project  was released. Unlike
what the Greens have just said in that last speech, where they seek to blame the
Ministers, the point of  the report, I th ink, is clearly that there is blame to go around for
all parties, and, sadly, nobody has acquitted themselves with great distinction in the
introduction of this project. There is a bigge r question, actually, because this is not the
first information and communica tions technology project that has had issues. In fact, it
is not the first information and communicati ons technology projec t with the education
payroll that has had issu es. In fact, you can go back to the mid-1990s and the
introduction of a payroll unde r another company’s name where there was again an
inquiry, this time by the head of the Ministry  of Education, about concerns in the way
that that particular programme was intr oduced. The net result wa s that a number of
changes were made, and it was thought that  these things would not happen again. So
rather than just leaping to the political conclusion that the Greens seek to leap to, and no
10644 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
doubt other members of the Oppos ition as well, it is important  to take the time to at
least read a few pages of the report and ask yourself what actually went wrong here.
Sadly, what went wrong was that in a number of ways the people whom the public
should be able to rely on—som e of the staff, some of th e suppliers—in this instance
were not able to or did not fully perform their role well. The problems with Novopay, as
the report notes, have affected public trust a nd confidence in the Ministry of Education,
and, of course, also in the wider public s ector. The report iden tifies weaknesses in
project governance and project leadership th at allowed the system to go live, with a
number of significant risks that the ministry  and its vendors, including Talent2, were, in
the words of the inquiry, “over-confident of managing.” These risks, as we now know,
resulted in service issues that the minist ry and Talent2 were unprepared for and they
were overwhelmed by their nature and scale.
The report goes into the history of what happened in the whole saga, and it goes back
many years, right the way to 2005 and ear lier. It makes the observation that New
Zealand’s school payroll is very  complex. It compares it with  the health sector payroll.
But it is also very complex, with some very unique elements to it. As a result there was
extensive customisation of the Novopay software. The ministry notes there was a failure
by the ministry to involve the users of the Novopay system in the schools and appreciate
their requirements. So those two things alone indicate some of the difficulties that you
can see happen in these situations when the project that was set up did not first seek to
simplify its business processes, and did not stay close enough to the users of the system.
Probably one of the biggest issues was th e lack of accountability for independent
quality assurance. Ministers were entitled to expect that the quality assurance processes
that the State sector has would have applie d in this case, and, unfortunately, despite
assurances that they did, this was not the case. The result is that Ministers were not well
served by the information they were given on the project. The report notes that reporting
to Ministers was “inconsisten t, … unduly optimistic and so metimes misrepresented the
situation.” I think it would be important to quote, in light of what Ms Turei has just said,
what was said in regard to the June 2012 docum ent. This is on page 88 of the report. It
says: “We were particularly concerned about  the 5 June 2012 document, which invited
Ministers to approve the Mini stry’s Go Live decision. This  report misrepresented the
situation in two significant ways. It suggested that the Go Live decision was supported
by three members of the ICT Council, whic h was not the case; and it stated that
Confidence Point Two criteria had been met, wh en in fact a number either had not been
met or were ‘deemed’ to have been me t (a lower criterion). These factors
overrepresented project readiness and its chan ce of success.” That was the paper that
invited Ministers to make a decision to proceed with the go-live situation with
Novopay. I think it is important, whenever  members get up in this House, to
acknowledge that, because irresp ective of your political ba ckground it is important that
Ministers are able to accept th e written word of their advise rs in the ministries. If you
cannot do that, then the Government processes break down very quickly.
Overall, this report makes for very sober reading. It confirms the view that there is a
lot of blame to go around for the problems with the software program. It does provide a
greater understanding of the level of fau lt between the organisations involved. It
mentions the ministry at significant length. Actually, you do not have  to go far to know
that the ministry has had issues that stretc h back, again for some period of time, many
years in fact, including the period of the previous Government. The performance
improvement review, or PIF review, for the ministry just a couple of years ago was very
sobering reading indeed, and, unfortunately, it s difficulties are reflected in this report.
But it is also the case of being able to rely  on other advisers, and I note that the primary
consultancy, PricewaterhouseCoopers, has been  mentioned in the report, and the State
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10645
Services Commission, and Treasur y as well. So it is fair  to say that nobody—none of
the agencies involved and none of the organisations contracted—has come out of it very
well. Of course, it mentions the key supplier,  the Talent2 organisation, which failed to
meet a number of deadlines. But again, ev en that process was fraught, because it
becomes apparent as you read  the report that the ministry  changed the specifications
significantly over the period of time the project was in development.
So I think there are many places where pe ople who have perhap s already read the
report online this afte rnoon could shake their heads and say: “This is a real problem.
This is a difficulty. Why did this happen in th is way?”. I think if we come back to the
issue of independent quality assurance, unfor tunately, in relation to that, I think you
could make the observation, as I did myself ear lier this afternoon at a press conference,
that a process of groupthink developed, where there was a drawing in of those who were
there to provide that indepe ndent assurance for Ministers into the project itself. The
State Services Commission, PricewaterhouseCoo pers, and others were drawn into that
project—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Go on. Just take a little bit of responsibility, just a little bit.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —Mr Robertson, and basically were not able to give that
independent approach, that potential to say “We should blow the whistle and not
proceed necessarily with the project at this time.”
Like I say, these issues that the report very adequately lists bring a number of
questions and lessons that need to be learnt  for the future, and the inquiry report lays
those lessons out quite clearly for the public sector.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Pretty basic.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member may say it is pret ty basic, but, actually, it is
pretty basic that some of the things should have been done at the outset. Seeing as we
are laying a bit of blame around the place, and obviously the member seeks the desire to
lay some blame, those members on that side of  the House who were part of some of the
original decisions perhaps should have actua lly called for some process simplification
before the process actually began, instead  of sitting there now , today, saying: “It’s
nothing to do with us. Nothing actually happened when we were there.”, when quite
fundamentally it happened over a significant period of time.
So where to from here? It is very impor tant to address the i ssues that go forward.
There will be some issues that arise out of this report. One of those issues will be, as the
Secretary for Education has announced, an investigation into some employment matters.
That is appropriate. There will also be  other consequences of some of the
recommendations in this report. More specifically, there needs to be a real think forward
about how to handle these projects in future. For my money, one of the key parts of it is
to actually go through that business process assessment—to go there and say: “Can we
change and simplify some of these processe s before we make a big change in an
information and communications technology sy stem in this regard?”. I think it is
incumbent on every agency to go through that exercise and to encourage the
Government of the day to try to make these simplifications before the process starts.
For this particular system, we are in the process of remediation and we have made
some significant progress, although nobody would sa y that the system is fixed at this
point. We have improved dramatically the performance pay period to pay period. We
now have the situation that for five out of th e last six payroll periods the error rate has
decreased to less than 0.5 pe rcent of transactions, which is good progress. Last week
88,500 people were paid a total of $173.53 milli on, and 29 staff were notified as being
not paid. That has been reasonable progress.
The second stage is, of course, the remedi ation and dealing with the backlog of
issues in the system. Firstly, there is the outstanding work, and there have been very,
10646 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
very large numbers of transactions that ha ve to be caught up with. We are making some
pretty good progress in terms of outstanding pay instructions, the backlog of inquiries to
the ministry, and leave balances. I am hopeful that these would be back to business-as-
usual levels by the end of June. However, overpayments resolution is taking a longer
period of time, and additional work is being done into the overpayments resolution
system to speed up the clearance of those issues. The next area that has to be resolved is
the resolution of software defects. This last  weekend a further 58 defects were closed.
We are now down to 14 category 2 or very se rious bugs left, nine of  which are targeted
for closure in June. If we achieve even half of that number, then we will have fewer
than 10 category 2 bugs by the end of June. We are on target to achieve that.
But going forward there are a number of th ings that now need to be addressed.
Firstly, usability to encourage people to use the system online is very important.
Secondly, the end-of-year and start-of-year issu es that we had last year need to be
solved. Thirdly, we need to close the service gap that has been identified by schools.
There has been good progress with the schoo ls. We have done some surveys of the
schools, and generally they have noticed improvement. But, as I said, nobody, including
myself, would say at this point that we are satisfied that the project has been
satisfactorily remediated.
I would like to take the opportunity once ag ain to acknowledge the hard work being
done by everybody involved in th is system, particularly th e school administrators, but
also the teams of people working hard at th e ministry, at Talent 2, and around the place
to get the system back on its feet. Ther e has been some hero ic work done by any
number of people involved in de aling with the challenges that  this system has laid out
for them. I would also like to thank for their patience—severely tried at times—the staff
involved with the issues that  have been apparent for i ndividual staff members. Again
they have my assurance that we are workin g as quickly as we can to resolve those
issues.
Finally, I would like to take the oppor tunity—although I appreciate the opportunity
for sober reflection may or may not be avai lable in the House this afternoon, depending
on how the next speakers—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I’m as sober as a judge, Steven.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —decide to take their view. No doubt Mr Robertson et al.
will immediately decide to disappear back in to the political cartoon that is their lives,
and try to lay political blame where quite clea rly, as set out in this report, there is a
much more serious issue for the whole public s ector that we need to address. Perhaps it
is not too much to hope that at least some of the speakers this af ternoon would seek to
address that issue, rather than laying po litical blame. But, for my money, I know that
every member of the Government is very  disappointed in the outcome of this
programme. I personally apologise to the teac hers and administrators for the pain and
suffering that has been caused to them. They, again, have my absolute assurance, as the
Minister responsible for Novopay, that we are seeking to address these issues as quickly
as possible, and that the lessons that are c ontained in this report will be learnt. Thank
you.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: If ever New Zealanders needed a clear
example of the fact that they have a hands-off Government that is not up to the task of
running the country, they got  it today—yet another example today—in this, the Report
of the Ministerial Inquiry into the Novopay Project . I will quote from page 1, the
foreword to the report, which says: “This stat e of affairs and the wider disruptions that
were caused were avoidable.” This, all of th is, this entire shambles, was avoidable.
Steven Joyce talked about there being plenty of blame to go around, and then proceeded
to try to scatter it anywhere except with the Ministers who actua lly made the decisions
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10647
to sign off on the Novopay project. He blamed  the officials and he blamed the past
Government. And, of course, the Government has tried to blame the schools. It has tried
to blame everyone except for the three pe ople who actually signed—put their names on
the piece of paper—to say to go ahead with  Novopay. Bill Englis h, Hekia Parata, and
Craig Foss were the three people who signe d off on the implementation of Novopay,
and ultimately they are the ones who are responsible.
It is great that Steven Joyce has apologise d to all the people who have been affected
by this, but why on earth did it take such a long time? Why did Hekia Parata not front
up and apologise? Why did Hekia Parata, the Minister of E ducation, not front up and
apologise for the massive turmoil that she ca used within schools? I agree with another
comment made by Steven Joyce. He said th at Ministers should be able to trust the
advice that they receive from officials. I ab solutely agree with that. But Ministers get
