paid $250,000 a year, and one of the reasons they ge t paid that is to test the veracity of
the advice they get and to ask some difficult questions. When officials give advice that
is inconsistent, as was clearly the case here, it is up to the Ministers to say: “This advice
is not good enough, and I want better.” They did not do that.
They got given advice that said, in the same  report, that the milestones had been met
and that the milestones had not been met. A nd that was signed off by three Ministers. I
can tell you now that if that sort of advice were given to me as a Minister, I would not
sign it off. I would go back to the officials,  and the very first question I would ask them
is: “Well, which is it? Were the milestones met or were they not?”. Apparently, that was
too difficult for Bill English, Hekia Parata , and Craig Foss—three senior Government
Ministers, and not one of them  was able to spot the inconsistency in that report from
their officials. Not one of them turned r ound and said: “I’m not satisfied with this
advice. I want more information.” Not one of  them thought to ask: “Has this actually
been tested? Have we actually got some results to show whether this is going to work or
not?”. Not one of those three Ministers aske d for that advice. Had they done so, we
would not be here having this debate, because it was abundantly clear before Novopay
went live that it was not going to work, and any Minister doing their job properly could
have established that in a very short order of time. They did not do so. They did not live
up to the expectations that the public should, rightly, have of them.
Did they ask whether schools were involved in the development and the design of the
new payroll system? Had they asked that basi c, fundamental questi on, the answer that
would have come back was a resounding no, and all of the alarm bells should have been
ringing at that point. The people who had to use the system, the people who had to make
it work, were not actually involved in the pr oject. Had it been tested? Did they ask that
question? No, they did not.
There are a whole lot of questions left unanswered by this report. The report talks
about the removal of the contingencies, the phased roll-out, and th e old system running
in parallel. It talks about the fact that that was removed. Well, who signed that off? Who
signed off the removal of those contingencie s? If any Minister signed off on the
removal of those contingencies, they  should resign immediately, because the
responsibility is very, very clear. The report is suspiciously silent  on that. There is not
one word on whether the Minister has signed off on the removal of the contingencies,
and why not? If they did, they have to go. It is as simple as that. If they signed off on
the removal of the contingencies, then the Ministers are responsible for the chaos that
followed, and the blame for that rests s quarely on their shoulders and nobody else’s.
They can blame officials, they can blame previous Governments, they can blame the
schools, but the Ministers were the ones who signed o ff on the implementation. The
Ministers are the ones who should accept the responsibility for that.
10648 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
There were known faults—multiple known fa ults—with the system. There was clear
evidence that even if the system was ready, the sector was not ready for the
implementation of it, and yet it was still sign ed off, anyway. The report finds, and I will
quote directly, that “levels of trust between  the Ministry and the sector that were
necessary to ensure the success of the project were not al ways evident.” Well, goodness
me! That is the understatement of the decad e. There is very li ttle trust between the
Ministry of Education and the entire educat ional community. The responsibility for that
rests with Ministers as well, because the Mini stry of Education is ultimately left with
the task of implementing the policy agenda of this Government, and it is the policy
agenda of this Government that has result ed in the massive breakdown in relationships
between the Ministry of Education and just about everybody who has to actually
implement the policies that the Government is trying to ram through. Whether they be
national standards, charter schools, performan ce pay for teachers, and all of those other
things that this Government talks about all of  the time, those things have contributed to
this breakdown in relationship and clearly that has had an impact on this project as well.
So what is the Government going to do next? What happens now? Well, there are
some interesting comments in the report. It talks about removing unnecessary
practices—i.e., banking staffing. Is that not interesting? Basically what it is going to do
is take away the ability of  schools to keep and retain and use any underspend in their
staffing allocations. Basically, this is an other Bill English clawback—ripping more
resources out of schools, ripping more m oney and more staffing away from schools.
This is how it will make up for its failed experiment with bigger class sizes—by
removing banking staffing. What does banking sta ffing do? It allows schools, if they do
not use up all of their staffing within the period  that they have been allocated, to roll it
forward. The Government wants to take th at away, and it wants to use its Novopay
shambles as the excuse for taking away banking staffing. It also talks about reducing the
complexity of collective employment agreements.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ah!

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Ah, now here we go. Performance pay is on the way. It is now
going to reduce the complexity of the collec tive agreements, and we can expect to see
this Government trying to ram through major changes to the way teachers and those
working in schools are paid. This report is  all part of the G overnment’s plan to
change—[Bell rung] Oh, that is the second 2-minute be ll, Mr Assistant Speaker. That is
very good; I am just getting warmed up. The Government is going to use this as an
excuse to ram through changes not just to the payroll system but to the collective
agreements and the very nature of teachers’ employment, and that is so totally wrong.
Ultimately what people wanted from St even Joyce—an apology was good—was for
him to stand up and say that he accepts that the Government made a mistake, the
Government should not have signed off the implementation of Novopay, and, yes, this
National Government accepts responsibil ity. And, no, nobody heard that from Steven
Joyce today, and they have not heard that all the way through this debacle, which has
been now going on since August of last year . It has been going on since August, and
still the Government tiptoes around the edges and tries to shed the blame elsewhere.
Steven Joyce even had the audacity to try to shed the blame on to the previous Labour
Government, yet that was actually one of the few positive findings—that the original
procurement of the payroll system was actually  OK. That was the bit of it that was all
right.
It became a shambles when Hekia Parata and Bill English and Craig Foss got
involved. They were the Ministers who signe d off on the go-live decision. I am looking
forward to Craig Foss’ contribution because  I have seen him taking extensive notes
during this debate. As he is the person responsible for signing it off, I look forward to
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10649
him standing up and apologising to schools, apologising to teachers and to support
staff—because it is not just teachers, it is all the other staff who work in schools who
have been affected by this. In particular, I want Craig Foss to stand up and say that he is
sorry for trying to blame the schools, because when the system first went live, and all of
those problems came up, Craig Foss came to this House and tried to blame the schools.
He needs to stand up now, take a call in this debate, and give them an unqualified,
unreserved apology, because he was totally wrong. The responsibility for this fiasco
rests with him.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. This would be a
comedy of errors if it was not so serious. Th is is not funny, and it is a shame to have
Ministers stand up in this House and, as has been said several times already, pass the
buck. They passed the buck to officials. They passed the buck to the Labour
Government. They passed the bu ck to school staff. I think that was the lowest, lowest
part of this conversation. Part of the probl em has been that this was a money-saving
exercise. We have not seen the end of it yet. I agree with my counterpart Mr Hipkins
that this is the third time or fourth time th at Mr Joyce has menti oned the complexity of
the pay scale structure inside our schools. Ca n I just say that when an IT system is
developed, the machines serve us. The machin es are supposed to serve us. We are not
supposed to change how we do something to make it easier for the machine. When we
move to that part of the world, then I hope I am not in it.
So one of the suggestions at the beginning of  this process was that it was actually the
front-line payroll staff who were too dim to  actually input the data correctly. Not only
was no training offered to payroll staff, not  only did they then halfway through this
process show up to training and have to t each the Talent2 people what they were doing,
but the suggestion was made in this House by an elected Minister  that it was payroll
staff who were the problem. Yet, ultimately,  the reason why a Minister stands and
answers questions as the Mini ster responsible is that th ey are responsible. The buck
stops there. That is why they get paid all those bucks. The buck stops there.
When I first stood for election, one of the things I said in a public meeting was to
elect somebody who reads the stuff. Elect peop le who read the documents that they are
going to make decisions on. Then elect a person who when they do not understand
something that is written in those documents has the courage to ask: “What does that
mean?”. Elect someone who has the courage to say as a Minister: “Explain this to me
again. That doesn’t make sense to me. Bri ng in somebody else who can make this clear
to me.” At the end of the day this is mini sterial responsibility. There are Ministers here
who need to take responsibility. They need  to do that for the New Zealand public, and
they need to do that for the staff who have  been insulted through this process. They
need to do that for the staff who are like th e young first-year teacher down in Tauranga
who lost her flat and had to move back in with her mum and dad because she did not get
paid for the whole first 6 mont hs of this year. Ministers ne ed to take responsibility for
the staff member who has a $17,000 accumulation of overpayments sitting over here
waiting for the debt collector to bang on his door while his wife has not been paid for 3
months. The Ministers need to take responsibility for that st ress. It is very easy to do
that and to say: “It was my call and I was wrong. I was wrong. I apologise. I am sorry.”
We did not hear Mr Joyce say sorry. We  heard Mr Joyce say thank you. He said:
“Thank you for your patience. Thank you for your time. Thank you to all the people
working hard behind the scenes to put the patches on.” But we did not hear him say
sorry. We have not heard an unconditional apology from anybody. I know it is the
hardest word to say, but it actually gets you th e furthest along the tr ack and that is all
the staff want.
10650 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
This Government is exceptionally lucky th at teachers love children and love their
jobs and are committed to their work, because any other industry would have walked
off. Any other industry would have thrown it in and said: “Until you pay us properly,
we’re not going to do this any more.” But these people did not do that. These citizens
stayed in the classroom and all they as k for now is, first, for somebody to take
responsibility and truly say sorry; secondly, that you do not muck around with their
payroll system until you get this one right; and,  thirdly, they want recognition that it is
still broken. The bank staffing, which Mr Hipki ns referred to, is not going to wash out
for another 12 months. When the headlines over this issue have gone, it will be another
12 months before schools may have to e nd up fronting with cash to the ministry,
because of the payroll stuff-up around this, a nd the ministry will have to take it from
their operations grant.
There are several, several th ings wrong with what has gone on, and we know it and
we need to move on and we need to move forward. But there is obviously something
wrong with the relationship between the Mini sters involved here a nd the ministry, and
that is probably more serious. If the minist ry does not feel confident or brave enough to
say to the Minister that “Thi s is wrong and we can’t do this  any more.” and that “Yes,
we’ve spent $10 million, but to spend anot her $23.9 million trying to patch up a system
that is terribly broken would be a mistake.”,  then we have got an issue. The Minister
must allow people to come into his or he r office and give him or her the truth.
Whichever Minister it is must be able to let those officials come in and provide the
truth, even when it is bad news. Then we need to take the steps to make it right for the
mass, for the citizens inside our schools.
There are many recommendations inside th e report and it will take some time to
digest. I hope that most of the recommendations will be listened to, but I would strongly
urge the Minister who now has oversight for this issue to please talk with the sector,
stop fixing it away from them, stop siloing it off, and actually go and see them, and
have them input into the solutions. Do not use it as a doorway to change the pay scales.
Do not use it as a doorway to save more money. Do not use it as a doorway to change
anything else, because you do not have a lot of—I beg your pardon, Mr Deputy
Speaker. The Minister does not have a lot of trust now, and any attempt to change the
structure of pay to hide what are actually fundamental errors w ith a base computer
system will do nothing to restore it. We  have patch upon patch upon patch on this
program. So even when we fix all the backlog problems and we are running at, say, only
about 23 errors per pay period, it is full of pa tches. We are going to have to do this all
again. This is not a clean program. This is not  going to be the end of the issue. We now
have a base program with several errors that  is being patched over the top. It is not the
best practice when it comes to an IT system, and I would suggest that in the next 5 years
we are going to be looking at another one.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I agree with and endorse and join
with Mr Joyce when he apologised, and I apologise to all those who have suffered
through the unfortunate outcomes from the wa y in which Novopay has played out over
recent months—albeit it has got quite a bit better in recent months—and the issues that
have been of major concern over recent months. School sta ff, support staff, boards of
trustees, principals—you name it—have suffere d because of what this report released
today points to.
I will not get political, as one or two members have done, but what I would like to do
is just point out some of the facts in the report and actually let the report speak for itself.
I do acknowledge members around the House not questioning those who produced the
report, and I join them in respect of the professionalism and standing of the people who
were in charge of it. Just a couple of things—for example, on page 79, under the section
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10651
“Leadership—The Secretary for Education”. I will quote the first sentence: “The two
former Secretaries for Education told us that they were clear that final accountability for
the Novopay project lay with them.” That  is quite clear. Ye s, Ministers have
responsibilities; of course they do. But Mini sters—those who have been in a ministerial
role or in a ministerial office—know that Ministers rely on the advice that they get from
officials in response to questions asked, reports required, Cabine t guidelines, etc.
Perhaps, as this report shows, unfortunately, at least in this instance, that has not been
able to be relied upon.
I will just make a quote again. On page 88, which is one of the findings, it quite
simply says in bullet point one: “Ministers were not always well served by the quality of
advice about the project from the Ministry.” And then there are points two, three, and
four, and Mr Joyce read out point four, particularly in relation to the 5 June 2012 report,
which essentially recommended that Minister s sign off on the go-liv e. The assumption,
of course, was that that advice rested on robust governance, intern al audit monitoring,
fairness, robustness, transparency, peer-r eviewed testing and reporting, and quality
control—and no unintended, perhap s, conflicts of interest and not being captured by
processes that, in fact, st arted in 2003, as members do, I think, know. The timeline is
very interesting. About eight or nine Mini sters have been involved in this Novopay
system. So the assumption that advice rests on robust public service ethos is, perhaps, a
fair assumption. Not just in education but across Government, across Cabinet, and
across Governments, the advice of professi onal, well-meaning public servants is relied
upon and used every single day. Unfortunatel y, the report here outlines some instances
where that does not seem to have been the case, and the Acting Secretary for Education,
Mr Peter Hughes, is investigating those matters right now.
I do note that the Acting Secretary has also ju st put out a press release, and I do want
to take a couple of quotes from that. Esse ntially, what it does say is: “The acting
Secretary for Education, Peter Hughes, says  he accepts in full all of the findings and
recommendations of the Minist erial Inquiry that relate to  the Ministry.” Further down,
where he is talking about the system, not just  since go-live but the bits leading up to go-
live and the system as a whole, he goes: “I n the end those efforts fell well short. The
Ministry did not have the capacity—skills, processes and governance—for a project of
this scale and complexity. Th ere was not enough oversight from the leadership.” He
repeats: “Government Minister s were not served well by some of the advice and
reporting they received, and that is unaccepta ble. I have apologised to them.” I accept
that apology, of course, and, as  Mr Joyce and other speakers have noted, the system is
running much better now, perhaps now where it was intended to be—albeit there were
the problems with implementation.
But, sadly, many agencies mentioned in th e report, both Government and outside of
Government, have in various ways and fo rms somehow been captu red by the changes.
The customisation, contracts not being finalised, and schedules customisation have been
captured by that. All that has led up to advice that is not robust, and perhaps
misrepresented advice, being given to Mi nisters, which led to them making the
recommendation to their colleagues to pick up  on the ministry’s a dvice and to go live.
So I repeat, as unfortunate—and I do genera lly apologise for all of those—as the
angst—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Your time has expired.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I was listening from my room
and then I came into the House, and it might  have happened in the minute or so that it
took me to come down, but I think that that member, Craig Foss, did not apologise. He
did not say sorry. He was the Minister in  charge of the project—the Minister
responsible for Novopay—he was the Minister  who did not ask the questions that
10652 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
needed to be asked, and he was the Minister who was not getting the weekly reports that
he should have been getting. He is sitting be hind the Minister of Education, and it is
hard to tell whether she did it deliberately or not, but someone did not do their job.
It is no good whatsoever, as is made clea r to everyone who has studied Westminster
democracy, to say that it is the fault of the officials. You are to blame, Minister. The
Minister is to blame, and, in this case, the two Ministers are the ones—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: And Bill English.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: —and Bill English, but Bill English is to blame for a
lot more than that. Hekia Parata’s job was to make sure that she had systems set up
within her ministry whereby she got at leas t weekly reports on at-risk projects. Did she
do that? No, she did not. That Minister does not even get proper weekly reports on her
area of responsibility. And I sort of wonder why we pay her a quarter of a million
dollars a year, when—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Clothes.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Well, you know, when that is appropriate, it is
appropriate. But in this case we have a Mini ster being paid a quarter of a million dollars
a year, she has the highest-ri sk project going on in edu cation—something that involves
the payment of teachers—and did she ask them a single question before she signed the
paper?

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Yes, many times—many times.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Did she ask—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: “Many times.” She said “Many times.”

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: She said she asked questions many times. Well,
clearly, as is made clear in the report, there were issues at the time she signed off the go.
She signed off the go, not the officials. She signed—and she is nodding; she agrees that
it is her responsibility. Well, have we heard an apology from her for being an
inadequate Minister who does not know how to ask a questio n? What is the point of
having officials and blaming th em? You might as well abolish the ministry if she is
going to be run by officials—although that, I understand, is the approach that she
prefers to take. Hard work and Hekia Parata do not go in the same sentence.
That Minister Craig Foss used to have pot ential. Craig Foss at one stage was seen in
the same class as John Key. He was brought into the party by Brash, Boag, and that
team, apparently for the difference that he  was going to make. What a disappointment
he has been—what a disappoi ntment he has been. One would have thought that
someone with some business experience would not just sign the paper that was put in
front of him. Frankly, under Helen Clark, both those Minist ers would have been gone.
Both those Ministers would have had the sa ck. They would have been out of Cabinet
because they just did not do their jobs.
Nothing can be worse for people—maybe those people over there do not understand
it. People who are lords and ladies and ri ch former business people do not care about
income and wages, but most New Zealande rs do. Most New Zealanders care about
getting their pay, and not only the teacher s but the support staff in schools. The
members opposite might think that  payroll is not that import ant because it is not that
important to them and it is not that important to their funders and to their mates. This is
a classic case of those members getting too cl ose to the people who have things and not
understanding people who do not. If those me mbers did understand how important pay
was, how important salary was, how important wages were to ordinary New Zealanders,
they would have made sure that they read the papers that were put in front of them, that
they took the warnings, that they asked th e questions, and that they did their jobs
properly. But instead we have over there two very guilty Ministers—Ministers who do
not do their work. I do not know whether it is ignorance or laziness. I really do not
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10653
know whether Hekia Parata is as silly as she pretends to be, or whether Craig Foss is as
lazy as he pretends to be. It does not really matter whether it is laziness—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! Your time has concluded.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: Pay period 5 has just fi nished, and in that pay
period 88,524 people were paid a total of $173.55 million. The PricewaterhouseCoopers
report shows that complaints and notifications were recei ved regarding 0.39 percent of
staff across the country. Twenty-nine staff were notified as not paid, 115 were overpaid,
and 199 underpaid. Affected staff were from 234 schools, or 9.5 percent of schools in
the payroll system. This is obviously unaccepta ble. This is totally unacceptable, and the
Report of the Ministerial Inquiry into the Novopay Project makes sobering reading. The
inquiry was undertaken by the former Chief Executive of the Department of the Prime
Minister and Cabinet, Sir Ma arten Wevers, and chairman of Deloitte, Murray Jack.
Their 113-page report contai ns 15 significant recommendati ons and was presented to
the Government just last Friday. The ministerial inquiry team has produced a
comprehensive report outlining the history of , and issues within, the school payroll
system, and it concludes that there were ma ny factors over many year s that contributed
to the problems with Novopay.
I understand that Peter Hughes, the Acting Secretary for Education, has written today
to all school princi pals and board chai rs to personally apologis e to them. He has also
written an open letter of apology to all staff in schools. I personally, as a foot soldier in
the National Government, someone passionate  about education, and chairman of the
Education and Science Committee, express my sincere regret to all staff members, who
do an outstanding job throughout the country. Of course, these problems have made
their task a lot, lot more difficult. We acknowledge that, and th e Government will be
acting upon these findings.
What were some of the key findings? Some of the key findings were to do with the
project life cycle: “The school s payroll environment is overly complex as a result of an
accumulation of historical changes. There was no serious attempt to simplify collective
agreements or Ministry or school business  processes before embarking on the Novopay
project.”—the retrospectoscope is a hugely useful instrument in medicine, and so it is in
this instance—“This was an underlying cause of  later problems. The strategic decision
to change from purchasing software to an outsourced service was valid, but the rationale
was simplistic. Customers’ perspectives, part icularly those of the boards of trustees”—
and I acknowledge Tracey Martin, who ha s spoken earlier—“were insufficiently
considered in the business case. The Ministry’s requirements for the outsourced service,
as outlined in the Request for Proposal, were too high leve l to convey the full
complexity of the required solution.” So, as I say, it is easy to be wise after the event,
but these are the results of this very in-dep th and comprehensive re port that we have
received from two very able investigators.  The report continues: “The process of
gathering user requirements was poorly ma naged and took too long. The failure to
involve users appropriately was a key w eakness. The Ministry was negotiating on
behalf of the users in the schools sector without an appreciation of all of their
requirements.”
One of the points that did come out was that the papers presented on 5 June 2012 to
the Ministers, following the so-called “Conf idence Point Two”, actually misrepresented
the state of the project. It was found that “Min isters were not always well served by the
quality of advice about the project from the Ministry. Reporting to Ministers was
inconsistent and at times unduly optimistic, and sometimes misrepresented the situation.
In oral briefings to Ministers, official s often expressed conf idence and reassured
Ministers”—who were asking the questions—“that  risks were in hand … We were
particularly concerned about the 5 June 2012 document, which invited Ministers to
10654 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
approve the Ministry’s Go Live decision. This report misrepresented the situation in two
significant ways. It suggested that the Go  Live decision was supported by three
members of the ICT Council, which was not the case; and it stated  that Confidence
Point Two criteria had been met, when in fact a number either had not been met or were
‘deemed’ to have been met (a lower criterion).”

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: I think that to start off with it will be worth
making a statement—a very common and well-used statement—and that is: something
that has been made crooked is hard to make  straight. When we stop and think about
those original decisions, it is easy to be wi se afterwards, as has been communicated in
this debate. The Report of the Ministerial Inquiry into the Novopay Project  certainly
does leave us with some very strong messages. As the member for the Kaik ōura
electorate, I want to say a special thankyou to the teacher s, the principals, and the
boards of trustees of the 36 schools that have  had to endure this whole process, which,
once it started rolling out, has been an incredibly bumpy ride, to say the least.
The ministerial inquiry has certainly taken its toll, when you stop to think that we no
longer have either of the two Secretaries fo r Education with the Ministry of Education.
The problem with Novopay has also affected  the public trust and confidence in the
Ministry of Education, and no doubt concerns us  all, as it does us on this side of the
House. Given the weakness of the project gove rnance and of the project leader, it is
clearly evident that the governance and leadership were not adequate, and that a number
of significant risks with the Ministry of Education and its vendor s, including Talent2,
showed and displayed an overconfidence in approaching this situation.
I would have to say that the complexity of anything like Novopay is well beyond the
member for Kaik ōura. However, there are people w ho practise these fine arts, and
everybody who goes to work in New Zealand expects that on a given day—a
predetermined day—they will be paid. For that not to happen is a disappointment and an
utter failure on the part of any employer. Whatever came at the ministry and Talent2,
they were totally unprepared for it. One’s thoughts do go out to those Ministers who had
oversight, in the way that information was relayed back to them. How do you cut
through and ask those searching questions and get into areas that are dark and dingy and
that people are espousing as being ready to go?
When you talk about the school payroll, it is complex, but that is not an excuse. In
the very essence of a systems analysis, complexity should have been a fundamental part
of the life cycle of the deve lopment of the Novopay system . The fact that it is now
extensively customised is a concern. It need s to be very quickly stabilised. It is
heartening, though, to see that 0.5 percent or le ss of mistakes have been recorded over
the last quarter or two. Howeve r, there is a long way to go to get out of the woods. We
have just got to be very, ve ry aware of the lessons that we have learnt during this
miserable process. There was no overall accountability for independent quality
assurance—some very fundamental failure s there. The project has cost $23.9 million
more than was estimated, and has a total cost to date of $56.8 million.
So what have we learnt? Well, we have le arnt that implementing a system with the
complexity of Novopay—of a payroll system  involved with the education system—is
incredibly difficult and high risk. We on this side of the House certainly welcome this
report. We offer our sincere apologies for an y difficulty, frustration, and hardship that
have come upon the fraternity of teachers, boa rds of trustees, and schools as a whole. In
conclusion, I would like to make the commen t, as quoted by the Minister responsible
for Novopay: “There are substantial lessons to  be learned by the Ministry of Education
in a number of areas which the Acting Secr etary of Education is taking steps to
address.” Thank you.
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10655

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I think it is very important at
the outset to say that this report on the Novopay system does scatter around the blame
for what happened. We have had Ministers on th eir feet, and they have talked about the
problems with the Ministry of Education, the problems with the State Services
Commission, the problems with Pricewat erhouseCoopers, and the problems—goodness
only knows—probably inside the schools. And we have got a whole lot of blame in here
about how complex it is to pay people who do not all work a 40-hour week in one place,
and how terribly, terribly difficult all of that is. But there is something missing from this
report, and what is missing from this repo rt is the acceptance of blame from the
Ministers who got the 5 June report in 2012 and said “Go live”. That is what is missing
from this report, and that is fundamentally flawed.
This report ought to share the blame across not only those officials who were
working on this issue but also  those Ministers who finally  took the deci sion to go live
on 5 June 2012. Those Ministers are Hekia Para ta, Craig Foss, and Bill English. It is a
fundamental principle of our Westminster syst em that Ministers will  take responsibility
for the actions of their agencies. It is unaccep table to have Ministers come down to this
House and tell us that they are not going to take that responsibility. The speech that
Craig Foss delivered in this  House was disgraceful. He we nt out of his way to find
quotes in the report that would mean that he did not have  to take responsibility. He took
a press release from Peter H ughes, who says that, yes, th e Ministry of Education is
going to take its share of the responsibility, a nd he used that so that  he did not have to
take responsibility. That is wrong. It is wrong for Ministers to stand up in this House
and not take their share of the blame. We on th is side of the House are not saying that it
is just the Ministers. Of cour se it is not just the Ministers. But, as Trevor Mallard
pointed out, what is the point of having a Mi nister, or Ministers, paid a quarter of a
million dollars if they are not prepared to stand up in this House and say that they got
this fundamentally wrong on 5 June 2012?
It is important to look at the report. Mr Foss alerted us to page 88 of the report. It is
actually important to look at the report and see that Ministers were briefed in May 2012
about what was happening. And in that pape r that they were briefed on they were
invited to consider arrange ments for rapid decision-making if it became necessary to
terminate Novopay. So Ministers were being told in May that  things had got to such a
point that it was possibly necessary to terminate the contract with Novopay. A matter of
mere weeks later they received a briefing th at gave contradictory advice about whether
or not all the milestones for the project had been met—only weeks after being told that
they might have to terminate the contract—a nd the Ministers said that it was all fine.
They said that that was all fine and that they were going to sign it off. That is not
adequate oversight by Ministers.
Ministers are paid the big bucks to ask th e hard questions. They are meant to ask
those questions, and they completely failed to do so in this case. They got a report in
June that said that there were 150 soft ware defects and 5,913 payslip errors in the
testing. That is just the testing—nearly 6,000 errors in the testing and 150 software
defects, and that was just weeks after be ing given advice that they may need to
terminate the contract. Yet all three Ministers—Hekia Parata, Craig Foss, and Bill
English—signed it off. That is not the kind of ministerial oversight that New Zealanders
would rightly expect.
This was a complex process; there is no doubt about that. That should be all the
more reason for Ministers to give it an ev en more thorough oversight than they might
have, but knowing these risks existed, the Mi nisters signed it off. That is bad enough,
but what makes it so much worse is that the Ministers have failed to take responsibility
today. We have had all kinds of faux apologi es over the last few months. We have had
10656 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
people apologising for the difficulties that have been caused and apologising for the
extra work that has been put on staff. Th ey are not real apologies. They are not
apologies that say: “I am the Minister, a nd I stuffed up. I made the wrong decision. I
didn’t ask the right questions.” There has b een no sign of that ki nd of apology up to
today, and no sign from Minist ers who have spoken in the House today. They would
much rather get the officials and throw th em under the bus than actually admit their
role. That is, as I said, a fundamental br eakdown in what we call the Westminster
system of Government.
There is a chapter in this report called “Lead ership”, and it starts off by talking about
the Secretary for Education. That is a flaw in this report, because if we are talking about
leadership, then leadership comes from the Minister of Education. The Minister should
be the person at the top of th at section, and instead what we see immediately is the term
“The Secretary for Education”. There have been faults by officials in this process—
quite clearly. Where is the acknowledgment of  fault from the Ministers who said “Go
live” in June 2012 when they were presented with contradictory evidence?
I also want to pay tribute today to the sc hool staff who have dealt with the problems
that have come up from this. As most MPs in  this House will have done, I have been in
schools in my electorate as th ey have tried to grapple w ith Novopay problems. I have
seen school administrators with decades of  experience reduced to tears because they
could not make this system work, and, in the early days particularly, they got the
reaction from Government that it was basically  their fault. That was the message. Craig
Foss, when he was the Associate Minister of Education, was sending out the message
that it was the fault of the school administ rators. They deserve a proper and thorough
apology from Craig Foss and the Ministers on the other side of the House because of the
stress that they went through. School admini strators have had to give up their jobs
because of the stress—that is what has happened across New Zealand—and those staff
deserve better.
I also think that the teachers and the othe r school staff who have been affected by
this deserve a tribute, because they have show n up to work day in, day out. It is not just
the teachers; it is the support staff. It is the teacher aides, who are often paid just above
minimum wage, who need that pay. They re ly on that pay. They live week to week.
They need the money. Minister s over there may not understand  that, but that is what
was at stake here: people who need the money.
When New Zealanders go to work they deserve to expect to be paid. When people go
to work in New Zealand they should know two things: that they  are going to come
home safely after a day’s work, and that they  will actually get paid for their jobs. That
did not happen here, and that did not happe n for far too long before this Government
actually got up and said it was going to try to  do something about it. That was the fault
in leadership that should have been found in this report.
It is not only in respect of 5 June that we need to look at this. I am interested by a
line in the report that talks about the cont ext in which this happened. I will quote from
page 83 of the report: “The Ministry’s relati onship with the schools sector has in recent
times been uneasy, and sometimes highly politicis ed.” That is what it says in the report.
Where do the politics come from? The politic s come from the National Government. It
is the policies of the National Government th at have been imposed on the sector, which
the sector knows are wrong and will damage  educational outcomes. It is that
environment of politics, which has come from the Minister and this National
Government, that is mentioned in this repor t as the context in which the ministry was
managing Novopay. I think that is a very interest ing line, and what that speaks to is that
this Government should be shouldering its shar e of the blame for this debacle. It has
failed to do that in the past, and it has failed to do that today.
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10657
I just want to finish—very briefly—on the point that Chris Hipkins raised about two
of the recommendations. One of those is ar ound the recommendation to modernise the
collective agreements in this sector. We will be watching that like hawks, because that
sounds to me like more from this Governme nt to undermine collective agreements. We
will not accept this debacle being used as an excuse by this Government to undermine
collective bargaining rights. There is also  the idea of cha nging banking staffing
arrangements, which allows schools to accumulate hours.
This Government has made a mess of this  payroll system, and this Government
should apologise for what it has done, but what it must not do is put pressure back on to
schools. They have had enough from this G overnment, they deserve better, and they
deserve a proper apology and some responsibil ity being taken for this debacle by these
Ministers.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak in this  snap debate on Novopay. I think it might
be helpful if we just review what was in tended by the introduction of Novopay. First of
all, it was intended that we have an up-to-date payroll system that would manage the
complexities of over 100,000 pay instructions every fortnight to a diverse workforce,
with different arrangements, across the c ountry. Everyone who ha s been involved with
Novopay set about it with the best inten tions. There was no one person who decided
that they should get involved in this and work it so that it would be difficult; it would be
a problem; it would underpay, overpay, or not pay teachers, support staff, and
principals; or it would create headaches for every school administrator. That was never
the intention. The intention was to have a much better payroll syst em, driven by a very
clear understanding some years ago that the pa yroll system that was then in place was
no longer going to be capable of meeting those needs.
Members in the Opposition—Labour and the Greens—seem to be under the
misapprehension that, somehow or another, there was an intention that this would all go
wrong. Nobody wanted that; nobody wants that now. There also  seem to have been a
number of allegations that Mi nisters on this side of the House have been completely
culpable and unwilling to take responsibility. Again, that is not true. What is clear from
this very comprehensive and very thorough report that has been written by the well-
respected, senior, experienced former public  servant Sir Maarten Wevers and another
very experienced businessman and adviser Mr  Murray Jack is that there have been a
range of people involved over the many years of this particular project. In fact, if one
looks at the report there are three pages about ministerial responsibilities, and there are a
number of Ministers who have held those responsibilities over the years, beginning with
the decision in 2003 and 2005 that the system  needed to be replaced, progressing
through the signing of a contract, which wa s done under Minister Mallard, then under
Minister Maharey, and then  Minister Carter, who in fact signed off the Novopay
contract with many of the schedules attached to it not yet filled out. Nevertheless, again,
it was with the intention that a better, fit for purpose payroll system would be devised
and implemented that would se e all of the complexities, wh ich have been much talked
about, dealt with and teachers, principals, and support staff paid.
Of course, our Government came in and inheri ted it, and we have also been part of
the process of design, development, and im plementation. This re port—a very thorough
and comprehensive report, as I said, prepar ed by Sir Maarten Wevers and Mr Murray
Jack—canvassed that very extensive history over all of that time,  from 10 December
1999 to the present date, and, as  the Minister responsible for Novopay made clear when
he first took over this responsibility, there is absolutely enough blame to go around. It is
not something that any of us celebrate on th is side of the House, nor should it be the
case on that side of the House. What was intended was that a fit for purpose, 21 st
10658 Urgent Debates 4 Jun 2013
century payroll system would be designed and delivered. Did that happen? No. We
know that now, we knew that comprehensivel y from when the system went live in
August last year, and we have seen a momentum  of errors that have  beset that system.
We know that many people were underpaid,  overpaid, or not paid, and we have
apologised to them and continue to apologise to them because that was never the
intention. We want people paid on time and pa id what they are owed in their banks, as
intended, and we want to see that occur.
Where are we now? Well, significant prog ress has been made. We have already
heard from previous speakers, including the Minister responsible for Novopay, that five
out of the last six pay rounds have been ve ry successful in terms of error rates. We
know that we have invested more money to  fix the problems and to recognise the
significant contribution that has been made by school administrators , in particular. We
acknowledge how hard it has been for them and the call on their time, and how difficult
it has been for everyone embroiled in this pr ocess. We are worki ng to get everything
fixed and we are making progress. Talk a bout taking responsibility: we instituted a
technical review, and the recommendations of that are being followed through. We
instituted a ministerial review , and today’s debate is driven  by the fact that we have a
113-page report that sets out in thorough, comp rehensive, and transp arent detail all of
the issues relating to the Novopay situati on. Where to from here? Well, a number of
findings have also been made in this repor t that we will be following up on because we
want to get this right—we want to get this right.
There have been suggestions from the Oppos ition that this has been an exercise in
shifting blame—not at all. This report is ve ry clear about where responsibilities have
lain at different points in the process. I want to make it clea r that not once—not once—
in the time that I have been Minister of E ducation, and that is almost 18 months to the
day, have I bagged the Ministry of Education, and I do not intend to start now. Novopay
has contributed significant difficulties and challenges, and they are being tackled. The
Acting Secretary of Education, in the 4 months that he ha s been in place—and I would
like to acknowledge and thank him for the work that he has done—has instituted a
number of immediate changes, seeking to ensu re that the systems and processes within
the Ministry of Education ar e robust. For instance, he ha s put in place new governance
arrangements across the ministry. He ha s implemented new project management
arrangements and accountabilities to deliver on the Better Public Services targets and
other ministerial priorities. He has put in place a new risk management approach for the
ministry. He has started an end-to-end revi ew on how we manage private and sensitive
information. He has talked to  a range of agencies, groups, and members of the sector
across the sector, and he has started a process of culture change in the ministry with a
focus on teamwork, service, and flexibility.
But there are also a whole lot of other things  that the Ministry of Education has been
doing, and is doing, successfully. It has focused significantly on our Better Public
Services target. We have a Better Public Servic es target that recognises that we need to
have more young learners involved in quality ea rly learning, and that we need to have
more young people at and above the national standards, and more young people—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Just say sorry.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: —passing National Certificate of Educational Achievement
level 2. If the member had been here in the House for the bulk of my remarks, the
member would know that I have canvassed  all of these issues, including the
responsibilities that relate to all Minister s since 1999 and the decisions that have been
made at different points.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Did she say sorry?
4 Jun 2013 Urgent Debates 10659

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Indeed, I have, and I am no w talking about the significant
contribution that the Ministry of Edu cation has been making, is making, and will
continue to make across a raft  of issues, including how we a ttend to and a ddress all of
those arising out of Novopay; the challenges to the repair of relationships that must
occur within and between the sector and us ; and how we ensure that the sector has
confidence that the system is meeting its ne eds. We know that that is increasingly
occurring.
We are focusing on fixing this because we want teachers, support staff, and
principals paid on time. We want boards of trustees and school administrators to have
all of this pressure alleviated. We want a system that works, which, indeed, was the
intention of the previous Gove rnment when it first signed of f this system. All of us, I
believe, have had the best intentions of ensuring a 21 st century, fit for purpose payroll
system. That is what the sector deserves and that is what we are bent on providing. That
is why we have this report today, setting out for us not just the technical detail, which
we have canvassed, but all of this detail he re. We have lessons to learn and we are
moving on with those. Thank you.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
Debate resumed from 30 May on the Appropriation (2013/14 Estimates) Bill.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: It is a great opportunity for me to talk
about the great way that the health budget th is year is dealing with the changing needs
of our population, thanks to  the stronger financial mana gement that the National
Government has brought to th e public health service. Health is, again, the biggest
recipient of increased funding in the Budget. The total health budget this next year will
be $14.65 billion, including capita l. When you contrast that with only 5 years ago, it
was $11.8 billion. So this Government has continued to invest in protecting and
growing the public health service in the last 5 years. In tight world financial times, when
so many countries are reducing their public  health spending or freezing it, we are
continuing to protect and grow our public he alth budget. In fact, the OECD found that
New Zealand had the third-biggest increase in public health invest ment of any country
in the OECD in the latest available figures  that it has produced. Vote Health in this
Budget gets an average of around $400 million available for each year over the next 4
years to meet pressures and initiatives. That includes $350 million in new money and
around $50 million in savings. It gets a lot better, because we are able to use that money
to invest in the changing needs of our population.
Let us just have a look at some of those ch anging needs. We have  been able to take
money that we had set aside fo r district health board defic its and risks, and, because of
our strong financial management, we have been able to take that money—about $35
million—and put it into a heart disease and diab etes initiative. This heart disease and
diabetes initiative is a very, very significant boost in funding that we have announced in
this year’s Budget. Why is it important? It is important because heart disease remains a
leading killer of New Zealanders, and, similarl y, so many of the risk factors associated
with heart disease are also a ssociated with diabetes. We know that diabetes is a major
challenge for New Zealand, but what is an  even more important challenge is the
prevalence of pre-diabetes and what we can do  as a country to deal with pre-diabetes.
So in our $35.5 million funding boost for diabetes  and heart disease in this Budget, we
are including $16 million to further increas e the number of New Zealanders getting
heart and diabetes checks. These heart and diabetes checks are an important preventive
health target. They are importa nt because they tell people of  an age that they have got
10660 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013
risk factors that may lead to them having heart disease or a heart attack, or maybe
having diabetes or being pre- diabetes. Once people know that they have got these risk
factors, once they know that they may be pr e-diabetes, they can th en make the lifestyle
changes that they need to make in order to better control their disease risk factors. So
we are doing that.
Secondly, we are going to double the number of Green Prescriptions that doctors and
nurses can give their patients. Green Prescriptions are a reference for a patient to go to a
provider who can help them with more phys ical exercise or be tter nutrition. We know
there are very, very sign ificant health benefits if people are more act ive, so that is why
we are going to double the number of Green Pres criptions over the next 4 years. It is a
really significant investment of over $7 million. For those who have got diabetes—
remember, this is very much about preven ting people getting diabet es; a very strong
focus on pre-diabetes and prevention—we ha ve got a number of local diabetes care
improvement programmes. We are going to si gnificantly increase that funding by about
a third over the next few years in order to expand those local diabetes care programmes
to provide more diabetes nursing and more podi atry services. That is dealing with heart
disease and diabetes, but so many of thes e people who have got  heart disease and
diabetes also have other diseases—they call th em co-morbidities in health. We want to
support those people to get better care from their general practitioners, so we are putting
$13 million into expanding the Care Plus pr ogramme, which is a general practice -
based programme that provides additional support to patients with long-term conditions.
So you can see, this is a Budget about the changing needs of our population.
Similarly, with aged care, we know that we are ageing, and we know that our country
is getting a greater prevalence of dementia. The prevalence of dementia is growing at 4
to 5 percent a year. It is going to be a very, very major challenge for New Zealand, so in
this year’s Budget we have got a very, very significant investment of $70 million extra
over 4 years for aged care and diabetes  and a $20 million boost for home support
because we think we should be supporting our older folks to stay longer in their homes,
if they want to, and that is a $20 million boo st to help those peopl e do that. Similarly,
there is going to be a $12 million boost to dementia bed subsidies. What we know is
that we are going to need a lot more reside ntial facilities for people who are demented.
As I said, it is growing at a ra te of 4 to 5 percent a year, so  what this will do is say to
rest home providers: “We need more dementia  beds. Switch on the investment signal.”
This is the third year we have had a pr etty significant increase in dementia bed
subsidies, and we are getting more of those beds.
We are also going to put $2 million into dementia awareness, because over the next
10 years dementia is going to affect everybod y in terms of their friends, families, or
someone whom they know who will be suffering from dementia. It is not a disease that
people should be frightened of. They should be  aware of the supports that are out there,
so we are investing $2 million to provide more dementia awareness programmes and to
assist our general practitioners and our ge neral practice teams with how they can
identify dementia, particularly with early detection, because that can better help manage
those people’s positions. Over $1 billion extra is going into training for our health care
workers, and there is also a $33 million incr ease for rest home bed subsidies across the
board. We increase those subsidies every year, a nd this is a very significant increase of
$33.2 million. So that is focused on our ag eing population but also on this increasing
prevalence of dementia—150,000 New Zealanders are projected to have dementia by
2045-50. So that is a very, very, very significant investment there.
At the same time this Government continues to invest very strongly in preventive
health, and we are almost doubling our rheumatic fever programme. Members will
recall that rheumatic fever became a national priority in 2001, and then that Government
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10661
did nothing. It made it a prio rity, and then it did nothing, other than more people got
rheumatic fever. So our Government came into power, and we have invested in two
Budgets in a rheumatic fever programme aimed at reducing rheumatic fever in our most
at-risk communities. What we know is—and even the Green Party, which did not really
want to admit this, but in its leader’s speech on Sunday it actually talked about the
fact—that where we have run this throat-s wabbing in parts of the Hutt Valley, we have
not had one case of rheumatic fever while we have been running that programme. So we
are running this programme right across the high-prevalence areas—Porirua, the Bay of
Plenty, Rotorua, the East Coast, South Auckland, west Auckland—and it is making a
very, very big difference.
But, of course, what happens when school is  not in? That is why we are investing in
this Budget $11.25 million in developing sore throat drop-in clinics. One of the key
messages is that one of the reasons why mums do not take their kids with a sore throat
to some doctors is the time they have got to  wait to be seen, because mums are leading
busy lives. So what we are going to fund ar e these sore throat drop-in clinics,
particularly in Porirua, South Auckland, a nd parts of west and central Auckland, where
parents will know that if their kid has got a so re throat and they need to be seen, they
can turn up at these drop-in clinics. There is  no charge, they can be seen straight away,
and they can have the throat swab taken and know whether their kid needs to get some
antibiotics to deal with streptococcus A. It is a really sensible initiative. It is backed up
by the $100 million investment on expanding th e home insulation programme. This is a
Government that acts across the life course and puts a huge investment into prevention.
You know, almost a quarter of a million homes were insulated under the first 4 years of
our insulation programme. Another $100 million is  going in, particularly targeted at
those high-risk homes.
So this is another B udget of another year of  record investment in  health, targeted at
the areas that matter most to patients: making sure we have got a strong investment in
prevention, making sure that we are dealing with the changing needs of our population,
and making sure that our hospitals continue to provide the quality services that New
Zealanders want. That is backed up by our 2,000 extra nurses and our 1,000 extra
doctors working on the front line of New Zeal and’s health services . This Government
came to power with the challe nge of repairing the damage of a decade of neglect,
wasteful spending, and clinical disengageme nt. In the last 4½ years this John Key
Government has delivered more operations faster, more preventive care across the
whole range of services, and a health system that New Zealanders can be proud of.
