items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: I am pleased to take the opportunity to speak in this
debate on the Appropriation (2013/14 Estimates) Bill, and particularly to talk about
Vote Corrections—the money we are committi ng to spend on our prisons over the next
12 months. It is interesting to note that the amount assigned th is year is in the order of
$1.2 billion or $1.3 billion, which is in line with what we saw last year, but it is
worthwhile going back 10 or 11 years, when the budget for the Department of
Corrections was to the tune of perhaps $460 million.
Vote Corrections has increased by some 250 percent over 10 or 11 years—two and a
half times more money is being spent this y ear than we spent a l ittle over a decade ago.
Increases of that order are not only unsusta inable, they are unacceptable given that one
would think that the expenditure of all that  extra money would be leading to better
outcomes from our prison system, but, sadly,  that is not the case. We are seeing
outcomes that are no better, and, indeed, in many situations are actually worse than they
10662 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013
were 10 or 12 years ago. We need to ask some serious questions about why this
considerable expenditure of public money is not producing better results.
We saw a very graphic example this weeke nd just past of a corrections system in
turmoil. We saw a major prison, one of our  newer prisons, with serious fires burning
and with 30-odd prisoners running amok. We saw a number of guards injured and a
number of inmates injured. We saw lives put at risk—and I must take this moment to
acknowledge the work of the corrections staff,  the firefighters, the police, and others
who were obliged to go into harm’s way to try to settle that very unfortunate situation.
You might dismiss this event as a one-off event, but the outbrea k of violence at
Spring Hill Corrections Facility was actually one in a series of events, and these events,
these violent outbursts, are becoming much mo re frequent in our prison system. Going
back to the middle of last year, we saw two major incide nts at Hawke’s Bay Regional
Prison of prisoners protesting, breaking out, and setting fires. At Pāremoremo, similarly,
about a year ago, prisoners were barricading themselves in a tower, trying to draw
attention to the absence of response to  their legitimate complaints. At Ng āwhā prison
last year we saw several rubbish fi res and damage to cells. At Rangip ō prison a few
months ago, in March this year, prisoners  were protesting about  poor conditions. In

items.speaker: April this year we saw two incidents
items.text: one  was when prisoners were fighting amongst
themselves, and then there was an assault on guards a few days later. Two weeks ago
there was a serious stabbing at P āremoremo, and now we have had a major riot at
Spring Hill.
These are not isolated incidents; these are indicative of a system in turmoil. We are
spending a great deal of money but we ar e not getting good outcomes. A lot of the
reason for that can be sheeted home to th e general culture, the attitude, over the
previous two decades. There is more and more of a punitive culture in our prisons.
There is much more of this nonsensical polit ical contest to be seen as being tough on
crime, which actually means being tough on  our communities be cause, ultimately,
inmates in our prisons, with very few exceptio ns, are returned to the wider society. To
the extent that we treat inmates poorly, do  not respect their human rights, and do not
provide humane conditions in our prisons, inev itably we will see th e knock-on effect of
that when these people come back into our communities brutalised, dehumanised,
paranoid, and wanting to strike back at the system that has struck them.
We need to do a great deal better. The m oney assigned in this Budget is sufficient to
do better. We do not need to spend more money; we need to spend it differently.
There is one obvious place to spend that—there  is one safety valve in our prisons,
one opportunity for prisoners to attempt to have their rights and their conditions
respected, and that is the complaints process. We know the complaints procedure, which
is an internal process managed within the corrections department, is failing badly. We
are seeing too many complain ts going directly to the Ombudsman. The Office of the
Ombudsmen is being overwhelmed with quite  low level prisoner complaints because
there is no confidence within the prisons and within the families. Those who know what
is happening in our prisons know that the internal complaints system is failing. The
Ombudsman is being over burdened. That would be one very good place to start making
a difference, to get a system that works.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I would like to focus my a ttention in this short call in
the Budget debate on the issue of housing, which is indeed an issue that has dominated
much of the coverage and deba te of this year’s Budget. I guess, to start on a positive
note, the Government does deserve to be c ongratulated—in the sense that it has finally
cottoned on to the fact that we do have an affordable housing crisis in New Zealand. I
must say it took it long enough. As we know, this affordable housing crisis is absolutely
the worst in Auckland, where the average hou se price last year  was $735,000. That is
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10663
the average price to buy a new home in Auck land and that increase d 12 percent in the
last calendar year alone. So any time you hear the Minist er of Housing crowing about
low interest rates and how affordable housing is I would just remind you of that figure.
Not only that, but in Auckland it takes a staggering 71 percent of the average take-home
pay to service the mortga ge on a house that is priced in the first qua rtile. That is, this
house is one of the cheapest quarter of houses in Auckland and it takes 71 percent of the
average income to service the mortgage on that house. When we talk about housing
affordability, anything over 30 percent of your income spent on housing is considered to
put you in housing stress, and for that house to be severely unaffordable. We have a
situation in Auckland where it takes 71 percen t of the average take-home pay to service
the mortgage on one of the cheapest houses in th e market. So that is your crisis for you,
and it is a pretty severe one.
Well, the problem is supply and demand, ri ght? We know that in Auckland we need
about 13,000 new dwellings to be consented each year. We have been averaging only
about 3,000 so it is no surpri se that we have a severe hous ing crisis in Auckland. It is
worst in Auckland but it is actually bad ev erywhere. That equivalent figure for the
national average in New Zealand is that it  takes 49 percent of the average take-home
income to service a mortgage on a lower-qua rtile house. So, again, remembering that
anything over 30 percent is  severely unaffordable and puts a household in housing
stress, we have got a problem across the whol e of the country. In places like the Central
Otago lakes, Nelson and Marlborough, We llington, and Waikato that problem is
elevated above the national average, so we have a major problem.
What we have seen from the Government in terms of solutions is the Housing
Accords and Special Housing Areas Bill, whic h I look forward to beginning to hear the
submissions on in the Social Services Committee tomorrow. In recognition of the fact
that the housing crisis is wors t in Auckland, this bill is eff ectively giving effect to the
Auckland Housing Accord that the Governme nt reached with Auckland Council earlier
this year. That might be all right if that was all that it did. Clearly it has spoken with the
council in Auckland, it has identified the pr oblem there, it believes it has identified a
solution to it, and it has brought some legi slation to the House to deal with it.
Unfortunately, the legislation does not deal wi th the issue just in Auckland, it actually
applies to the whole country. Not only that  but Auckland Council itself, because it was
not consulted on the drafting of  the legislation, once it sa w it actually f ound that there
were inconsistencies between the legislation and the accord that it thought it had signed
up to with the Government.
But there are serious problems with the m odels that are proposed in the Housing
Accords and Special Housing Areas Bill. First of all, it is based on the idea that the
development at Hobsonville Point is the answer to affordable housing in Auckland.
Given that the so-called affordable houses at  Hobsonville Point cost  either just over
$400,000 or $485,000, which is not affordable for most people, that is not a great model
to base it on. There is also  no guaranteed percentage of affordable homes in the new
special housing areas that are going to be created, and they  override local democracy.
Those other regions that I mentioned, where housing affordability is also a problem, had
better watch out because the Government is coming to create special housing areas in
their region whether they like it  or not. All the power is with  the Minister, and, if they
cannot negotiate an accord with the Minister, he can just put a special housing area in
place, regardless of whether the local c ouncil actually agrees , overriding both the
Resource Management Act and the local democracy for that area. And remember, at the
end of all of that, there is absolutely no guarantee in that special housing area that a
percentage of those houses that will be provi ded will actually be affordable for the New
Zealanders who are in severe  housing stress at the moment. So congratulations to the
10664 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013
Government on identifying a problem—it is a shame that none of the measures do
anything at all to address it.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am very pleased to stand and
speak on this debate on Budget 2013, a Budget th at keeps us on course in a consistent
and a steady way. I recall the comments of the chief executive of the T ātua dairy
company, who said that consistent is good, pred ictability is even better. I think that we
have produced a Budget that certainly th e business community, and consequently, I
think, families and industry around this country can rely on. I think that has been par for
the course under Bill English, our finance Minister, who over this last number of years
has enabled this country to be seen as  a standout country amongst many economies
around the world because of our solid track record and where we are going with this
economy. We are right on track. We are delivering what we said we would.
I think that today is a very hard day for the Opposition, which is having to throw up
all sorts of objections and criticisms when we know that so many things are going right.
It is to do with the leadership, the vision, the stability, and the safe pair of hands that we
have in our Minister of Finance, as well as our Cabinet colleagues.
We have the lowest mortgage rates sin ce 1965, after-tax wages have increased 22
percent since September 2008, and we know the co st of living increases have been their
lowest since 1999. This is good news for New Zealanders. It is not just statistics and
information coming out from the Government benches; this is what Statistics New
Zealand says. Just over a month ago it reporte d that grocery food prices for the year
ended April 2013 decreased—that means they  went backwards, went down, became
more affordable for New Zealanders—in th e last year. Fresh milk went down 7.4
percent. I can remember that before the last election in the Commerce Committee there
was such a hue and cry for an inquiry on th e price of milk because everybody thought it
was out of control and that we were payi ng huge international prices. We know that
even just this last week Fonterra has announced a record payout for farmers, and yet we
see in the last 12 months that the price of  milk has come down. That is, I think, the
response of a good economy that is tracking along nicely. We also know that cheese
went down 7.8 percent. Butter is  down 23 percent. Meat, pou ltry, and fish are down 6.7
percent. There were a couple of things that  went up: avocados we nt up 48 percent. So
when you go to the shop to buy your avocados, sorry. It was such a small production in
2012, compared with a bumper season in 2011.
This is all good news for New Zealanders. This Budget is sensible and it is solid. It is
what New Zealanders want right now. We  do not want big sweeping and novel ideas
like capital gains taxes and wholesale electricity monopolies. We do not want all of that
stuff that those people are throwing up there because they are desperate. They are trying
everything they can to attract the atten tion of New Zealanders. It is voodoo politics.
They are hoodwinking people when we have got  it right for 5 years now, getting it right
all the time for New Zealanders.
Labour believes that it can enhance competitive pow er pricing by becoming the
monopolistic buyer of wholesale electricity in the country. Pull the other leg. Come on.
We are wide awake to that. The only people who are doing that are people who are
moving away from monopolistic purchasing into a market-driven economy. Those
members know that, but they will not say it. It is a daft idea, and we do welcome all
their daft ideas because they just go to prove how solid and sensible this Budget and this
Government are for the sake of all New Z ealanders. Colin Espine r—who, as I said in
my last speech, is no friend of the Gove rnment—says: “This is Third World, funny-
money stuff.” The New Zealand Herald referred to it as a 1930s command economy
solution. We need to understand that we live in a society where, when we get the
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10665
balance right around competition, it brings thro ugh all the benefits of not only better
innovation but better pricing for New Zealanders.
I think that this is what the Government is doing in this Budget.  We are responsibly
managing the Government’s books. We are building a more competitive and productive
economy, and we are delivering better public services.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What about households?

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: We are doing a lot in the housing space. It is not pie-in-the-
sky stuff. It is steak on the plate, while you  wait, and that is so  good. We are delivering
better public services. We ar e rebuilding Christchurch. We are building the foundations
for future success. We need to understand that this is something that we need to build
into the economic DNA of this country. It ta kes time. It takes time to get things right,
because it took 9 whole year s to get it wrong—we know that . We know what a stuff-up
they made of this economy, and we know the ha rd work that we have put in place, the
hard thinking, and the hard yards, and it is  starting to pay off. There was 3 percent
economic growth this last year. It is fa r above the growth of the UK, America,
Australia, and the European Union, of course . It is better than all those economies and
all those nations that we look up to. They ar e looking up to us now because we have got
it right, and this Budget is doing a great job.
We are increasing education investment. We are not just aiding people, we are
enabling people. There is a difference there. There is something there. We are putting
tools in the hands of people so that they can have choices. They can be predetermined in
their life because we are ensuring that they  are getting education where it is really
needed. We are pouring more and more mone y into early childhood education to ensure
that those young kids are getting their foot on the first rung of education early on, so
that they are not st ruggling and trying to climb up la ter on. We are putting more and
more money into tertiary education, and more and more emphasis on, and
accountability into, tertiary education. This is so that our young people—and not just
young people, but all New Zealanders—who go through these educational programmes
can have their foot on the ladder of employ ment in a very successful way. They are
coming out of our high schools with National Certificate of Educational Achievement
level 2 in far greater proportions and number s. We are seeing alre ady that this is
shifting. Already we are seeing some great re sponses. We know all the controversy and
criticism that we have narrowed education. Bu t we have not. We ha ve a broad base on
our education.
What we are getting right is the fundament als. We are getting the foundations right
so that people can go into tertiary edu cation with really good linguistic skills and
abilities, and so that they have really good numeric skil ls and abilities. These are the
foundations for future learning, and we have got to have them right. We cannot keep
seeing our polytechs having to do level 1 and level 2 courses. They need to be doing
levels 3, 4, 5, and 6. We need to make sure that our secondary schools are getting all the
fundamentals right, and they depend on the primary schools to get that right. So we
have this complete pathway of learning, and every single step on this pathway has to be
strong and fit for purpose, and has to be  achieving for our young people. We cannot
have one part of this system falling over, because it is like a domino effect.
We are getting it right. We  are putting the money where it really counts. We are
investing in education. We are investing in  innovation. We are investing in all these
areas that, in time to come, even as we see it now, progressively we will see more and
more. We are seeing New Zealanders succeed. This is incredibly important for this
nation. We are just a small nation of 4.4 m illion, competing in a huge world market of
talent. We have got to maximise our talent. We are innovators, we are dreamers, we are
thinkers, and we are inventor s. And when we have our education strong and robust,
10666 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013
when we have fewer people needing Gove rnment support and more people bringing
resources to Government and to their commun ities, what we are going to see is a nation
with its head up. We are going to see a nation that forges ahead, and we are going to see
a nation that internationally, economically, and educationally will continue to forge
ahead. We are going to take those high places of achievement and we are going to earn
them. This Budget is very much a part of that  long-term future for the future success of
all New Zealanders. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: As we discuss the Budget that this
Government has handed down I think it is important to consider  the Government’s
progress through its agenda to exploit all of New Zealand’s natural resources. In that
context, it is necessary to look at the im portance that the Government places on its
environment budget. I have taken a look at Vote Environment and I find it absolutely
remarkable that there has not been one single policy initiative in the environment
budget—not one new idea, not one new progr amme, not one new policy initiative to
protect, maintain, and enhance our environment.
The Minister for the Environment has done things, but they are not reflected in this
Budget. Let me give the House some exampl es. The budget for Vote Environment is to
be set against our claims—our diminishing clai ms, and our claims that are consistently
under criticism—of being 100 percent pure. We  have poor and declining water quality.
We have erosion of our protections for our  environment, proposed in the Minister’s
second tranche of Resource Management Ac t amendments, and we have some self-
interest reflected in the water recommendati ons and proposals that the Minister put out
earlier this year. I would real ly like to know whether the Minister even put in a bid for
her environment vote, because it is not apparent from this Budget.
I will just list some of the things that ar e contained in the Vote Environment part of
the Budget—let us have a look at them. E nvironmental management obligations and
programmes—there is no change, absolu tely no change. Improving resource
management—there is a drop of $2.4 million from the previous year, so improving
resource management, as a Budget line, gets a cut. This needs to be explained. If the
members opposite wish to give the Minister a heads-up, that will be asked in the
estimates questions when she appears before the select committee.
I will tell the House where one area of increase has happened, and it is in the funding
to service the Minister. Funding to service the Minister has gone up by $313,000, and
the note attached to that in the vote is that  the ministry expects that there will be an
increase in ministerials as a result of  the Resource Management Act and water
management reforms. Clearly, the Minister is aware that the Resource Management Act
reforms and the water management reforms are go ing to be controversial, so in order to
bolster her own ability to answer the quest ions that are going to flood in and the
challenges that are going to be taken agai nst her, she has increased the funding to
service her office by $313,000. That does not enhance the environment one iota.
Advice on environmental hazards and waste— there is no change; no change there.
The waste levy administration and assessm ent of projects for funding by the levy—
there is a drop of $600,000; $610,000, actually. But it is a $600,000 drop in the waste
levy administration and assessments of project s that are funded by that levy to see how
various industries can minimise their waste production. So th ere is not any vision about
next year or the year after, and whet her or not our waste production and our
minimisation of that is going to improve. There are no new targets. There are no new
ideas. In fact, there is a cut of $600,000 in  that area. The Contaminated Sites
Remediation Fund—there is no change there. There is no change in the Contaminated
Sites Remediation Fund. How is the Minister intending to deal with new contaminated
sites as they emerge?
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10667
She has only to look in her backyard at the Ōwaka Pit in her electorate, which has
had medium-density fibreboard combusting sp ontaneously and releasing toxins into the
air. This has been happening for months. The fi re has gone out only just in the last 2 or
3 weeks. The Minister clearly does not bothe r about that, even t hough it is in her
electorate, because the prevai ling wind makes those toxic fumes blow over the people
who live in the electorate of  my colleague Megan Woods. The Minister is not so
concerned about the people in that electorate that she thinks there is anything that needs
to be done about the burning of formaldehyde and the release of t hose toxins into the
atmosphere, creating an unpleasant smell and an irritating set of toxins that have caused
some discomfort. So even for the Minister’s  own backyard she ha s not appropriated or,
it would seem, even asked for additional f unds to address contaminated sites. The
Ōwaka Pit is now in a state that needs re mediation. The fire is out; now the ground has
to be recovered.
The Contestable Waste Minimisation F und—no change. This fund has a certain
allocation per year. Sometimes the funds are not spent in 1 year and they are moved into
future years, but there is no change. Where there has been an increase—and here we go
again—is to the Envi ronmental Protection Authority, which gets an increase of $1.9
million. Why? It is so that the Environmen tal Protection Authority can implement its
functions under our exclusive economic zone  legislation and the Exclusive Economic
Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Ef fects) Act 2012, so that when challenges
are brought about the illegality of the law that  this Parliament has passed in respect of
controlling shipping above the continental shelf—which, I am still of the opinion, is not
legal—then there will be sufficient resource s in the authority for it to address those
things.
There is no change to the Fresh Star t for Fresh Water Clean-up Fund for New
Zealand water bodies—no change to that . For the Rotorua Lakes Protection and
Restoration Programme there is  a slight re-phasing of f unds between the years but no
overall change. Lake Ōkareka in Rotorua is suffocating from hornwort. It is a hugely
invasive aquatic plant, and there has been nothing in the way of additional funding put
aside to restore Lake Ōkareka, which is one of the Rotorua lakes. I have been to the
lake. I have seen it myself. The people there work hard at  trying to deliver quality. The
fund for the Waikato River clean-up—no chan ge. There is an amount of funding over
30 years, but the real value of the funding will reduce over time. There is no change to
the Waikato River co-governance, no change to the Waikato River co-management, and
no change to the waste disposal levy disbursement to local authorities.
The environment budget is a disgrace. The environment budget is lacking in any
vision, any foresight, and any pr otective measures, and simply plays into the hands of
this Government’s agenda to mine and dril l everything it can get its hands on in terms
of our natural resources. It does not matter whether we have the legal right to do it or
not, this Government will proceed to expl oit our environment in order to produce
dollars, and usually for its friends. So Skycity was sold the gambling laws, Warner Bros
was sold the employment laws, and now we have Shell being sold the Crown mineral
laws. Thank you.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Budget 2013 is Bill English’s fifth
Budget and it is, indeed, buildi ng momentum. It confirms that  New Zealand is back on
track, with more economic growth, more jobs, rising wages, and a return to surplus by
2014-15. That is all great news for New Zealand, and very bad news for the Opposition,
which is bereft, as we have heard this afte rnoon, of any fresh ideas or policies. Both
Labour and the Greens are, of course—and ha ve proven it time a nd again—anti-growth
parties. They are opposed to a ny and all initiative s that would create jobs and boost the
economy. The Opposition’s policies of borrowi ng more and spending more would take
10668 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013
our economy backwards at a great rate. A nd when no one would lend us any more
money, what is its solution? It is to print more, of course. That is the sort of madness
that the unholy alliance of no ideas would deli ver. It is the tired old tried and failed
policies of Labour and the “Watermelon Gr eens”—those individuals who are green on
the outside and socialist red at heart, and who think they are doing so well.
This Budget 2013 is a defining document from a Government that is spending
prudently, not spending up large, which is  all Opposition member s can come up with.
So I am not going to waste any more time th is afternoon on them. Instead, I intend to
focus on the very positive measures that we re introduced in the Budget in the vitally
important areas of health, housing, and welfar e. As our very competent and successful
health Minister, Tony Ryall, outlined at the start of today’s Budget debate, this John
Key - led Government is investing more in  health than ever before. The Minister
outlined the number of green prescriptions and the strong focus on investing in
preventative care. To recap, we are making a $1.6 billion investment available over 4
years. That has boosted the total health spending to a record level of $14.7 billion.
Let us look specifically at where that is be ing targeted. As our population is healthier
and we are living longer, it is projected, as the Minister indicated, that by 2045 or 2050
there are going to be 150,000 New Zealande rs with dementia. As I and many New
Zealand families know only too well, the painfu l reality of living with dementia is a
terrible struggle for the sufferers and for their families, who have to watch as the people
they love gradually decline and need mo re and more high-level support. My late
mother’s 10-year decline with multi-infarct dementia was not untypical. It was very sad
to see a once independent, successful businesswoman and vibrant personality struggling
to do the simple things like making tea a nd toast, and desperately wanting to stay
independent and in her own home for as l ong as possible. To help people in these
difficult situations, we are investing an extra $70 million in aged care and dementia
services. That money is being very carefully targeted into the areas where it will help
most.
As my mother, Agnes, lost her ability to recognise people and places, it became even
more important to her to stay in her own home, because it was a safe place and it was a
place where she was familiar with all he r surroundings and her garden. She was a
happier and calmer person there. But, as that eventually took its toll on her, Mum
needed more and more support to stay at home. Although I was able to pay privately for
much of the assistance that she needed, it is a very difficult thing to manage long term. I
know that the $20 million that has been allocated in this year’s Budget targeted
specifically to be invested in home support se rvices will be invaluable. Some things are
priceless. It will provide practical help so that people can stay in the familiar
environment of their own home for as long as  possible. With an ageing population, we
need to ensure the best possible quality of life for dementia sufferers and for their
families. It is very clear to me that it is important to detect dementia as early as possible.
I know of many families who were in denial  for a long time, and who were just not
aware of the onset of dementia  and its early signs. So they  experienced, I am afraid to
say, heart-breaking misunderstandings and fami ly rifts, actually, un til they understood
what was happening.
Overall, as a society, we need to have  a much better and earlier awareness of
dementia and its inevitable pathway. When  the time does come for more expert
intervention and residential care options, we need a workforce that is equipped with the
right level of training. There is no questi on in my mind that caregivers need to be
compassionate, and they need that quality in abundance. I believe it is basically a
vocational guidance—it is a cal ling, really, to look after people who are losing their
minds to dementia. There is also the need  for better training and more specifically
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10669
skilled people to meet th at growing demand. To meet that, we have allowed $3.2
million towards training for health professionals and towards awareness programmes,
and also for early detection assistance for th e clinical teams. These kinds of conditions
require that high level of skill as well as that high level of compassion. Believe me, I
and people who have experienced it think that  is money well spent. It will make a huge
difference to the quality of life for the pe rson suffering from dementia and for their
families. With the best will in the world it is very difficult, once the condition has
reached a certain stage, for most New Zeala nd families to look after dementia sufferers
at home. That is why the $12 million increase in funding for bed subsidies and the vital
encouragement for further investment in demen tia beds are essential. So over the next 4
years we are also funding, through the district health boards, an additional $33.2 million
on aged residential care subsidies.
In the vital area of housing, the Minister Dr Nick Smith is as determined through his
portfolio as the health Minister, Tony Ryall, is  with health, to help the vulnerable in our
society. We know that crowded, cold, and damp  conditions contribute to dismal health
outcomes. So making homes warmer, drier, and healthier is one of his priorities. It is the
right thing to do. And, unlike the waffle a nd the weasel words of the Opposition, Dr
Smith is not leaving that to chance. An extra $100 million investment in the highly
successful home insulation programme is goi ng to boost the number of homes insulated
to 230,000 by September this year. That is a clear and measurable thing. So all State
houses that are capable of being insulated will be. It is a measure of the standard of our
State housing stock. He is developing and tr ialling a Housing Warrant of Fitness to
apply to all 69,000 Housing New Zealand Corpor ation properties, so that over the next
3 years this Government is making a record investment of $2.9 billion in State housing.
It is also making very bold changes to the way that we deliver housing assistance, and it
is targeting it to the people who really need it.
The shift from State dominated housing to community housing has been very
successful in Europe, in North America, and in Australia. So in Budget 2013 our
Government has announced that we are al so going to extend in come-related rent
subsidies to community housing providers. Churches, charities, and other NGOs often
integrate housing with other wraparound services  to people with disabilities, to people
with mental health issues, and to people with drug and alcohol problems. These sorts of
wraparound services can often do, let us face it , a better job of m eeting their clients’
complex needs. This Government is determined  to create the right environment to grow
the community housing sector.
Quality affordable housing is good for the economy and it is also very good for
communities. High housing costs ultimately rais e debt and increases demand for social
assistance. Under this Government, the Ki wi dream of owning your own home will
again become a reality and within reach of low and middle income New Zealanders. We
have announced a raft of measures to make housing more affordable. We are looking at
increasing land supply, we are streamlini ng consent and compliance costs, we are
looking at better delivery of core infrastruc ture to support that new housing, and we are
also getting on top of the costs around build ing materials and cons truction. We are not
just sitting back and leaving it to chance;  we are doing somethi ng about it. We have
concrete, measurable things.
As my colleague Jonathan Young said in hi s earlier call, we ar e not just aiding
people, we are enabling people. That is why I come to our welfare reforms. They are
increasing, and under Budget 2013 low-income families will be receiving greater
support. It is really a combination of what we have been doing—extending proven
programmes and also introducing new initia tives, targeting res ources and targeting
support. This is complemented by the G overnment’s $139.3 million investment through
10670 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013
the Social Housing Fund, which others ha ve detailed. Helping people to help
themselves is what is at th e heart of this Government’s Budget. This is a Government
and this is a Budget with real heart and m easurable outcomes th at will really help
people because it is targeted, it is precise, it is measurable, and it is going to work.
This Government has put another $1.5 million to support budgeting services, as well,
for people who have not ever really been ta ught how to grasp the reality of budgeting,
and making sure their cheque books work a nd making sure they are not overspending.
Those are lessons that perhaps the Labour colleagues across the way could well benefit
from.
To end, I will say that the people in my No rth Shore electorate have given me very
positive feedback on this Budget 2013 and all its measures. Measures relating to ACC
were some of the things that they have b een looking for. They wanted to have some
better provisions there, and what we are doing there with  the reduction in the levies has
been outstanding. They have told me that they love the significant levy reductions of
around $300 million, which will extend to $1 billion the following year. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: I listened very carefully
to the Budget speech from the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, where he
said that anyone standing for the Christc hurch City Council should look at the finances.
He said—and I want to quote him—“do not be deceived by what you are being told by
the people who are presenting those figures.” That is an extraordinary statement coming
from a senior Minister in the lead-up to  a council election. I pl aced the Minister’s
speech on my Facebook page, and the response was immediate: what does the Minister
know that we do not know? There was a consid erable amount of fear expressed that the
Minister knows things about the council’s finances but is  not telling the people of
Christchurch exactly what those concerns ar e, even though the council is at the moment
going through its 3-year plan process. Ch ristchurch City Counc il is not going through
the 10-year plan process that other councils  are going through. It has had its planning
process reduced to 3 years, but, more sign ificant, the Government has decided not to
make the council subject to the usual Auditor-General oversight.
So, on one hand, the Minister sa ys that we should be c oncerned about Christchurch
City Council’s finances, and look at them very carefully and not be deceived by those
presenting the figures—he is referring to th e mayor and the chief executive, who have
signed the 3-year plan; he cannot be refe rring to anyone else, because it is their
signatures that actually app ear on that document—and yet the Government has decided
in its wisdom not to make it subject to usual Auditor-General oversight. The Labour
Opposition members asked that that Auditor-General oversight be included in the Order
in Council when we were asked to comment on it, but we were not listened to. Why did
the Government allow this process to proc eed with no proper scru tiny, clearly knowing
things that the people of Christchurch do not know, and with an election looming?
Add on top of that the extraordinary pressu re that the Government is placing on the
council to pay for the Government’s blueprin t, even though the people of Christchurch
had absolutely no say whatsoever with regard  to the major anchor projects that it
announced. I do not think that the people of Christchurch  need a Cabinet Minister—the
Minister for Canterbury Eart hquake Recovery—to stand here  in this debating chamber
firing shots at the council down in Christchurch, but also in  the same breath can I say
that we do not need a council that shows that it is incapable of being the kind of partner
that a Government needs in a recovery situation.
The Minister warned us about these peopl e who are presenting these figures, and I
think that deception is a pretty strong a llegation. But how does the Government have
confidence in the council when the front pa ge of the paper has been dominated by a
chief executive who is blatantly double-dipping, both as the chief executive receiving
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10671
his extraordinarily high salary—which re ceived huge feedback, in a negative sense,
from the public—and also as a director receiv ing director’s fees fo r sitting on the Civic
Assurance company? He is now having to appe ar in front of the council to explain why
Civic Assurance is taking so long to pay the council’s insuranc e bill. He is double-
dipping. In any situation like th at, a chief executive of an organisation would pay their
director’s fees directly to  the organisation that they were representin g on that body.
Only three or four councillors have actually  consistently stood up for transparency in
Christchurch, but they are accused by the ma yor and the chief executive of being the
problem.
I have to say that this has got to stop. It  absolutely has got to stop. The people of
Christchurch need their leaders to really step up at this time. We are going into our third
winter—our third winter—and peopl e are still living in  unacceptable situ ations that we
would not ordinarily tolerate in a First World country. The pressure that is being
brought to bear on ordinary Ch ristchurch residents living in  areas where the land is the
most challenging is unbelievable. They do not need to read in the paper about what can
only be described as sheer greed, and then, at the same time, hear that the Minister is
making these allegations in Parliament wit hout giving the substanc e to the people of
Christchurch. I think it is absolutely vital that the people of Christchurch are told the
truth about what is going on at Christchurch City Council.
The Government’s blueprint is part of the problem. It is  a big part of the problem.
The people think that they have been forgotten—put to one side while we talk about
what buildings are going to be built in the centre of the city. We see a campaign bid for
City First or Christchurch First, but really it should be the people fi rst. If the people are
dealt with first, then surely the rest will follow.
In the last couple of weeks the Prime Minist er has said that “big-ticket Christchurch
recovery projects could be scaled back to help bridge the funding gap between local and
central government.” But whose funding gap is that? Who created the funding gap? The
Government manufactured the funding gap wh en it decided that it would completely
rewrite the city’s draft Christchurch Central Recovery Plan  and would then hand the
bill to the people of Christchurch. That is what has happened in Christchurch. John Key
says that major projects like the new conve ntion centre and the roofed sports stadium
could be downsized to save money. But whos e money would that sa ve? They were not
our decisions. Christchurch City has never had the opportunity to have a say about these
major anchor projects that the Government has foisted upon us.
John Key said the council had only three ways of paying its share of recovery
projects: borrowing the money, significantly ra ising rates, and “it changes its asset
mix”. Well, what does “it changes its asset mi x” mean? It means selling Christchurch’s
strategic assets that we have held on to because those assets have actually been a part of
ensuring that we had revenue -generating opportunities but al so the strategic ability to
govern our ports, both the airport, which is  the gateway to the South Island, and our
seaport, similarly, in term s of goods coming in and out  of the country, and also,
obviously, Orion, which was the standout performe r after the series of  earthquakes that
we had. I have never seen an organisation ope rating the way it did, but the work that it
did in advance, the resilien ce that it built into its netw ork ahead of the disaster
occurring, was what saved Christchurch and, indeed, saved New Zealand a considerable
amount of additional cost that would have otherwise applied.
So when the Prime Minister says “it changes its asset mix”, the Prime Minister is
saying: “People of Christchurch, you must se ll your revenue-generating strategic assets
and fund loss-making facilities, where th e council cannot even tell the people of
Christchurch how much they are budgeted to  lose, because the Government has not
even prepared a business case for any of th ese so-called anchor projects.” This is a
10672 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013
National Government and there is no busines s case prepared for any of these assets.
How can the council pay its share when we do  not know as a city what our share is?
And why should we pay for any share that was not part of what we, as a city,
determined was in our best interests?
John Key then said it was up to the counc il to ask whether residents wanted the
“nice-to-haves” in the city’s rebuild. What  are these “nice-to-haves”? No one in
Christchurch has been told that any of the anchor projects are negotiable. Many people
feel that John Key has relegated the repair and rebuild of homes on the most challenging
land in Christchurch to being a “nice-to-have”.  We in Christchurch say it is not a “nice-
to-have”; it is a “need-to-have”. That need is  very, very real. We need the Government
to be working alongside the council in pa rtnership with the community. Take the
community with us as we rebuild our city. I am extremely optimistic about what we can
achieve in Christchurch, but we need central government, local government, and
community all working together on the rebuild and repair of our city.
