items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I move, That the Education
Amendment Bill be now read a third time . The Education Amendment Bill amends the
Education Act 1989. It will play a key role in supporting the Government’s objective of
how we get five out of five  students achieving educational success. This Government is
absolutely focused on that. We do not want educational success for a few—for some—
but for all, so we have focused on a full range of measures that will deliver that
possibility to all New Zealand school students  and learners. This bi ll helps deal with a
number of things, in fact. It creates th e legal framework by which we will establish
partnership schools or kura hourua. It also looks at the provision for how school staff
may exercise search and surrender provisions, in order to ensure that schools are safe
and secure places while protecting the rights of students. It also  makes provision for a
number of other areas that will allow greater flexibility in the delivery of education in
New Zealand.
Starting with the two significant or substa ntial provisions in te rms of creating the
legal framework for partnership schools or kura hourua, we know that it will help us
deliver a third option for educ ational provision in New Zeal and. It will enable us to
have a legal framework that allows for pa rtnership between the community sectors,
business, and education, because this Government recognises that there is not a
monopoly on how quality education can be delivered. In fact, it can be delivered
through a number of ways, and we are interested in exploring all of those ways, because
we will leave no option uncons idered in how we ensure that we raise educational
achievement for five out of five kids.
We know that our education system in Ne w Zealand is world class but not world
leading. We know that it is top performing as  an education jurisdic tion. It performs for
the vast majority but not for all. We know  that those who have been traditionally
underserved by our education system are the same groups of people year in and year
out. So there is a system response that we need to make. We want those parts of our
education system that are performing well for the majority of our students to continue to
perform well and, indeed, to perform better, bu t we also want to address those parts of
the system that are not performing as well. That means working with all of the schools
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10673
that we have—and we have over 2,500. T hose 2,500 schools already canvass a range of
options. We have single-sex and coed; we ha ve total immersion in English and total
immersion in Māori, and bilingual units; we have faith-based and secular-based schools;
we have small, medium, and large schools; an d, of course, they ar e spread the length
and breadth of our country.
What partnership schools do is offer us another optio n—another option that is
focused on results, on transparency, on ensuri ng that the sponsors who propose and go
through a very thorough approval process are focused on how they will deliver
educational results for the students whose parents choose that they should go there.
There will be no compulsion in  this. Partnership schools pr ovide another option, but it
will be transparent in terms of what is exp ected. It will be transparent in terms of the
conduct of its business. It will be transparent in that the disciplinary provisions of the
Ombudsmen Act will apply. It will be transparen t in that all of the requirements will be
specified in a contract between the Ministry  of Education, on behalf of the Crown, and
the successful sponsor, and all the reporting th at will be expected in respect of that,
whether financial, operational,  or educational, will be reported to the Ministry of
Education, which, of course, will ensure that it is captured by the Official Information
Act.
The bill provides that the sponsors may recommend that a proportion of their staff
may not be registered as teachers, but that  is not to be confused with not having
qualifications and not having skills. Indeed, kura kaupapa had the same kind of difficult
birth that the Opposition w ould try to attend partnershi ps schools with. There was a
belief that kura were so different from the re st of the mainstream system that they could
not possibly be good, when the facts, which have been incontrovertible since they
started, are that children and young people who go to kura by and large, on average, do
better—Māori kids—than they do in the mainstream system. The kura will tell us that
much of that success is due  to experts in te reo me ōna tikanga, who may not be
registered teachers but nevertheless deliver learning in ways that ensure educational
success. We envisage the same sort of track  record occurring here with partnership
schools. So what this legislation does is put around it a lega l framework that makes this
option clear, stable, transparent, and focuse d on getting five out of five kids being
educationally successful.
As I have said, there will be no compulsion for a parent to send their child here, as
there is no compulsion for a pare nt to send their child to any particular type of school.
And, as I have said many times before too, it is not the type of school; it is the quality of
performance. We will be holding these school s to the highest standards. We will be
expecting that they will be able to deliver successfully to these kids, and if not, the
ultimate sanction will apply, and that is that they can, and will, be closed.
A second part of this legislation focuses on ensuring that we are very clear about
what the rights are of not only teachers and pr incipals but also othe r authorised staff to
ensure a safe and secure environment wher ein learning can break out, potential can be
realised, and educational success can be within  reach of every one of our students. But
we are realistic. We know that schools are also microcosms of society and that there can
be dangers and unsafe instruments or behaviours that are brought into schools. We want
to ensure that our teachers and other authorised  staff have the ability to exercise search
and surrender responsib ilities that ensure th at where staff suspect that a student may
indeed be harbouring inappropr iate equipment or anything th at might present a danger
to other students, staff have the ability to require these young people to disclose those.
The Education and Science Committee members have worked really hard together,
and with the sector, to strike a very good balance between ensuri ng the safety of all
students and protecting the rights of the dignity  and privacy of other students. This has
10674 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
been a very challenging balance to strike, an d I think that this le gislation does that. It
will be reinforced by the establishment of guidelines, which will be formulated under
the Secretary for Education’s auspices, but also through involving a working group
from the sector. After all, principals and teachers are the ones who every day face these
challenges and want to know that they ar e going to have sensible and practicable
provisions by which they can exercise these cautions.
The final part of this legisl ation deals with a range of ot her provisions, all of which
are dedicated to this Government’s commitment to raising educational achievement for
all kids. One of the things it starts off with is a recogniti on that boards of trustees are
Crown entities but, unlike every other Crown entity, they have no purpose articulated at
law. This legislation remedies that omissi on by making it very clea r that the role and
purpose of boards in everything they do is to focus on ensu ring that every student has
the opportunity to do well educationally. So, wh ether it is the management of property,
financial responsibilities to be discharged, the kind of curriculum programme that is to
be taught, or the kinds of skills that are to  be employed at the school, the board is doing
all of that with one clear focus, and that is to raise the achievement of all.
Allied to that is a provision for making timetabling flexible. We learnt from
Christchurch that by enabling schools to have flexibility in their timetables, they could
cater for a whole range of students, but in pa rticular for that very  permeable interface,
which this Government has made more perm eable, in the secondary -tertiary transition,
where young people go off to trades academies fo r 2 or 3 days a week, or take up other
options such as internships, practicums,  and so forth. We do not want a hidebound
structure within schools that precludes that possibility. We want educational success to
not only be in reach but also be achieved by five out of five students, and this legislation
puts that within their grasp.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Before I begin the substantive comments
that I want to make on the Education Amen dment Bill, I have a quick question for the
Minister of Education. I would like her to name one school boa rd of trustees that is not
focused on student achievement. Which one?

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: We’re providing a legal basis for all of them.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Oh, right, there we go—the Mini ster of Education cannot name
one school board of trustees that is not focused on student achievement, because the
reality is that when parents put their names forward to be on school boards of trustees,
they do so specifically because they care a bout their kids’ educational achievement and
because they care about the educational ac hievement of other kids within their
community. I think it is absolutely disg raceful that this Government does not
acknowledge that and that it seems to think it  has to legislate for something that is
blatantly obvious. It is blatantly obvious because parents, teachers, and everyone who
works in the education system go into it w ith the view of improving the lives of young
people in New Zealand. They already want to do that. They do not  need to have the
Government come in here and accuse them  of not doing that, wh ich is what Hekia
Parata is constantly doing all of the time.
This is a sad day for the public education system in New Zealand. It is a very sad
day, because it is a day when the National Government put politics before education. So
when did this all start? We know how this bi ll came to be in the H ouse. It was all to do
with the cup of tea between Mr Banks over there and John Key—the one that was
inadvertently recorded, and the one that they went to court to try to cover up. The cup of
tea between John Banks and John Key is why we are debating this legislation in the
House today. It is not about education. It is not about wh at is going to be good for
education. It is riding ro ughshod over public opinion, which is something that we are
well used to this National Government doi ng. Eighty-two percent of New Zealanders
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10675
are opposed to the idea that charter schools should be allowed to employ unregistered
teachers, yet this Government is bringing this bill to the House to deregulate the
teaching profession, effectivel y, and it is ignoring the pub lic’s concern about that
matter. It voted down Supplementary Order Paper 221, which I put forward, which
would have ensured that there were qualified, registered teachers in schools.
Seventy-one percent of the New Zealand public are opposed to the idea that a charter
school operator should be able to make a profit, because New Zealanders know that
money taken out of charter schools in profits is not money—

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Specious numbers.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: “Specious numbers.”, Hekia Parata says. I think it was a One
News poll.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: We don’t make up stuff like the Opposition does.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Oh, she says they do not make up stuff. They do not make up
stuff like the Opposition does. I am sure this is going to get better.  Seventy-one percent
of New Zealanders are opposed to charter schools making a profit, because they know
that the money that is sucked out of the edu cation system in the form of profits is not
money that is going into educating kids. And why should the taxpayer be lining the
back pockets of the National Party’s and AC T Party’s mates who want to set up their
charter schools, rather than putting that money into education? This Government is
putting $19 million into these charter schools, and in the very same Budget it cut the
funding for a programme like Te Kotahitanga.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: A programme that has a proven track record of lifting student
achievement has been cut by this Government . Hekia Parata says that is rubbish. How
much money is going into Te Kotahitanga next year?

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: It is called building on success and actually—

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: No. That is right. That would be no money going into Te
Kotahitanga next year—no money at all going into Te Kota hitanga next year, not one
cent. The Government has cut the funding for it, because it has decided that charter
schools are more important—charter schools, which the international evidence proves
do not actually work.
Let us look at the United States. The Govern ment seems to be so in love with the
charter school system in the US. Stanford Un iversity did research into charter schools
and found that for 37 percent of learners, they produced significantly worse outcomes—
for 37 percent. For 46 percent they made no difference at all, and only 17 percent did
better in charter schools. These are the sort s of numbers that the Government thinks
justify its experiment in charter schools in New Zealand. This is not an experiment that
is designed to improve the outcomes in education. This is an ideological experiment that
is designed to privatise as pects of the education system, when what we should be
focused on is ensuring that every school in  New Zealand is a great school, and that
every New Zealander has the opportunity to fulfil their full potential—their full
potential—through access to lifelong learni ng opportunities and a quality public
education system.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: No, every New Zealander hasn ’t—not under that Government.
They’ve just wrung their hands and said: “Isn’t it terrible that every year more kids are
not passing—more Māori, more Pasifika.”

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Hekia Parata has got the audacity to talk about M āori
educational achievement, when that Mi nister cut the fundi ng for the best M āori
education programme in the country—cut th e funding completely. It is gone. It is
completely gone from next year, an d Hekia Parata is  talking about M āori educational
achievement when, actually, she has been th e Minister who has cut the one programme
10676 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
that had outstanding results. Why? Because  it was too expensive. And what was her
excuse? “Oh, well, we have got to come up w ith something that is a lot cheaper.” She
has decided that it is going to be cheaper to cut corners and to cut the programme that
works. That is how much Hekia Parata cares about M āori students’ educational
achievement. She wants to cut the one programme that actually works.
And Hekia Parata wants to put unregistered and unqualified teachers in front of these
Māori students. They are not going to have to  learn the New Zealand Curriculum. They
are not going to have to learn the New Zeal and Curriculum in these schools. If Hekia
Parata is so confident that they are going to be such good-quality schools, why are they
not going to be subject to th e Official Information Act? We hear nothing from the
Minister. Deathly silence—nothing. Because the Government does not want the public
to know what goes on within these charter sch ools. If the Governme nt is so confident
that these charter schools are goi ng to act in a manne r that is totally appropriate, why is
it that the Ombudsman’s powers do not apply to the entirety of the charter schools’
operations? Another deathly silence from the Government. No answer  to that question.
We know that the Ombudsman’s powers in rega rd to the State school system have been
used judiciously and have highlighted major systemic problems—

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Bullying.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: —including systemic bullying in one particular school, which
the education agencies did not pick up. This is the sort of stuff that the Government
wants to hide in charter schools by making them  not subject to the Official Information
Act and not allowing the Ombudsman the power to investigate. In short, the
Government wants to shortcut the democratic pr ocess. It wants to hide what is going on
in these schools.
The Government talks about the priority l earners. Here is another question for the

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: name one learner who is not a priority learner.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: All of them are priorities, but that Opposition—

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Oh, all of them are priorities. So when the Government talks
about its priority learners, what on earth is the point? They should all be priority
learners. So it is absolute weasel words when the Govern ment talks about priority
learners. What is it that Hekia Parata has ag ainst parent-led boards of trustees? What is
that Hekia Parata has got against parent-led  boards of trustees? She wants to allow
private charter schools to be set up as profit-making businesses with no parental
involvement whatsoever in how they are run. Th at is what this legi slation allows, plain
and simple. This is a failed ideological experiment that is being imported from overseas.
It is not about improving educ ational outcomes for New Z ealand students. It is not
about making sure we pick up the best examples  of what is working in this country and
what is good for New Zealand st udents. It is not about that at all. It is about importing
failed ideology. It is about the failed ideology that says that if we increase competition,
we will get better outcomes. Well, actually, we have had several decades of increased
competition in our education system, and the very priority learners whom Hekia Parata
talks about are some of those who have b een most disadvantaged by that competition
that we have within our education system.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Under that Government. Didn’t care enough, just published
reports, and cried about it.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Oh, no. No, actually, it was a Labour Government that set up the
Te Kotahitanga programme, which that Mini ster has now cut the funding to. It was a
Labour Government that estab lished schools of special charac ter to recognise that there
is a gap within the existing public educa tion system. Schools of special character
already allow that gap to be filled, yet th is Government is turning its back on that,
saying that it does not think that  schools of special character ar e of any use at all. It is
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10677
turning its back on that, and it is saying that it wants to privatise education and
deregulate the teaching profession instead. A nd deregulate the teaching profession it
will, because we saw from the Novopay inquiry  today the veiled references to further
deregulation, to renegotiating the collective ag reement to make it simpler. Oh, yes, that
is the agenda. We know that Treasury has been working on it. The Government is going
to use any excuse it can to deregulate th e teaching profession in New Zealand, because
the National Party never learns  the lessons of history. When  we look at the countless
examples of where deregulat ion of professions has gone wrong, we see that we do not
need another one. The future of New Zealand’ s education system and the future of the
young people in it are far too important to experiment on, which is what this bill does.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: The Education Amendment Bill amends the
Education Act in the two principal ways that  we have heard. The Mi nister of Education
gave a very lucid explanation of how it sets  out a legal framework for a new type of
school, the partnership school. It  alters another very import ant area by establishing
powers around surrender to schools of harmful items, and retention by schools of
harmful items. These harmful items may be defined as items that pose an immediate
threat to the physical or emotional safety of  a person or that detr imentally affect the
learning environment. These might include such things as knives, drugs, grenades, guns,
and items stored in electronic form.
This is a bill that, as introduced, include d a number of new s ections intended to
clarify the powers of schools in searching and retaining students’ property. We made
some key recommendations towards that. The Education and Science Committee looked
at this in a huge amount of detail, and so me of these key recommendations are worth
delineating because these were not clear in the original bill. I have to once again
acknowledge the hard work of most members of the committee for achieving this end.
Some of the key recommendations on the bill are as follows. We recommended
allowing authorised staff members to exercise  surrender and retention powers. I want to
acknowledge Mike Sabin and his work in this area for a number of years. He made an
outstanding contribution. We recommended a llowing teachers to require the removal of
outer clothing or the surrender of bags, with  safeguards. The Minister alluded to the
safeguards in this legislation. We recomm ended allowing teachers to require the
removal of any head covering, gloves, footw ear, or socks; clarifying that students may
be encouraged to participate in voluntary drug programmes; clarif ying that drug dogs
can be used to search school property; and making it mandatory to have rules and
guidelines about the implementation of th is. I hear some barracking from the
Opposition. This is crucially important. This is  legislation that this committee can take
great pride in because it has made the lif e of students throughout New Zealand a lot
safer. It has made the life of  staff, principals, and member s of boards of trustees a lot
clearer. So I want to acknow ledge this work by members of the committee. There were
some who stood to one side, but, in fact, those opposite an d Tracey Martin from New
Zealand First did work hard on this.
We have mentioned the key recommendations. I would like to now come on to why
we have this extra strand in our cable of  lifting student achievement that is called
partnership schools. One of the simple reasons for it is that  the only area in which New
Zealand is leading the world is inequalit y. The gap between our best students and our
lowest-performing students is the biggest in the world—the biggest in the world. As one
submitter asked—I will repeat it—are we liv ing in two different countries? Can we
afford to be complacent? The committee h eard that the Partnership Schools Working
Group had received from sponsors 34 indications of interest in setting up a partnership
school. Groups were saying that they want to do something about this.
10678 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
Contrast that with the unions, which were  ineluctably locked into opposing anything
that showed the leas t bit of innovation. Most of those 2,300 submissions were form
submissions, and there was not a lot of orig inal thought, but the people who are actually
wanting to get involved with these partnership schools were  saying that they want a
chance to do something about this. They want  to use innovation to enable their kids to
engage in learning and get a decent start in  life, and they are willing to be held
accountable for doing that.
The significant point is th at it is a matter of choi ce. Nobody has to go into a
partnership school. As outlined earlier, th e most fundamental difference in the
relationship between the Minister and the partnership school is that the relationship with
the Minister will be contractual rather than  regulatory. It is a contract to deliver
engagement and achievement outcomes—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member. The time has come for me to leave the Chair for the dinner break.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I want to start my final contribution to
this debate on this Education Amendment B ill by paying tribute to the parents and the
teachers throughout our country who have the be st interests of their children and their
education at the front of their minds, and that  is what leads their actions. Unfortunately,
this is a group that has come under attack  during the course of this bill’s passage
through the House. We have seen attack af ter attack from memb ers of the National
Party on the fact that we had members of teacher unions come to the Education and
Science Committee and offer their opinion. Well, these are the trained teaching
professionals in our country, the people who have the expertise in  education, and, yes,
they did have an opinion. They had a unanim ous opinion that this legislation is going to
do nothing to further educational outcomes in New Zealand.
This is a dark day for education in Ne w Zealand. Before the dinner break my
colleague Chris Hipkins mentioned in his cont ribution that this is a fundamental change
to what we understand about education in New Zealand that we are passing through this
House tonight. I do not see this as anything to celebrate. I also want to pay tribute to the
number of parents who are putting themselves  forward for boards of trustees as we
debate this legislation going through the H ouse and who have stood to be part of the
community governance of their schools, because  this is something that charter schools
will not have. This is something that the kind s of schools we are crea ting tonight in this
House are doing away with—the very thing that has led New Zealand to have one of the
most innovative, one of the most creative,  and one of the most community-involved
education systems in the world. We are doing away with that system with the passage of
this legislation tonight. It is absolutely nothing for us to celebrate.
I want to make it very cl ear about the future of ch arter schools under a Labour-led
Government in 2014. The ongoing funding and support for charter schools will not be
guaranteed under a future Labour Government . We will not guar antee any charter
school established during this term of the present Government the right to integrate into
the State school system. We do reserve the right to impose additional contractual
obligations on any charter school establishe d, such as a requirement to employ
registered teachers and the removal of exem ption from the Official Information Act
1982. No further charter school will be esta blished under a New Zealand Labour Party
Government, and legislation allowing for their establishment will be repealed. Let us
not make any mistake about what Labour’s position on these charter schools is. We do
not agree with them, and we do not agree with  them because they are not in the best
interests of the children of our country.
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10679
Throughout the various stages of this legi slation colleagues have outlined exactly
what our problems are with this type of school  being set up in New Zealand. It has been
well rehearsed. Our objection to unregistered  and unqualified teachers is on the record.
We would not let unqualified doc tors treat any of us, but members opposite think that it
is OK to put unqualified teachers in front of classrooms. We do not.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: They don’t respect them.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: We respect the teaching profession and the expertise that
they bring to their job. This is not something that we are willing to undermine.
We also object to the lack of scrutiny that these schools will be subjected to—the fact
that they will not be subjected to the Offici al Information Act, that parents will not get
that level of scrutiny, and that they will not have that recourse. We have talked
throughout the various stages of this legisla tion and shown examples of when this has
come into play and where it has been very useful, and, indeed, needed. I have talked
already in my speech about the lack of community engagement by doing away with
something that has become a New Zealand in stitution: the rights of communities to be
involved in decision making about their schools through the role of boards of trustees.
But, most disturbing, we know these sc hools will not work. The international
evidence points us in that direction. The very examples that have been thrown across the
House by members opposite are actually the very  failed experiments. They have touted
Sweden as the great example. Well, edu cational achievement in Sweden went down
when they introduced their freedom schools.  And, actually, if they had read their
Maxim Institute documents, they would know this, because the Maxim Institute has told
them this. Right-wing thinktanks are telli ng them that charter schools do not work, so
why do we not actually look at an eviden ce base for what we are doing with the
education of our children? It just does not stack up. What we want is to celebrate the
innovation that exists in our education system and to pay credit to the people who have
been doing that and the wonderful things  they do. Throughout the select committee
process we had submitter after submitter come  to us and tell us about the wonderful
things they were doing and that nothing they were doi ng now—or, indeed, wanted to
do—they could not do under the present legislation.
But for me as a Christchurch member of Parliament one of the most disturbing
aspects of this is the guinea pig nature of Christchurch children in the Government’s
thinking—that we are having the closure of school s in the Christchurch network to
make way for charter schools. In fact, in que stion time today the Minister of Education
refused to rule out establishing charter schools—or “partnersh ip schools”, as she
preferred to call them, because she could not quite stomach those words “charter
school”—on the site of Christ church schools that she closed  down last week. She is not
ruling this down.
Before our select committee we had Karran Harper Royal come and tell us of the
experience in New Orleans and the way in whic h natural disaster is used as an excuse
for experimentation. Today in this House we had the Minister confirm that is exactly
what she is thinking. She will not give that  commitment to the people of Christchurch
and the communities of Christchurch. For the schools in my electorate—for Branston
Intermediate School and Manning Intermedia te School—that are being closed down, I
want the Minister to give a commitment that a charter school will not be established on
those sites. This is something these people de serve. They need to know that their school
closure is not about building capacity in the network so this Government can implement
its charter schools, which are the price of coalition with John Banks. That is right.
Christchurch children are being used as the pawn in this coalition game. It is the price of
a vote. It is the price of getting through all the pieces of legislation that this Government
has been able to do by that one vote. This is not something that we on this side of the
10680 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
House feel is anything to celebrate—in fact, it is something that we should all be very
sad about, and something that we should all se e as a shameful day for education in our
country.
This evening I received an email from a cons tituent. The Minister also received this
email from this constituent of mine. She was very, very upset after hearing what
happened in question time today and the fact that the Minister  was not going to rule out
establishing charter schools at the very schools that she was closing. She wrote to the

items.speaker: Minister and she copied me in
items.text: “The schools you have closed, and you decide to replace
them by using the land for charter schools, to me  is another kick in the teeth.” This is
how people are feeling. This is  how people in Christchurch  are feeling on the schools
that have been closed. The people of Phillip stown are feeling like this. They know they
have been let down by their lo cal member. They know they have been let down by this
Government. They do not have a school in that community any longer.
This is something that is straight from th e playbook of New Orleans. That is one of
the most distressing parts of this. We could have sat back and predicted this, given this
Government’s commitment to playing from  that playbook. This is what happened in
New Orleans. And it is nothing about educational achievement. The educational
achievement there has not gone up. Indeed, th e educational achievement has not gone
up anywhere where charter schools have b een introduced. Members opposite have not
been able to show us this, through all the stag es of this legislation, be it in debates in
this House or at the select co mmittee, and have not been able  to point to the fact that
these are going to lead to better educational outcomes. For Labour, that is the bottom
line: what will deliver the best educational outcomes for our children. We know it is not
these partnership schools. This is not the wa y to do right by our children, and Labour
cannot support this legislation. Thank you.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Charter schools have no future in our
country, Aotearoa New Zealand, and I am pleas ed that the Labour Party has also made
it very clear in the last addre ss that it too believes that ch arter schools have no future in
this country. We want to make it very clear to any of those who are considering
establishing one that should there be a change of Govern ment in the near future, your
schools will no longer exist as charter schools.  I have said that we may apply the
integration criteria to those schools just to give those kids, at leas t, a bit of a chance,
because changing schools is always very diffi cult. But if those integration criteria are
not met or there are other reasons why those schools should be closed, including the fact
that the legislation will be repealed, then charter schools will no longer exist in this
country. It is important for those who are considering setting them up to know well in
advance the risk they are taking in establishing charter schools in New Zealand. Why do
we say that? Because we believe that the public money for education should be spent on
a strong, free, and quality public education system, not on lining the pockets of a few
wealthy cowboys who will drain the public purse for their private profit.
It has been very disappointing that the Minister of Education herself has shown no
real awareness of her portfolio and the imp act that the policy d ecisions she makes has
on schools, teachers, children, and their fa milies. We have had the Novopay debacle
report today, showing that sh e did not even know who wa s responsible for managing
this multimillion-dollar disaster. In this charter schools legislation and the policy behind
it, we see exactly that same neglect and, fr ankly, incompetence from this Minister in
managing this policy.
One of the key issues that was raised toda y in question time was the fact that this
Minister will not guarantee that  the schools that she has just closed in Christchurch will
not then be rented out or used by charter schools for ma king a profit. Those schools
were closed apparently because of populat ion decline in those areas. Those schools
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10681
were closed apparently because of earthquake  damage that was too expensive to fix in
those areas. But she still retains the power and, obviously, the inten tion to rent those
schools out to the charter school cowboys who have no educational experience, who
will be able to make a quick buck off the public purse, and who will, in doing so,
exploit vulnerable New Zealand children, be cause that is who will be running these
schools—cowboys. There is no requirement fo r these cowboys to have experience in
education management or its delivery. Ther e are fewer checks on these cowboys than
are currently applied to principals and to teach ers. Not only that but they will be able to
employ untrained people—these are not teacher s; these are just ordinary people, but
without any training or expertise in education—to teach children who all of the research
in New Zealand and before th e Minister says need the be st-trained, most professional
teachers in front of them. If you want to teach vulnerable kids, they need the best
possible teachers—those who are skilled a nd trained in this profession. But these
cowboys will be able to get anybody they want, including their mother and father and
sister and brother and uncles  and aunties and cousins—a nybody they like—to come in
front of these kids, and get public money for that. It is significant amounts of public
money for that.
Not only that but they will be able to ge t money for, for example, dealing with
children with disabilities. I do not know wh ether people realise that. But they do not
have to spend it on those kids . There is no requirement for them to spend it on those
kids, and they can simply put it in their back pocket as a big fat profit from the public
purse. At the end of the day, it will be New Zealand children who are left to find a
decent education somewhere in their area, after being exploited and experimented on by
John Banks and his mad ACT policies.
Sometimes I think that Hekia Parata really does not believe in this policy. Sometimes
I think, more and more, that she is being bul lied into promoting this policy because of a
$19 million cup of tea that John Key had wi th John Banks 18 months ago. I do think
that Hekia Parata does know what works for M āori. She has certainly been told by her
own people, by her advisers. She has been told. She knows that kura kaupapa M āori are
excellent and enormously successful for M āori kids, because th ey are a kaupapa M āori
solution that is developed by the very families that this policy is supposed to be directed
at—Māori and Pacific learners. She knows that Te Kotahitanga works and she has been
told that Ka Hikitia—Managing for Success needs more resources to be even more
effective than it is, but she has had to cut th e funding to Te Kotahitanga in order to feed
public funds into John Banks’ ridiculous ACT policy and his experiment on our kids. So
the successful programmes are being cut and experiments that have a history of failure
are being promoted.
I think that she too is nervous about th e financial side. During the Committee stage
of this debate last week, I as ked the Minister very specifica lly to guarantee that if there
is an Official Information Act request to he r and her ministry about financial matters to
do with charter schools, she would never use the commercial sensitivity clause. She sat
here and said that it was OK that the Offici al Information Act did not apply to charter
schools because all of their financial inform ation would be made public. But she would
not guarantee that she herself would not hide that information from the public. It does
beg the question of why that is the case. I think that the whole reason why the Official
Information Act does not apply to charte r schools and why the Minister will not
guarantee that she will not hide financial information herself, using the commercial
sensitivity rule, is that J ohn Banks knows all about the im portance of hiding financial
information. John Banks, actually, is right in the middle of a serious debate, a serious
issue, where he has been accused of hiding financial information from the public.
10682 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
You know, this is the man who cannot reme mber how much money he was given by
Kim Dotcom for his mayoral campaign. This is a man who took a cheque from
Skycity—who took a cheque from Skycity—I understand with his very hand, and still
does not remember how much it was for. So this is a man who has deliberately hidden
information about his public financial affair s from the public. He is now facing serious
action elsewhere about this issue, and because John Banks thinks that he is such a
master at keeping financial information secret and clearly is unhappy to have it revealed
here in the House, he is making sure that all those charter school cowboys that he is
promoting through his party membership—a ll those charter school cowboys—also get
the chance to hide their financial information from the public. They will be funnelled
funds and funds and funds—millions of dolla rs; at least $19 million in this first
tranche—of public money, and John Banks will  make sure that they do not have to
reveal the information. John Banks, the master  at keeping financial information secret,
will make sure that so can charter schools.
So not only do we have all of  the evidence about how charter schools fail these kids
the most, fail the most vulnerable children—overseas, only 17 percent of them do better
than in the public system; it is less than one in five—but the information about how
public education money taken from our State schools will be used is being kept secret,
because John Banks wants to protect those cowboys so they can continue to make a
public profit. There can be no other excuse fo r keeping those charte r schools out of the
Official Information Act. There can be no other excuse for the Minister of Education
failing to guarantee that she will reveal all the financial information that is useful, that is
critical, for the public to see. She would do th at only if she is being bullied by this $19
million cup of tea that forces an exploitative experiment on our most vulnerable
learners. We oppose the Education Amendment Bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: The chairman of the Iwi Education Authority came to this
Parliament. He is one of the most distinguished M āori educators in New Zealand. His
name is Dr Toby Curtis  and he says that M āori undereducation in this country is
institutionalised and expected. Well, we say it is institutionalised, but it is not expected,
and we do not like it. We do not like kids going through 11 years of education and, at
the end of 11 years of education, not bein g able to read and write. The Labour Party
Opposition, the apologist for the teacher unions, might think that that is OK, but we say
that it is not OK, because we want five out of five kids to have a world-class education.
The leader of the M āori Iwi Education Authority came to the Education and Science
Committee and he said to it solemnly that this bill is well overdue. He wants it to pass in
its total content.
Tonight is a celebration. It is a loss for the Labour Party, it is a loss for the Green
Party, and it is a loss for the losers of New Zealand First, but it is a big win for kids
struggling out there in an education system th at has doomed them to failure, and that is
the 20 percent of our kids who leave school with no  educational qualification
whatsoever.
Almost 25 years ago Parliament passed the Education Act 1989 and put the Picot
report into effect, giving us Tomorrow’s Schools. Parliament wanted to empower
educators and school committees. Parliament wanted to educate educators and school
communities, as well. It wanted to decentral ise and liberate the compulsory education
sector. The then Labour Government said th at reforms would addr ess inequality of
achievement, but the teacher unions cried foul. The teacher union s said that only
education experts like teacher unions, not parents, would be able to govern schools. We
on this side of the House say that on th is the teachers unions have got it wrong. The
schoolkids who are underprivile ged, schoolkids who come fr om deprived homes, and
Māori and Pacific schoolkids we are putting on  a pedestal tonight, because this bill,
promoted by the ACT Party and suppor ted by the National Party and the M āori Party,
no less—the M āori Party, no less—says that this is well overdue. In fact, the teacher
unions said that Tomorrow’s Schools was a first step in privatisation. I was in
Parliament 25 years ago when the teacher unions came here, and the apologists from the
teacher unions on that side of the House said th at it was the first step in the privatisation
of education, and no such thing is happening.
All these arguments, tired and worn out, are ringing in our ears. The truth is that the
union opposition to partnership schools has been  straight out of the old playbook. They
are the same tired old lines they trot out at any attempt at reform of the education sector.
Twenty percent of the education sector is an  institutional failure to the kids in that
sector tonight, and that is what the Iwi E ducation Authority came to the Parliament and
told us. We have a long tail of underachievement in New Zealand. I say that it is not
good enough, the ACT Party says that it is not good enough, the National Party says
that it is not good enough, and the M āori Party says that it is not good enough. Tonight
kids are the winners. The Labour Party me mbers are losers, the New Zealand First
10684 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
members are losers, and the Green Party me mbers are losers on this philosophical
debate, because Parliament, on balance, has said that we are going to change it.
It is shocking that any system could ta ke a child through their formative years and,
after 13 years in the system, turn out a student  who is functionally i lliterate and in no
way prepared for the modern world. Partners hip schools will make a real difference to
New Zealand’s most disadvantag ed students, and for the li fe of me I cannot understand
why the teacher unions and th eir apologists on the other side  of the House are opposed
to lifting the tide that floats all boats.
The policy is not an attack on our teachers, who, by and large, do a fantastic job. The
policy acknowledges the contribution of the 35,000 support staff in our schools who are
so frequently belittled by the Opposition b ecause they are not registered. They are
belittled—35,000 people who help out in schools every day of  the week are belittled.
We acknowledge them.
No one is saying that this is a quick fix. No one here is saying that there are not a
number of ways of addressing institutionali sed failure. We are not going to spend this
money on education and find that 20 percen t of the kids leave after 13 years of
education as failures. Every second M āori has not passed National Certificate of
Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 1. Ev ery second Pacific student has not passed
NCEA level 1. The decision will be based on the needs of students, as it should be, not
on the needs of teacher unions, and not on  the needs of the Labour Party - Green
coalition of losers.
Both the Ombudsman and the Human Rights Co mmission have been invited to work
with the Ministry of Educa tion on these contracts. Than kfully, Parliament was not
swayed by the Opposition’s attempt to limit the types of organisations that can run
partnership schools. Achieving educati onal improvements and being accountable
always mattered more than whether a partne rship school is run by a trust, charity,
business, iwi, or church group.
I want to thank Cam Calder, the chairman of the Education and Science Committee. I
want to thank the Prime Minister and Hekia Parata and her colleague Nikki Kaye for the
support they have given us, and I want to thank the M āori Party, because the M āori
Party does not want institutionalised failure amongst Māori any longer. The Māori Party
does not want kids to leave school after 13 years with no literacy and no numeracy. The
Māori Party wants aspiration for young Māori, and the Pacific Island representatives on
the other side of the House should be ashamed of themselves for not supporting this—
ashamed of themselves. Every second young Pacific student leaves school after 13 years
without NCEA level 1 maths or English.

items.speaker: I have good news for the House tonight

turn education into an opportunity fo r everyone, and to make sure that M āori and
Pacific kids can foot it with the best of the other kids in the schools and have the dignity

It is a big loss for the small-minded apol ogists for the schoolteacher unions opposite,
and it is a big, big win for kids up and down the country who are wondering what they
are going to do when they have had 11 years at school and they ca nnot read and cannot
write. Partnership schools will be establis hed in areas that experience significant
underachievement, where students are underser ved by the current system. I cannot for

want a world-class education for everyone. They can sling the abuse and they do not
like it, they can wear the lipstick and look good on TV and make a big impression and
they do not like it—
