items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: The reality is that this is an emotive issue. These are our
children we are talking about. That is why it is emotive.  These are the children whom
each one of us cares about. I have no doubt that members of the Government care about
the education of children. I have no doubt th at Mr Banks believes somewhere inside
10686 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
himself that this is a good policy. Unfortunatel y, as Sir Peter Gluckman just said earlier
this evening, this is not evidence-based policy—this is not evidence-based policy. Peter
Gluckman was here earlier th is evening in the Beehive theatrette promoting evidence-
based policy, so that downstream these decisions are endurable. This is not an endurable
decision.
New Zealand First needs to join with the Labour Party and the Green Party in issuing
a warning. That warning is: please do not mortgage your home to open a charter school.
Please do not put yourself in debt to open a charter school, because it is very unlikely
that you have a long future. Any best practic e developed inside a charter school will be
brought inside the State school system, and it is possible that you may want to shift
from a charter school to a private school, but, please, I beg you, do not put yourself in
debt to do this, because its future is too unstable.
If this policy was about targ eting those children who ar e achieving in the tail—the
stanine 1 to stanine 3—and if th at was whom these schools ha d to direct their services
towards, that would be different. If these sc hools had to provide something that is not
currently supported for those students whom Mr Banks refers to being in the “tail of
underachievement”—for example, dyslexic or dyspraxic children—that would be
different. If these schools had closed rolls only to target those students whom we are not
supporting well enough inside our  public school system, that  would be different, but
they are not. Catherine Isaac came to my  office and said: “No, no, no, no, we are
targeting middle New Zealand.” There is no money in decile 1, decile 2, decile 3,
stanine 1, stanine 2, and stanine 3 children. They are very intensive work—and they
deserve it—but you cannot skim a profit off them. So there lies the flaw. If this was not-
for-profit, that would be different. But none of those things are in side this Education
Amendment Bill.
I am still trying to find out who is driving th is bill, because it is not the New Zealand
public. Private schools’ rolls have not increased from the 5 percent for the last 30 years.
They have not increased. There is no more demand for that style of education, and yet,
possibly—possibly—this door was opened when the recession began in 2008 and
private schools’ rolls starte d to drop. It may be—it just  may be—because the public
system is doing so well. The public system is  doing so well, particularly over the last
few years with the extra supports that needed to be in place, and with more professional
development, compulsory professional de velopment, around Te Kotahitanga and Ka
Hikitia—Managing for Success, then we might have seen even further leaps inside the
public system. But, perhaps because the mainstream public school system is doing so
well, private schools are under pressure. Perhap s that is what is driving this, because
there is no appetite for it out in the real world.
I need to also issue another word of warni ng. Under this legislation it is not possible
to have a school for M āori. It is not possible to have a school for Pasifika students. This
is an open-door policy. Mr Toby Curtis and Mr Pem Bird think that they will take 23
successful kura from inside the curre nt Education Act 1989—and I believe my
colleague Metiria Turei made the Minister give us volumes in her answer today at
question time, while she was trying not to say something. Toby Curtis and Pem Bird—
who is the president of the M āori Party, and therefore the M āori Party has a conflict of
interest in this House—are intending to take, and I predict, 23 kura outside the
Education Act 1989 and turn them into charte r schools. They can then throw away the
current curriculum, deliver what they believ e is more culturally appropriate, and do
what they like.
The word is that there is a contract he re, though. The Minister  says: “There is a
contract. Trust us. Trust us be cause there is a contract.” Ea rlier today we had a debate
about a contract. That was a pretty big contra ct. It had key performance indicators in it,
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10687
it had levels of achievement that had to be reached, or  it would be stopped. Why should
we be confident, with our children, that th ese contracts will be any different? The point
is that we will not know the key performance indicator s—we will not know the key
performance indicators. If it is a primary sc hool, we have a 6-year window. We have a
6-year window in which to get it right. Ar e we doing it 100 percent right? No, we are
not. But $19 million is taken, currently, out of Vote Education. Instead of supporting
literacy support for 5-year-old s and 6-year-olds with an identified need, instead of
supporting dyslexic and dyspraxic children inside our systems, and instead of
supporting truancy officers to make sure children go to school, we have decided to open
another competitor.
The other word that is being bandied about, th e other thing that is said to calm us all,
and to calm the public, is that this is about “choice”. But, actually, to have true choice,
just as Dr Gluckman said earlier today, you need to be truly informed. You need to
know all the pieces of information before you can make a choice. There has been
information withheld from the New Zeal and public. For one thing, there is no
transparency around the “high-quality appli cants” for the 35 schools.  I happen to know
one school that has found itself on that list but  never asked to be on it. I find that very,
very interesting. Apparently it was asked to speak at an ACT electorate meeting, and the
next thing it knew, it had its name on a charter school list.
There are things that have not been sai d. I cannot believe—I choose not to believe
that my colleagues on the Education and Sc ience Committee truly support this bill. I
understand their circumstances. I understand why they have had to  stand and say what
they do—very little, to be perfectly honest, b ecause there is very little they can say. But
I am sad for them because their names will be  on this legislation when it passes through
this House.
The other thing I do want to touch on is the clause that has been inserted around
governance and around making boards of tr ustees responsible for the academic
outcomes of all students. I find that very interesting. It is interesting because—
[Interruption] Why the boards of trustees, is the question. They are not the professional
leaders of the school. They are elected pare nt trustees who are there to govern the
school, not manage it. The School Trustees Asso ciation has warned that this blurs even
further the line between governance and manage ment. Is it possible that what this is
about is the fact that the Minister can re move boards of trustees but cannot remove
principals or teachers? The Minister has had a problem implementing national
standards, and there are still schools—even  more schools now, after the farce of e-
AsTTle and other testing—that realise that national standards are flawed beyond repair.
So possibly the ministry has suggested this is the way to place pressure on, to make sure
the national standards will be met.
The final thing is that Mr Banks forgets that of the 20 percent of children in the tail, 5
percent are children with special needs. Ever y one of those children has an individual
education programme, to attain their best . But Mr Banks holds so much ignorance
around the field of education that it is impossible to have a conversation with him.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call on the third
reading of the Education Amendment Bill. This bill represents very, very positive
options and choices for the public. I just want to put it on record that the House has
heard the venom that has come from memb ers on the other side, who have spoken
against the communities that have shown a passion to take ownership of the
underachievement in education. I stand here to night to say that it would be a lunacy of
any future Government, if the Opposition we re to get into power, to do away with
communities taking ownership of the achievement of their young ones.
10688 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
So, on that basis, let us clarify a couple of  points that have been falsely represented
on the other side. They talk about unqualified teachers. Sadly, when you hear
Opposition members speaking, when they are sp eaking to their friends, they are trying
to sound angry because they want to be believed to be wedded to that side of the debate.
The truth of the matter is that those people who are unregistered teachers will have to
show outstanding qualities in teaching in orde r to be in a charter school. There will be
police vetting. There will not be secrec y around the Teachers Council vetting of
teachers. The State system is not the only solution.
What has ever happened to the Labour Opposition? It is not since 1989 that it has
had any vision. What have we seen coming out of the National Party? We have seen the
Industry Training Act, the New Zealand Qu alifications Authority framework, the
private training establishments, the trades academies, and more. It gives me great
pleasure to support this great step forwar d, this addition to the Education Act. I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: This bill—the Education Amendment Bill; from the
crew who tried to convince us  that bigger class sizes woul d be better for educational
outcomes—just about says it all. This is the same bureaucratic babble and nonsense that
those members tried to foist on New Zealand parents when they said that having more
children in classes and fewer teachers in cl assrooms would be better for educational
quality. Well, they were trying to pull the w ool over parents’ eyes then, and they are
trying to do the same  now. Well, actually, they are not even trying to argue, let us be
honest about it. National members cannot even  sustain more than 1-minute’s worth of
arguments for charter schools. They are so embarrassed by their feeble attempts.
I challenge the next National MP who gets on their feet to talk for 10 minutes and
argue for charter schools, and not do what Cam Calder did. He is the chair of the
Education and Science Committee, and he co uld not even utter the words “charter
school” when he gave his contribution. He wanted to talk about search and surveillance.
He would not even address the issue, the main issue, in this amendment bill, and that is
that the Government is borrowing a failed system from the United States, like National
does all the time with all of its policies. It  cannot come up with New Zealand - grown,
Kiwi-based success stories, so it looks to wreck our education system by borrowing
from a failed system in the United States. Is not that the National Party all over? Is that
not also John Banks all over, as well?
The shameful thing about this piece of legi slation is that the Government is putting
politics before our children. It is putting polit ics before our children and the quality of
the education system. It is trading in our  world-class public education system—it is
trading that in—for a failed system. I am goi ng to disagree a little  with Tracey Martin
from New Zealand First on this issue, b ecause she said there is no evidence around
charter schools. Well, there is. The evidence is that they fail. The evidence is that they
fail. In every other country where they have been implemented, they fail. So we have
got the evidence. We know that charter schools do not work.
What is it that the Government does not get about its so-calle d 20 percent tail of
underachievement, which it keeps going on  about? The Government says that 20
percent of our children do not achieve. John Banks agrees. He has to agree. That is the
line the Government has been trotting out for about 5 years now—20 percent. There is
another 20 percent figure I want to remind th at Government about. Twenty percent of
our children in Aotearoa live in poverty. Twenty  percent of children in the land of milk
and honey live in poverty.
What do Government members not get a bout the correlation between those two
statistics? Twenty percent of our child ren live in poverty, a nd 20 percent of our
children, the Government says, are failing. What do those members not get? Why do
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10689
they not join the dots? [ Interruption] Join the dots, Mr Banks, because you and that
party over there will do nothing about addr essing poverty. They are doing nothing. In
fact, they want to pretend it does not exist. That is the way that party wants to address
poverty. It wants to pretend it does not exist.
Instead of dealing with the root causes a nd addressing the issues that New Zealand
families are crying out for, in terms of  support for their children, what do those
members do? They come up with a solution that no one has asked for. They come up
with a solution over a cosy cup of tea—well, act ually, a corrupt cup of tea, as we learnt
afterwards. That is the solution they have come up with—charter schools.
No one asked for charter schools. Well, actually, I may be wrong there. I apologise if
I am wrong, because I think John Banks asked for charter schools. This was the dirty
deal that was stitched up between ACT and National, so that National could get back
into power. They did a dirty deal over Ep som, and they did a dirty deal, over the
teacups, with charter schools as well. That today, sadly, is what our children are being
exposed to. That is what future generations are going to be exposed to, because of that
dirty deal over a dirty cup of tea and that dirty deal over the Epsom electorate.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Oh, diddums!

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: John Banks says “Diddums”. That is a really mature contribution
to the debate. That is about the level of it,  in terms of maturity. This is the man, New
Zealand, who is wrecking your education system and his response is “Diddums”. That is
as good as it gets. I want everyone in New Zealand to understand who the mastermind is
behind charter schools. The best defence he can  come up with is “Diddums”. Well, that
about says it all.
On the select committee we had a briefi ng from a woman from New Orleans, and
Karran Harper Royal was her name.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: How bad was that!

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Mr Banks wants to know how bad it was. I think he needs to
listen up. It was pretty propheti c, what she told us—not path etic, but prophetic. It was a
prophecy. She warned us that in New Or leans what had happened was that the
Government there used the opportunity of a na tural disaster to close down a number of
State-funded schools.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: It sounds a bit familiar.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It sounds a bit familiar, does it not? Those State-funded schools
were replaced by these failing charter schools. She came to warn us that she believed
that exactly the same thing would happen in Christchurch: a natural disaster, and the
Government comes along and closes down State schools, and then opens up on those
same sites privatised charter schools without any accountability to the public.
What did we hear today from the Minister of Education? I think the Minister pretty
much confirmed that that is exactly wh at this Government has planned. Members
opposite know it—listen; you can hear a pin drop. They know it. They know that their
Government has gone about closing down State-funded schools in order to slip taxpayer
money across to charter schools run by their mates, without any accountability.
And let me say, while I am on that issue,  that John Banks trie d to pretend—and so
did the last speaker, Colin King—that some how these are going to be community-run
facilities, facilities run by the community for the comm unity. Well, they are not
required to have a board of trustees; not like State-run schools. They are not required to
actually give any information to the public about how the public’s own money is being
used in running these schools. There is only one reason why the Government would
want to hide that information—no, actually, I can think of two: one is it does not want
the public to know how their money is being misused, and, secondly, it does not want
the public to discover how those charter schools are failing.
10690 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
The Government makes a lot of  the contracts that are going to be made between the
Crown and these charter school operators, whoever they may be—and they could be
anybody, quite frankly, because there are no ru les, there are no regulations, and there
are no standards when it comes to who can run a charter school. Is that not right, Mr
Banks? There are no standards at  all as to who can run a ch arter school. There are no
standards. The Government is dropping the st andards. It will not let anyone understand
what is going on, because it has deliberately kept charter schools out of the purview of
the Official Information Act. And it expects us to believe that this bill is about
improving the education system.
Well, if it were an ounce about improving the education system, the Government
would be proud of it; it would not be hiding it . While I am on the subject of who would
be proud and not hiding, can I say “Shame on the M āori Party.” Shame on M āori Party
members for not being involved in this deba te and for putting their votes to something
they are not prepared to even come and speak to in the House. They have not made a
contribution to this debate. They are inst rumental in forcing this upon our wonderful
education system, yet where are they when th e rubber hits the road ? Where are they to
stand up and be counted on why they are putting their votes—

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: What are you doing?

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: —beside these schools? I can tell that member what we did. The
Labour Government funded te kotahitanga . We did not cut the funding, like his
Government is doing. He does not care at all for M āori achievement if he can be a
member of a Government that will cut the funding to one of the most successful
programmes for M āori students—te kotahitanga. That  member need not take that
attitude, because if he really meant what he said, he would not be doing that.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am astounded at what I have heard from
the previous speaker, Sue Moroney—actually, at what I have heard from everyone on
the Labour side and from their coaliti on partners, their mixed-ownership model
partners, the Greens. It seems that it is OK fo r them to have choice but they do not want
New Zealand parents to have choice. They  do not want to see parties like the M āori
Party actually trying to do something about th e one in five students who is failing. They
say partnership schools will fail, but they do not want us to do a nything about it. What
are they doing, and what did they do, about  the one in five who is failing? Their
argument holds no water, much like many other of their policies.
I want to focus on just one aspect of the Education Amendment Bill, which deals
with the surrender and retention components.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Oh, search and surveillance, here we go.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Well, if that member actually took a little bit of time to talk to some
people out there in the school community—pare nts, principals, and boards of trustees—
instead of swanning around this place, she wo uld find that it is a challenge out there.
This bill actually provides them with the meaningful tools that they need to keep
students safe and the learning environment conducive to learning. That is what this is
about—that is what this is about.
I think I have pretty much nailed my point on this, but can I just say, over the din and
the ranting I am hearing from the other side , that the search and surrender components
of the Education Amendment B ill are about providing the t ools that these schools need
to keep their environments safe and protec t the learning environments of those students
who are there to learn. The guidelines ar e something I encourage the Ministry of
Education and the school community to get on with and to get sorted, and let us make
our schools function and work well.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A split call. Louisa Wall—5 minutes.
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10691

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora. Thank you very much for this
opportunity to talk about what is titled th e Education Amendment Bill but for me is
actually the “Anti - Public E ducation Amendment Bill”. This  bill is gutting community
involvement in education. It is gutting parents’ involvement in their children’s learning.
I want to say, from living in a community like Manurewa, that my principals and my
teachers are incredibly dedicated and hard-working people, as Cam Calder knows. They
are dedicated and hard-working people. So what is the biggest challenge in communities
like Manurewa? As Cam will know, it is not th at our principals and our schools do not
have the best interests of our children at heart. The reality is that we have two cohorts of
children living in Manurewa—and my coll eague Sue Moroney touched on this. We
have children who come from stable families.  They are able to go to school day in and
day out. They may not have an early childhood education experience, but what we know
from Jane Milner and Redoubt North Primary Sc hool is that if they can have our kids,
who are, on average, 18 months to 2 years behind as 5-year-o lds, for up to 3 to 4 years,
those kids can catch up. Our children are clever . They just live in circumstances beyond
their control that mean that it is hard for them to go to school.
So we have a cohort of children who are stable kids and who come from families
living in homes as part of the community. They can go to school and they can succeed.
The other cohort of children is called unstable children. Th ey come from homes from
which some are enrolled in ni ne schools in 1 year. So wh at does the Government want
to say? The Government’s solution, in term s of charter schools, does not address the
underlying issues. The underlying issues ar e that families do not have access to
affordable housing. That is the primary issue. Transience is a huge issue in communities
like mine. The solution that this bill proposes is actually incredibly flawed, and it is also
scientifically corrupt. It is an incredibly di shonest piece of legisla tion. But at the heart
of this legislation you are actually eroding parents’ rights to be on boards of trustees and
to be part of solutions to ensure that their children are getting the best education.
I am proud to say that of my 29 schools, eight have had Education Review Office
reports that say that they do not  have to be visited for 5 year s. Why is that relevant to
this debate? It is relevant to this debate because what it says is that my schools—the
schools that Cam Calder visits—are run by pr incipals and boards of trustees who are
doing a fantastic job for our children. I want to acknowledge the work that our teachers
are doing and that wh ānau who work in Manurewa are doi ng to better our children and
their education. But the reality is that they  cannot control the social determinants of
those children. They cannot control the fact th at the children do not have a home. They
cannot control the fact that some of the parents in my community are in low-paid work.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: What on earth has that got to do with this bill?

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: This bill is about charter schools and partnership schools being
incredibly flawed and corrupt. Did you not hear me earlier? The solution that this
Government is proposing is pathetic, and it is not going to achieve anything for
communities in my electorate.
I want to conclude by agreeing with my colleague Sue Moroney about the M āori
Party. It is only because of the M āori Party that this bill will be passed. It has tools
within the current Education Act—sections 155 and 156—for kura kaupapa M āori to be
designated as special character schools. We do not need charter schools and partnership
schools in New Zealand, and we will repeal this legislation as a priority. Thank you.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I am very pleased to be able to take a call in the third
reading of the Education Amendment Bill on behalf of my colleague Catherine
Delahunty. I am pleased to report for the bene fit of the Hon John Banks that I am not
wearing any lipstick tonight, so, unfortunately, he will have to put his sexism aside and
listen to the content of my speech.
10692 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
I am glad to be having my say because, I have to say, this is one of the most
appalling bills to pass through the House in my  time in Parliament so far. Basically, at
its heart, this bill is a $19 million cup of tea.  It is the result of the deal between John
Banks and John Key, which allows for a single  member in this House to insist on an
unpopular, undemocratic, non-transparent la w change, which no one publicly
campaigned for before the election. That is the $19 million cup of tea that we are getting
tonight in the form of this bi ll. It is yet another example,  I think, of this Government
governing for the benefit of its mates, and, in this case, for its mate John Banks.
What is so abhorrent about th is bill? Well, I have got five things, and I hope I have
time to talk about them all. The first is that there is no  requirement for partnership
schools—yes, I will use the terminology—to have registered teachers in their schools. A
university degree is apparently enough, perhaps not even that, to teach children—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: No, they don’t even have to have that.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: —yes, not even that—in the vital stage of their education.
Teaching is a highly complex job, it is vitally  important, and it is a job that we should
value very highly. It is informed by theory, pedagogy, culturally appropriate knowledge,
and having the right skills to work with vulne rable learners, none of which are going to
be available to people who ha ve not trained as teachers and who are not registered
teachers. So this bill is undermining the teaching profession and with unregistered
teachers it is an experiment, essentially, on our kids.
The second reason that this bill is abhorrent is that it is not subject to the Official
Information Act. So we have got $19 m illion of public money being spent on these
schools with absolutely no level of public over sight on how that money is spent. There
is no transparency, there is  no ability for the Ombudsman to investigate complaints
about the schools, of which I am sure th ere will be many, and it is basically an
inexcusable lack of accountability for the use of public money in our school system.
The third reason that the bill  is abhorrent is the use of  public money for private
profit-making businesses, and it is  straight-out corporate welfare. It is handing taxpayer
money to private profit-driven companies to allow them to run schools for profit and to
pocket public taxpayer money for profit. They  can receive special  funding for certain
elements of that, including for students with disabilities, but they do not have to provide
any level of accountability that that money is actually spent on what they say it is going
to be spent on. They can pocket it as profit if they want to , and that is taxpayer-funded
public money.
The fourth reason that the bill is abhorrent is what we heard toda y, that it is rubbing
salt in the wounds of schools that have been  closed. Today we heard in question time
that, first of all, the Minister of Educa tion could not even remember signing her own
Cabinet paper that suggested closed schools w ould be the logical first locations for the
new charter or partnership schools. She did not remember signing that advice, but that
was her advice to Cabinet. Then, when she was questioned about it, she could not rule
out that she might use closed school sites in  Christchurch to open charter schools. After
everything else that she ha s put the school community in  Christchurch through—trying
to tell them that their schools are irreparabl y damaged or that they do not have enough
students to stay open, and then closing thei r schools—she is now telling them that she
might allow private for-profit charter schools  to open up on the sites of the schools that
she is about to close. Talk about adding insult to injury.
The fifth and final reason why this bill is so  abhorrent is that it is an ideological
solution in search of a problem. We have a great public education system in this
country, and it delivers some of the best results in the developed world, in terms of
public education. There is absolutely no ev idence, including from  the United States,
from where this model was imported, that charter schools will ac tually deliver any
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10693
better results for those most vulnerable learners whom those on the Government
benches like to trumpet in th is debate, as though they are going to be solving the
problem of inequality and education through the mechanism of charter schools. There is
no evidence that that is requ ired and that charter schools actually achieve that. It is
already possible to establish special charact er schools to meet particular community
needs under the Education Act. There is no need for this legislation. It is abhorrent and I
am very proud to speak in opposition to it.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): Thank you for the chance to speak on
this third reading of the Education Amendm ent Bill. We have heard a lot of talk,
particularly coming from the Opposition, us ing the word “ideology”—that this is all
about ideology. There are two general elements that you can kick into here. The first is
that this side of the House has not used th e word “ideology”. In fact, it has been straw
man or “straw person” politics—we have to be gender-neutral tonight. It has been straw
person politics, arguing what supposedly the Op position has said. That is not what it is
about. You see, the key with ideology is that you can flush it out pretty quickly. I
suppose I want to suggest charging that this has been more about the Opposition.
Firstly, the thing that you see when ideo logy comes from the Opposition is that you
know it is ideology because it is highly emotional, it is yelling and it is screaming, and it
is that belief from the ideological left that if you yell louder, somehow it makes your
point more valid. The second side—and we have been hearing again about ideology,
and I am reversing this b ack on to the Opposition—is around consistency. We have
heard the Opposition talk about special charac ter schools and State schools. We have
heard about integrated schools.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How about Catholic schools?
SIMON O’CONNOR: Yes, very good Catholic schools as well. Of course, the thing
is that if you want to be consistent, then  a further option really  is not a problem. I
suggested during the Committee stage that act ually these parties—the Labour Party and
the Greens—would have been fighting agains t integrated schools in the 1970s because
they are different. What they want, and they have talked about it themselves, is to have
their hands on a singular control. I also get the sense that they just want to keep on
talking.
The third element where you know the Opposition is coming from an ideological
side is proportionality. When you look at a ny argument, it is all about proportionality.
We have heard tonight the “Chicken Little” approach to politics from the—

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Chicken liver.
SIMON O’CONNOR: Chicken liver, even, possibly. It is sort of a pâté, maybe. But
the Opposition has said the sky is going to fall in. This is going to be the end of
education. This is going to be the end of  childhood. Somehow this  is going to destroy
New Zealand, this approach here that attempts  another addition to help one out of five
children.
The final side—the fourth side—you realise, is not about ideology from the
Government’s side but from the Opposition’s side , and that is threats. You hear threats:
“We are going to change this legislation come  hell or high water.” It is the same with
the whole casino thing: “We do not like it, so we are going to make threats.” So you can
see that ideology is being spoken about and accused of the Government, but, actually, it
is coming from the other side—lack of cons istency, lack of propor tionality, lots of
threats, and emotionalism.
This Government—and, I think, all sides of  this Government—supports teachers. It
has a respect for the teaching profession. A numbe r of the people on this side have been
teachers. A number of us have friends w ho are teachers. We have respect for the
teaching profession and what teachers engage  with. This bill is not about replacing
10694 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
schools; this is about an addition. This is not removing the current system; this is adding
on to it in the same way that our special character schools work. Tracey Martin was
talking about how we have got a number of people who have special needs who are well
catered for, but there are still options. So this is not about replacing, it is not even about
replicating; it is about an addition.
I think there are other elemen ts we need to consider. Ther e has been a lot of talk, a
lot of mix-up, particularly from the O pposition, around the whole registered versus
qualified side. The language from the Opposition has been very imprecise. This bill says
that being a registered teacher is not an absolute condition; being qualified is. I want to
challenge one of the last speakers who wa s suggesting that somehow the only way you
can teach is to have gone through teacher s college—the only way you can teach is
through teachers college. That cannot make sense—that cannot make sense.
People all through this House teach their childr en in all sorts of different ways. Each
and every one of us teaches and imparts knowle dge in different ways and not all of us
needed to go to teachers college to do this. We did not need to do that. In fact, even
when you look at something like traditi on, if you would even use that word
“tradition”—dare I use that in the House—ther e is an element of teaching, as tradition
comes from the root word, the etymology, “to pass on”. That is something that each and
every one of us—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: My mother was a teacher.
SIMON O’CONNOR: Yes, yes. His mother is a teacher.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: My brother.
SIMON O’CONNOR: His brother is a teacher.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Sister went to teachers college.
SIMON O’CONNOR : His sister has gone to teachers college, on this side of the
House. But, see, teaching is about pa ssing on. It is about tradition—handing on—and
that is the core of the teaching professi on. So this is not about not having qualified
teachers; this is about registered teachers. Just a couple of final points—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Thank goodness!
SIMON O’CONNOR: Oh, we go “thank goodness”. I co me back to the ideology
and contradiction—contradiction. This side—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Tautology.
SIMON O’CONNOR : Tautology, even—repetitious  tautology. They have been
yelling and crying, that side of the House, that someone will not take a call. And then
when someone dares to stand up, it is “Oh no, we  do not want to hear that now.” This is
all about control.
I want to come back to what I was saying in the Committee of the whole House. This
is taxpayers’ money. Individual taxpayers cont ribute to the education system. If those
individual taxpayers want to come together to form a school with their money, well, all
power to them. They are taxpayers. They are individuals. They are families. They want
this education system. Let us pass this bill. Let us put it into law. I welcome 2014.

4 Jun 2013 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 10695
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I move, That the Land
Transport Management Amendment Bill be now read a third time . I thank members of
the select committee, particularly the Tran sport and Industrial Relations Committee in
this case, for the work that they ha ve done on the Land Transport Management
Amendment Bill. It has been given a ve ry thorough examination and a number of
valuable amendments have been made.
The bill amends the Land Transport Management Act 2003, known as “the Act”, and
it also repeals the Public Transport Management Act 2008 and carries over its
provisions, as modified by the bill. The bill is part of the Government’s ongoing efforts
to cut unnecessary red tape and to create better, more effective legislation.
The bill has three main components. Firs t, it simplifies the Act’s planning and
funding framework. Second, it streamlines  the Act’s tolling and public-private
partnership provisions, and, third, it implements a new public transport operating model.
Key changes made by the bill are, first, to planning and funding. The bill amends the
Act’s planning and funding framework by making it simpler, more streamlined, and less
prescriptive. To achieve this, the bill fo cuses decision making on three key criteria:
effectiveness, efficiency, and safety. It al so combines the former five national and
regional transport planning documents into three main documents. The bill simplifies
the Act’s consultation provisi ons and enables regions to tailor their engagement
processes to specific situations. The bill also allows the New Zealand Transport Agency
to borrow against National Land Transport Fu nd revenue to finance projects with the
approval of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport, should circumstances
suggest there is a good case for borrowing and it is prudent to do so.
The bill also amends the Act’s tolling a nd public-private partnership provisions. The
bill simplifies and streamlines the Act’s fr amework for assessing tolling schemes and
processes for improving public-private partnerships. These changes will reduce
potential barriers to the use of the Ac t’s tolling and public-private partnership
provisions while maintaining r obust approval processes. In re spect of regional fuel tax,
the inefficient and impractical regional fuel tax put in place in 2008 is repealed.
Finally, the bill establishes the public transport operating model in legislation. This
model provides a new framework for building long-term partnerships between regional
councils and public transport operators to de liver public transport services. The model
will deliver more competitive public transpor t services that are less reliant on public
subsidy. Over time, public transport users will  see better integration of services and
better-quality services with more focus on customer needs.
The Land Transport Management Amendment Bill is an important bill and I am
confident that it will only improve land tran sport planning and decision making, as well
as ensuring that central and local governme nt get better value for money from their
investment in public transport. It will also support all of our effo rts to cut unnecessary
red tape to create better, more effective legislation. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I rise to take a call on th e third reading of the Land
Transport Management Amendment Bill and to reiterate that Labour continues to
oppose this bill. Despite putting up some excellent Supplementary Order Papers during
the Committee stage that would have improved this bill, the Government kept its head
down. It remains stuck in the tarmac, dedicat ed to building roads,  roads, and more
roads, to the detriment of everything else.
The truth is that this Government wants th is bill to pass so that it can borrow more
and charge more on toll roads. The bill clearly shows that the Government’s direction in
10696 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
land transport is to build more and more  unsustainable roads and spend more on
motorways to nowhere. It seems that the Government woke up one day and realised that
the roads of national significan ce projects are too e xpensive and that it is going to have
to borrow to fund them or make them all toll roads. That is the truth of why it needs this
bill. That is what is at th e heart of this bill. Without increasing petrol tax beyond CPI
adjustments, the New Zealand Transport Agency would need to borrow $930 million
over the next 5 years to keep  the roads of national signifi cance on track. That is $930
million over the next 5 years that would need to be borrowed.
Meanwhile, this Government continues to underfund local roading. I am sure we will
hear about more local roads in this debate. We will hear more about local roads in this
debate, and I know my colleagues have many a st ory to tell on that. The current level of
subsidy sees State highways receiving $142,5 09 per kilometre, compared with just
$7,573 per kilometre for local roads. How unbala nced is that? That just shows you that
what this Government is up to—

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: More and more highways.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Yes—more and more highways. It  is addicted to tarmac, and
does not care about the local people.
When you look at the purpose of this bill, it says it all. The Government has removed
references to words like “affordable”, “int egrated”, “safe”, “susta inable”, “accessible”,
and “one that promotes public  health, environment, and social responsibility.” During
the Committee stage we sought to understa nd why the Government thought it could
remove those criteria and re duce them down to three, whic h is what it describes as
streamlined, project-level, decision-making criteria—three criteria—to give effect to the
Government policy statement, and to be effective and efficient.
What is being cut out? Let us remember what is being cut out. “Affordable”—what
is wrong with “affordable”? I thought this was a Government that prided itself on being
fiscally responsible, but it does not want to have  that as a criterion in this bill. It does
not want to have the word “integrated”. It  has removed “integrated”, which is about
incorporating not only roads but also rail  and coastal shipping. Coastal shipping has
died a death under this Government. We  were making progress under the last
Government, and it has died a death under th is Government, which is so committed to
roads. It is not committed to rail in real terms; it just wants to make sure that we have no
other way of getting around except by roads.
The Government wants to remove the word “safe”. Surely we want a land transport
management system that is safe. What is wrong with “safe”?

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Look at the road toll.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Well, roads have not—[ Interruption] No, he does not. Maybe,
as that member was saying, the roads of nationa l significance should not be safe. Is that
what the member is saying? Is that what he is saying? Look, we just had a fantastic
weekend when nobody was killed on the road. Nobody was killed on the road, and that
is down to the hard work of many, many peopl e over many years. Certainly, I am sure
that the people who were responsible for the wonderful road safety we had over the
weekend will be very concerned to hear that  this Government does not think “safe” is a
decision criterion.
The Government has also removed the words “responsive” and “sustainable”.
“Sustainable” is a dirty word for this Govern ment. This is a word that this Government
does not like to use. It does not understand it, but I thought it might understand assisting
“economic development”. Would you not think th at a National Government that, again,
prides itself on being fiscally responsible , and that boasts al l the time about its
wonderful economic management, would want to have a criterion that requires land
transport management systems to assist economic development?
4 Jun 2013 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 10697
And “improving access and mobility” has gon e. I think we saw during urgency the
disgraceful performance of this Government and the lack of regard it has for people
with disabilities, and that is what this means—that is what this means. Removing
accessibility and mobility, not having those as crite ria, is a slap in the face to the people
throughout New Zealand who have disabilitie s and who rely on the Government to
actually recognise that for them to get around, we have to take special care and provide
special access.
And then there are other things, like social  responsibility. Of c ourse, they are dirty
words for this Government. I do not think it would understand what social responsibility
meant. Here is another one: “environmental responsibility”.

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: No idea.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: There you go. We had the Hon Maryan Street speaking this
afternoon about the Budget and about the fact  that nothing about the environment was
mentioned in the Budget speeches—no new initiatives, no new money. So I guess those
are our concerns about the bill. This is w hy we are very concerned about it and why we
continue to be opposed to it.
There are other things about the bill. It a bolishes the ability to have a regional fuel
tax. That is just another cynical attempt by the National Government to prevent the
Auckland Council’s plans for its transport sy stem. The Minister of Transport already
has complete control of whether a fuel tax is created. We know that Steven Joyce and
Gerry Brownlee do not get along with Auckland, but some of us live there. Some of us

mayor and council, to ensure that we ha ve a future transport system throughout
Auckland that is fit for purpos e, that will cope with gr owing populations, that does not
rely on building more roads when we do not have any more room, and that actually
extends public transport. But abolishing the ab ility to have regional fuel tax takes that

And, of course, local communities, under this bill, have less say in supporting

into the transport systems. We in Labour strongly believe that every community should
have the ability to have its say about its transport systems, but this Government is taking
that away, just like it is taking away other things that  underpin our land transport
system. It is taking away the right of comm unities to have a say on their local transport
systems.
So this bill will do nothing to fix the shambl es the transport portfolio has been in
since this Government took over, with years of wasteful mismanagement. The sad thing
about it is that future generations will pay th e price for the very, very stunted and short-
term thinking that this bill demonstrates . It is a missed opportunity, and it undoes much
of the good work that Labour did when it was in Government around progressing and
upgrading land transport management systems. It is a real shame, and that is why
Labour is opposed to this bill.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I just want to thank members of
the Transport and Industrial Relations Comm ittee and the Minister of Transport for the

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: You have taken over the Labour Pa rty policy on transport. It is
wrong, it is not what the public  wants, and you are going to lose votes for the Labour
Party. And those New Zealand First members there, who are still trying to work out
what transport actually mean s, you are also going to lose votes by sitting with those

This is a good bill. It is good for transport, it is good for the solutions that we want,
