items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: It is a shame that the senior member of
the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee, David Bennett, could not summon up
more thought, more intelligence, more subs tance, or even more wit in that last
contribution. It is really a shame that a bill as important and far-reaching as the Land
Transport Management Amendment Bill did not  get a more serious treatment from the
member opposite, who gave it only 3 minutes.
There are a number of reasons why the La bour Party opposes this  bill, and Darien
Fenton summarised them very well. It is true that this bill narrows the principal
legislation’s purpose statement a nd decision criteria in a way th at we feel is retrograde
and unhelpful to the future of New Zealand’s tr ansport system. It is true that this bill
reduces the say that communities all around Ne w Zealand have in setting the transport
priorities that they pay for with their petrol tax and their road-user charges. It is true that
this bill, perhaps most damagingly, opens the door and facilitates more long-term debt
and use of toll roads to f und a National Land Transport Programme whose priorities are
fundamentally wrong, and that is why we oppose this bill.
More than ever—more than ever—the tran sport system in New Zealand needs to
take account of sustainability. It needs to take account of social well-being, the needs of
4 Jun 2013 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 10699
communities, the environment, and economic efficiency. Unfortunately, what this bill
does is cement in place the very narrow and distorted definition of economic efficiency
that this Government has used to justify its roads of national si gnificance. The National
Government has gone on this motorway-building binge for the last few years, wasting
billions of dollars of ta xpayers’ money, building white elephant, duplicate, over-
engineered, and gold-plated motorway proj ects that will be an albatross around the
necks of future generations of motorists.
The bill also abolishes the regional fuel tax, which is just part and parcel of this
Government’s systematic stripping away of  the powers and the options that local
government might have to fund its own transpor t priorities. We have seen it recently in
the debate in Auckland, where within minutes  of the report of the Auckland Council’s
consensus-building group on funding options being released—and noting that he had
not even read the report—Gerry Brownlee, the Minister of Transport, ruled out the very
recommendations that that body of expert  opinion recommended, including a regional
fuel tax to fund Auckland’s future transport agenda.
But I want to focus the rest of my comme nts tonight on an issue that has not had
much attention in the debate so far, and that is a really insidious part of this bill, which
strips away the democratic rights of Aucklanders in setting the priorities of the transport
programmes, services, and infrastructure—tra ins, buses, and ferries—that they pay for
with their road taxes, with their road-user charges and petrol excise duty, and with their
rates. This bill takes away the power to make decisions about Auckland’s transport
system, and hands those powers to Cabinet. It puts those powers in the hands of the
executive, at the expense of local government  and the elected representatives of the
people of Auckland. I think that is just unforgivable.
It is just the latest move by this Government to clip the wings of the Auckland
Council, which it cannot abide. We have seen so many examples now that it is hard to
keep track of them. There is a whole debate going on about the response to the housing
affordability crisis in Auckland, and we will come to that on another day.
What this bill does is it strips Auckland Council of its right to determine the priorities
for spending what is currently about $459 mil lion a year. Thirty-three percent of the
rates that Aucklanders pay goes to Auckland Tr ansport. This bill takes away the ability
of Auckland Council to have a say in setting those priorities. It is the only council in the
country that is losing its democratic right. It is the only one, and why is that? It is
because this Government has a difficult, problematic relationship with Auckland
Council. The wrong guy won the mayoralty, and the Government has never ever got
over it. That is its problem, and it will come back to bite it.
There are two reasons why the measure in this bill is particularly offensive. The first
is that it amounts to a giant loss of acc ountability for that $459 million a year that
Aucklanders contribute out of their rates to  transport. They are losing representation
while they are being taxed. It  is taxation without represen tation. It is a fundamental
democratic principle that does not seem to be a matter of any importance to the National
Government. It is quite happy to say to Aucklanders: “Never mind what you think.
Never mind that 63 percent of Aucklanders want to see the city rail link built as a matter
of priority. We in the National Government  are going to impose this from Wellington.”
Gerry Brownlee, the “Minister of Gridlock”, from his comfortable ministerial office in
Auckland, is giving the big middle finger to 1.4 million Aucklanders and saying:
“Never mind what you think, 1.4 million Aucklanders. You pay your rates, you pay
your taxes, but I know best, and I am going to set your pr iorities for Auckland. Never
mind what you think.”
This Government loves to treat Auckland with contempt. It is its No. 1 sport. We saw
it, actually, right back in the setting up of the Auckland super-city, when Treasury and
10700 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
the Ministry of Transport advised Cabine t that Auckland Transport would be more
accountable if it was set up within Auckland Council as a department. But Steven Joyce
knew better. Steven Joyce advised Cabinet: “No, set Auckland Council up as a council-
controlled organisation—that way we can better control it.” That is exactly what this
Government has set out to do. It wants to control Auckland Transport by requiring in
this legislation that it act consistently with the Government policy statement. So
Auckland Transport will take its marching or ders not from the people of Auckland but
from Cabinet. That is what is going on with  this legislation. It is Cabinet telling
Auckland how it is going to run its city, and what the priorities are for its transport
system.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: They always do that.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: That is exactly right.
There is another basic principle of politi cs in Government called subsidiarity.
Subsidiarity means that deci sions should be made as close as possible to the location
where the consequences of those decisions  are felt by those people who live with the
daily consequences. It is Aucklanders who ha ve to live with the consequences of this
Government’s policies and its priorities. It is  Aucklanders who sit in traffic for an hour
in the morning and an hour at night because  this Government doe s not give a damn
about their transport system, and continues to want to impose a 1950s ideology of
suburban sprawl and motorways. That is the mindset of the Nationa l Party, and it does
not give a damn. It does not give a damn that Aucklanders are actually crying out for
something different.
I want to say something, to conclude, about  what National has done in the transport
area. It has poured billions of  dollars into gold-plated, wast eful motorway projects. It
has neglected public transport. Not a single new piece of public tran sport infrastructure
has been initiated since thes e turkeys have been on the Tr easury benches—not a single
piece of new public transport.  It is an absolute bloody di sgrace. National has neglected
rural roads. It has neglected State highways . It has run down KiwiRa il. And now in this
bill it is doctoring the legislative framework fo r our entire transport system in order to
take power away from local communities and give it to Cabinet. What an absolutely
disgraceful record. And I say to the National Government that it has gone too far. There
is not a shred of consensus left in the transport sector after 4½ years that this
Government has been in power.
If there is a good thing that comes out of  the wasteful, mismanaged, ideologically
blinkered management of transport by this National Government, it is that the next
Labour-led Government will lead major refo rm. It will lead major reform, and the
legacy of the National Government will lie in tatters. I say to the members over there
that all the things that you have done for the last 4½ years will be swept away, because
people do not want the kind of transport syst em that you have ushered in over the last
4½ years—not you, Mr Assistant Speaker; these people on the National Treasury
benches. There will be major reform. Peopl e will notice the difference. There will be
public transport in our cities. The local road s will be maintained properly. There will
not be billions of dollars wa sted on motorways, as the Na tional Government has done.
And that, actually, will be the legacy of that party’s tenure on the Treasury benches.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: I rise to speak on the third reading of the Land
Transport Management Amendment Bill. I would like to start out by talking about the
cost of transport, because I think it is so mething that Government members probably do
not know that much about. What we know fr om the regulatory impact statement and
from the Government books is that central government spends $3 billion a year on
transport infrastructure and services, and local government  spends $1 billion to $1.5
4 Jun 2013 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 10701
billion a year. So all togeth er we are talking about $4 bi llion to $4.5 billion a year of
spending on transport from local and central government.
Of course, that money that they spend co mes from New Zealanders. It comes from
petrol taxes, from road-user charges, and from  rates. But, of course, a much larger cost
is the cost of vehicles and fuel to run th em, so our road network does not work unless
households and businesses have vehicles a nd have fuel to run those vehicles. New
Zealand households and businesses are spendi ng in the order of $12 billion a year on
vehicles and fuel to run them.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Twelve billion a year. So wh ile the Government is taking
our tax money and spending it on transport in frastructure and spending in the order of
$4 billion a year, households and businesses are actually having to spend three times
that much on vehicles and fuel to run them. An d, of course, all of that contributes to our
current account deficit, because in this count ry we do not manufact ure vehicles and we
do not produce petrol that is used in the tanks of cars. Ev en if we did find oil off the
East Cape, we would not be using it in the tanks of our cars and trucks, because we
produce light sweet crude oil here in New Zealand and we export all of it.
So the total cost of our transport system is more than the amount  of taxpayer money
that the Government is spe nding on infrastructure. It is the money that households and
businesses have to spend on vehicles and fuel  to run them because they have no other
choice, because subsequent Governments have spent all of the money on infrastructure
for vehicles and cars rather than looking at  a more cost-effective solution, which would
look at what the best way is to move peopl e and goods. What is th e most cost-effective
way to move people and goods? What the Green Party is advocating is simply a rational
approach to assessing the problem of what the most cost-effective way is to move
people and goods.
It turns out that since we ha ve a very extensive road sy stem, the biggest bang for our
buck is going to be in improving the productivit y of our road system and of our existing
rail network. That means investment in capit al expansion of our ra il network so that we
can deliver better servic es for exporters who are using rail freight to get their products
to market and also investment in passenge r transport and safe walking and cycling,
because New Zealanders would actually like thei r kids to be able to walk and cycle to
school, but they simply do not have the choi ce. And, of course, it is much more cost-
effective to provide safe walking and cycling infrastructure than it is to constantly
increase the supply of roads for more and more vehicles.
We live in an interesting time. It turns out that the trends of the past 50 years are no
longer continuing in the direc tion that they were going in. Yet another report has come
out of the United States, there have been re ports from Australia, and there have been
reports here in New Zealand that show that the fundamental drivers of transport demand
are changing. What we have seen is absolu tely no increase in traffic volumes on State
highways since 2004. We have seen no increase in heavy-vehicle traffic volumes since
2007. This is an opportunity that the National Government could be seizing to catch up
on the lack of investment in alternatives—t hat means safe walking and cycling, public
transport, and rail freight. Al l of that enables our transp ort network to work more
efficiently. But instead it has declined to take a rational approach to the assessment of
transport infrastructure.
What it has done through the Government Policy Statement on Land Transport
Funding is have three measures by which it is goi ng to define the effectiveness of the
projects: one is efficiency, one is strategic fit,  and one is effectiveness. Efficiency is the
benefit-cost ratio, or BCR. That is the amount of benefit the project provides divided by
the cost; that gives yo u the benefit-cost ratio. What we  have seen is that the vast
10702 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
majority of spending from the National Government on transport infrastructure has very
low economic efficiency. The Ne w Zealand Transport Agency has that data available. I
have brought it up in the House many times. We have seen the rela tive benefit of our
spending start to decline, and it is actua lly all very low right now because the
Government is prioritising projects that do not have very great benefi ts relative to their
costs.
But it justifies these projects on two other criteria: strategic fit and effectiveness. The
strategic fit means whether they fit the strategy as defined by the Minister. The Minister
of Transport said the strategy is to build the roads of so-called national significance,
which are just some pet project motorways th at the Government thinks are going to win
it votes. So it is a very circular logic, obviously, because to meet the strategic fit when it
is defined as building this particular mo torway—well, only building the motorway is
going to meet that strategic fit. It is a bit of circular logic there in terms of what the

items.speaker: Minister has said
items.text: “We want to build these motorways. Never mind that they have very
low economic efficiency; we will say they ha ve high strategic fit because the Minister
said we had to build them.” Effectiveness is very similar. Effectiveness is how effective
the project is at achieving the strategic fit. We have got tw o circular logic reasons for
justifying projects. We have one that is about economic effi ciency, and by that test the
roads of so-called national significance absolutely fail.
Unfortunately, we are talking about the singl e largest bit of spending in the National
Infrastructure Plan. When the National Gove rnment talks about its plan for lifting our
economic competitiveness and productivity, it often refers to investing in productive
infrastructure, but about 90 percent of the money it is spending on productive
infrastructure in the National Infrastructure Plan is on these roads of so-called national
significance, which have low economic efficiency. It is spending tens of billions of
dollars on projects that have very little benefit relative to their cost. There is an
opportunity cost. Most people do not see the opp ortunity cost of not spending that $10
billion on projects that would have greater benefits and actually re duce the costs that
New Zealand households and businesses are ha ving to spend on transport. Instead of
reducing the costs that we are spending on  transport by investing the money in a
network that works more efficiently, the Government has decided to spend the vast bulk
of the money on new infrastructure—on a few projects that will win it votes.
There is one other point that I would like to  raise right now, and that is clause 14 of
this bill and what it does. Clause 14 of this bill takes away the right of regional councils
to determine the strategic direction for transport in their areas. In particular, it takes that
away from Auckland Council and gives it to Auckland Transport. Clause 14 says that
the strategic direction they are setting for transport in their region has to be consistent
with the Government Policy Statement on Land Transport Funding . Of course, the
Government policy statement is written by th e Minister, who just says: “We want to
build these projects not because they are eco nomically efficient, not because they are
going to deliver benefits for the country, but because we think they are going to win us
votes.”
So what the National Government has done with this bill— there are many bad
aspects to this bill—is take away the ability of local ratepayers to determine what their
money is going to be spent on. It also takes away the right of Aucklanders to determine
what their money is going to  be spent on, what transport solutions are going to work
best for them, and it puts it all in the hands of the Minister , who is writing his
Government policy statement on a whim.
Ultimately, those roads of so-called national significance in the Waikato, north of
Auckland, and in Wellington are not going to be used by very many people, and they
are certainly not being paid for by the users.  If you look at the traffic volumes on these
4 Jun 2013 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 10703
routes, they are much smaller than the averag e daily traffic volumes on an arterial in
Auckland. Auckland Council will not even have that much money to spend on
upgrading those arterials or investing in productive infrastructure that would mean there
were fewer cars on those arterials. Ultimately, what is going on here is the National
Government is saying to Auckland that it is not going to let it have its regional fuel tax,
it is not going to let it fund the solutions that would actually work for its communities; it
is going to make its rates be spent on Nationa l’s electoral priorities and it is going to
make sure that the fuel taxes of Aucklanders stuck in traffic well into the future are
going to pay for some very low-value motorways. Thank you.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am pleased to pick up after the member
Julie Anne Genter has resumed her seat. She talked about circular logic. What happens
when the member speaks is that the logic go es round in a circle, because what she says
makes so little sense that by the time I am speaking I am actually seeming like quite a
luminary, so I appreciate the member’s contribution to this debate on the Land
Transport Management Amendment Bill.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: It ain’t as good as you make out.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Bring it on—bring it on. The Land Transport Management
Amendment Bill goes to the heart of openi ng up the highways and byways that are
fundamental to the economy of this country . The members over there say we should all
be travelling around on unicycles or buses  or something—I do not know—assuming
somehow that they must levitate, that they  are hoverbuses or something, because buses
actually need roads as well. But so does a region like Northland, where $800 million of
that Northland economy makes its way to Auckland via State Highway 1. The State
Highway 1 roads of national significance project is a project this Government is
committed to, and this bill goes to the heart of  saying that this is about getting priorities
and synergies right in terms of economic priorities, because when we do not, what we
know is we end up with clogs and bottlenecks, and every Aucklander will know that.
For every member on that side of the House who says they are going to get rid of the
Pūhoi to Auckland road, the party vote fo r the National Party goes through the roof,
because everyone in Northland knows that the P ūhoi to Wellsford road is so important
to Northland’s economy. I commend this bill to the House.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : I am surprised that the last speaker, Mike Sabin,
gave a 1½ minute speech on such an impo rtant bill. I felt th at the speech was
undercooked, unpalatable, and indigestible, and so is this bill. The Minister of Transport
said that the Land Transport Management Amendment Bill is about cutting red tape and
saving money. In fact, it is about much more  than that. It makes some fundamental
changes. It alters the object ives of the Land Transport Mana gement Act. It changes the
funding framework for land transport activities, including roading, public transport, and
road safety; it repeals regional fuel tax provisions; it changes the framework for
assessing toll road schemes; and it establishes a policy framework for the relationship
between regional councils and public transport operators.
So I am starting first with the objectives of the New Zealand Transport Agency. The
bill changes those objectives from the achievement of “an affordable, integrated, safe,
responsive, and sustainable land transport syst em” to the achievement of “an effective,
efficient, and safe land transport system ”. The deletion of the words “affordable”,
“integrated”, and “sustainable ”, and all that those terms mean, will be a huge mistake
for New Zealand. Essentially, the bill means that  the Government is interested only in
saving money as its first priority, but, actua lly, much more is at stake. The agency
should be seeking much better integration of transport modes. As the era of the
dominance of fossil fuel transport comes to  an end—and it certainly is, mostly because
of the increasing costs and risks of producti on, and the increased competitiveness of
10704 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
alternative energy sources. As the dominance of  the use of cars for peak-time travel is
increasingly non-viable in the big cities, especially at peak times, and as the
competitiveness of other modes and the huge increases in the cost of the road network
expansions and maintenance continue, then, increasingly, it is going to be necessary to
ensure a properly integrated system, so that  the best use can be made of all modes and
of the alternatives to more and more car s and bigger and more expensive motorways,
which is what the Government’s agenda is really about.
Similarly, it is essential for New Zealand to  design a transport system, especially for
freight from one end of this country to th e other, and especially also for personal
transport at peak times in the larger cities, so  that the system is sustainable. That means
economically, socially, and environmentally sust ainable, and if that ceases to be an
objective, as proposed in this bill, then the vast effects of the tr ansport system will not
be adequately controlled or mitigated. As a result, the very environment that we rely
upon for healthy lives and a good quality of life will be significantly degraded, as,
indeed, it has been in many other countries in the world.
The bill will also entrench the current situ ation that has been with us for decades
under successive National and Labour Governments, in which we do not have a genuine
and comprehensive New Zealand transport st rategy. The intent of the bill, under which
the Government will issue a Government policy statement on land transport, will not be
a sufficient basis upon which the planning an d funding of our future land transport
needs and options can be properly assessed. La nd transport will continue to be, I think,
a political football, kicked about in different  directions by whichever political flavour is
in power at any given time. It will ensure th at there is no coherent long-term strategy
that we can work towards. It will mean the wasting of huge amount s of public funds on
doing what we have always done: failing to provide for fundamental future changes that
will be imposed upon us by global conditions and developments.
We need an entirely new approach that converts our system to  one that, over time,
firstly, makes better use of our vast rene wable energy opportunitie s, especially to
produce electric power; secondly, reduces the dependence on imported liquid fuels; and,
thirdly, replaces more clogged motorways with attractive, safe, comfortable, and
affordable public transport options, as well as  facilitating more cyc ling at peak times.
The bill is going in entirely the wrong direction.
We should be learning from the lessons of  other countries, where the headlong race
to build more road capacity has resulted only in more and more demand, especially at
peak times. You only have to look at cities li ke Los Angeles to see that—the city that
has basically destroyed its own environment with the demand for the use of the motor
car.
You can also see, on the same west coast of the United States, the city of Portland,
which shows the right way to go. I went there and saw where they stopped building
more motorways. There is actually an off -ramp that is cut off and does not go any
further, because at that time that city decided on a new direction, the sort of new
direction that New Zealand should be going in. That city provided a very
comprehensive light rail system for its popul ation, which is now extremely popular and
goes to most parts of that city—a city, by the way, that is not too different in population
from our own city of Auckland. The effect of  feeding demand with capacity is a vicious
circle that costs vast sums of capital expe nditure and increased maintenance costs, and,
in addition, causes very large increases in ex ternalities such as th e cost of accidents,
health care, and deaths, and increased cost s in relation to pollu tion, waste, delays,
community severance, business dislocation, and so on and so on.
I also note that some of the best aspects of regional transport administration will be
removed by this bill. Firstly, the non-voting representatives of a prescribed list of
4 Jun 2013 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 10705
interests as members of regi onal transport committees ar e removed altogether. This
reinforces this Government’s disregard for the integration of land transport modes and
its determination to favour road transport over all other modes through planning and
funding mechanisms. From my experience, whic h in local government is considerable,
the quality of the input of volunteer experts in public transport, transport safety, cycling,
walking, business operators, transport opera tors, the Automobile Association, and on
facilities for disabled people was very significant and is too valuable to lose. Worse still
is the intention to remove th e option of regional fuel ta xes, and that means that a
regional council will no longe r be able to persuade its population in favour  of such a
tax, which could offer an inexpensive, eff ective, and fair way of funding important
regional transport options. That will be lost too.
Finally, one has to wonder what is really behind these chan ges. It seems to me that
this Government is excessively influenced  by road transport interests. New Zealand
First is focused on a modern, sustainable tr ansport system for New Zealand. This bill
will not deliver that. We will vote against it.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I commend this bill , the Land Transport
Management Amendment Bill, to the House. We should pass it.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I rise to take a ca ll on the Land Transport
Management Amendment Bill. I begin by e xpressing my considerable disappointment
in the last member who spoke, Chris Auch invole, a member who in the past has
attracted my admiration and, indeed, on occasions, respect for his worthy contributions
to this House, but that speech, frankly, is an embarrassment. But it is more than an
embarrassment, because it demonstrates the ongoing contempt and disrespect in which
this House is held by members of this Gove rnment. To stand up in the third reading of
this bill, an important bill that makes radi cal changes to the administration of land
transport policy in this count ry, with a cursory, barely tw o-sentence submission by that
member is, frankly, a disgrace. Mr Auchi nvole knows better, as, indeed, do the leaders
of his party in this House tonight. It is in cumbent, of course, on the Opposition to take
the debate on these important points.
This bill makes considerable change to th e administration of land transport policy in
this country. It changes, amongst other th ings, the purpose of the primary legislation
and, therefore, of the New Zealand Transpor t Agency. In what has until now been an
agency that has been driven by a sense of a comprehensive approach to land transport,
an integrated approach to land transport, this bill now minimises it and reduces it, in the
reductionist sort of approach that this Government favours,  to a much narrower set of
parameters and drivers. It replaces what is a comprehensive and integrated approach to
transport with one focused almost entirely on efficiency, whatever that means. So it
changes our approach to road planning. It introduces scope for more tolling and,
therefore, for the privatisa tion of more roading, over an d above the approach that
typically, until now, has been taken, which is to regard roading, in a long, narrow
country like New Zealand, as being integral to our total transport networks. But this bill
will replace that.
You know, the irony of that is, of course, that only weeks ago—only weeks ago—we
had rammed through this House, rushed th rough under great urgenc y, legislation that
will increase excise duties on petrol by 3c a ye ar for the next 3 years on the basis that it
was needed for transport funding, but, indeed, what this bill does is  give greater scope
for toll roads and the privatisation of roadi ng. So we cannot even get consistency in the
approach that this Government adopts. We cannot get members opposite to defend this
bill—to defend the approach taken in this le gislation—so that we can better understand,
and so that the members of the New Zealand public who are tuned in  tonight, on this
cold, windy, “haily” night, when people have got nothing better to do than to listen to
10706 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
Parliament, can understand. The citizens of New Zealand will be none the wiser from
members of the Government, who choose not to  defend this important and this critical
piece of legislation. What a disappointment—what a disappointment.
I want to comment too on the other thing that, of course, this bill does. This bill from
this Government, which purports to be th e Government of regional voice and local
voice, provides for and portends the greater centralisation of roading decision-making. I
know that Mr Auchinvole, now that he realises  the folly of his ways, is alarmed at that.
He had not understood that that  was in the legislation, and he expresses in his facial
expressions great alarm and horror at that prospect. I can see it—I can feel it from here.
But I would be remiss in my duties if I di d not come to the House tonight to talk
about State Highway 3 and north  Taranaki, because they will be sorely affected by this
legislation—sorely affected. I want to talk about Taranaki, my t ūrangawaewae, the area
that is dear to my heart and close to my mind right now. I wa nt to say that in Taranaki
what we desperately need is a sense of coherence and cohesion in our roading planning,
and this bill will not give it to us—this bill w ill not give it to us. What we also need to
ensure in Taranaki and on State Highway 3 is that the local voice is heard, and this bill
will deprive the people of Taranaki of that opportunity. You see, we need a good,
coherent plan for State Highway 3, that section north of New Plymouth, and not just the
Waiwhakaiho bridge and the 100- odd metres of that bridge and the stretch to Vickers
Road but the 100 kilometr es through to the lit tle village of Piopio, wh ich is actually in
the King Country—it goes from New Plymouth to  Piopio there. I also want to mention
that little stretch of road just north of H āwera around Normanby bridge, because that
has been a big challenge to the people of Taranaki, as well.
Fifty-seven percent of the Taranaki ec onomic output is geared towards export.
Whether it is for oil and gas, or dairy, or so me of the engineering activities that are
there, 57 percent of the Tara naki economy is geared to wards the export economy. That
is twice the national figure. That is the significance of Taranaki  and, therefore, the
significance of the Taranaki infrastructure. We need roading that reflects the economic
contribution that is made by the people of Taranaki. The province of Taranaki produces
the highest GDP per employee in the country—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: That’s right—$120,000 per FTE.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is the highest GDP per employee in the country. Cam
Calder, who once hailed from that great re gion and who made the mistake of settling
way further north of that region, knows. He is  ashamed to be living in a region that is
making far less of a contribution per capita than the people of Taranaki. One of the
consequences of having a region that contributes so much to the economic well-being of
the country and that contributes so much to our GDP, and whose employees contribute a
disproportionately greater amount than any ot her employee in the country, is, of course,
that it demands a skilled international workforce. Those people are travelling up and
down the roads of New Zealand, and, therefore, in and out of  Taranaki, all the time. Of
course, the products of Taranaki—not only the goods that come off our farms but the
products of our heavy engineering industry—demand good-quality roads, and we do not
have them.
Here is what the local economic development agency said about State Highway 3
only last year. This is Venture Taranaki, the local economic development agency, which
is one of our best economic development agencies in the country. Here is what it said in
its report on State Highway 3 last year: “B ut there are some roadblocks that are
preventing the Taranaki economy from meeti ng its growth aspirations and thereby
contributing to the national economy. Our re gion’s roading network, particularly the
central artery of State Hi ghway 3—between Taranaki and the Waikato, and then on to
Auckland—is failing to fulfil its economic poten tial.” It went on to sa y, because it is by
4 Jun 2013 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 10707
intelligent people: “Where considerable effort has been made to get central Auckland
moving, insufficient attention has yet been given to reviewing the critical links
connecting Auckland to the rest of New Zealand—and thereby New Zealand to the
world.” That illustrates the problem for Taranaki.
The people of Taranaki will l ook at this bill and they will  say: “There is nothing in
this bill for us. There is not hing in this bill that will improve the prospects of State
Highway 3 for us.” This Government is doing nothing for Taranaki. It talks big and
large about Taranaki and about the contribu tion that it is making, but the reality about
the National Government running New Zealand in 2013 is that it could not give a toss
about State Highway 3 and the infrastructure in Taranaki. It talks long and large about
that region that contributes di sproportionately to the great benefit of this country, but it
will do nothing for the people of Taranaki to improve their roads.
That is an issue that the people of Ta ranaki and New Plymouth are getting angry
about and agitated about. I am talking to th em all the time, and they are going to see
some action. They are going to see some ac tion from the Labour Party. When Labour
leads the next Government, we will see action on State Highway 3, on Mount
Messenger, on Awakino Gorge, and on all that stretch of road. That  stretch of road
includes 65 kilometres of road heading north without a single passing lane. What person
travels 65 kilometres in this country wit hout a passing lane? On ly the people of
Taranaki, and they have had enough and they want it changed. This  bill will not do it,
and we will be—
Hon Damien O’Connor: West Coasters do.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: The West Coasters do. We will change this legislation to
ensure the people of Taranaki  have a better voice, a str onger voice, and soon they will
have a stronger MP representing them in Parliament.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: Improving our nation’s infrastructure is a
significant part of this Government’s Busi ness Growth Agenda. The key aims of this
legislation, the Land Transport Management Amendment Bill, are to simplify the way
transport projects are planned, funded, and under taken; to eliminate the duplication that
exists throughout the system; a nd to better align the region al and nationwide strategies.
I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Gerry Brownlee said in his opening remarks that
this bill, the Land Transport Management Amendment Bill, was about cutting red tape
and saving money. Well, I think we would ca ll that an exercise in political spin,
because, under this piece of legislation, the Government has to do only three things—
that is, give effect to the Government policy statement in terms of transport, for any
transport decision that the Government makes to be effective and efficient. So I guess
when you consider what the Transport Agency used to have to take into consideration, it
is cutting a lot of red tape. But let us l ook, because it is always the case with this
Government that the devil is in the detail—the  devil is in the detail. What kind of red
tape are we cutting here? The Transport Agen cy used to have to take safety into
consideration. It used to have to take that in to consideration, but th at is red tape under
this Government so let us get rid of that. After Queen’s Birthday weekend, during
which we had no deaths on our roads—an d congratulations on that to everyone
involved—we are removing the need for safety to be taken into consideration when this
Government is making its roading decisions. Under this Government, the safety on our
roads is red tape, so it should be cut.
Let us look at what else the Government is removing from those things that we have
to take into consideration. Our roading solu tions are being integr ated. So now we are
10708 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
just going to keep building more and more motorways. Do not worry about what freight
we move on the sea. Do not worry about our air transport. Do not worry about our rail
transport. Let us just blindly keep building roads. That is exactly what this National
Government has been doing. And, funnily enough, we also no longer need to take
account of—because this Government thinks that it is red tape—the environmental
responsibility that we, as New Zealanders, have around the building of our roads. We do
not need to worry about the environment any more when building our roads. Let us just
build it whatever happens to the environment. Let us just do it. Do not worry about it,
because, under this Government, being environmentally responsible is red tape. Let us
cut it. Let us get rid of it. It is gone in this bill.
And one that I am going to get into more de tail around what is happening in my area
is that this Government says that it no l onger has a social responsibility when it is
building roads in our communities. So damn the people and damn the effects that the
roads will have on communities. Do not worr y about the people. Let us just build the
road. Let us just get it done. The Government  no longer has to take that into effect. The
feelings of people in those communities are re d tape, so let us cut them. Unfortunately,
that has been the situation for the communities of Raumati South, Raumati Beach, and
on the Kāpiti coast, where this Government wants to build the Kāpiti Expressway.
Mr Brownlee also said that this b ill was about saving money and economic
development. Well, that is not necessarily the case, because the Government’s plan to
build the expressway rolled over the top of a $350 million plan that Labour introduced
late in its last term. This National Government introduced an expressway, a monstrosity,
through the K āpiti coast, which is going to cost New Zealanders $515 million, a
considerable amount more than what was planned. When you talk in terms of the
economic benefit of the K āpiti Expressway, which this Government is going to build, it
is a dog. A leaked report last year from the engineering consultants Beca Group showed
that the economic benefit ratio of the K āpiti Expressway is 0.2. For every $1 that New
Zealand taxpayers spend on this road, we are going to get an economic benefit of just
20c. In terms of economic developmen t and a good return for money, the K āpiti
Expressway is an absolute dog. The New Zeal and taxpayer is going to lose money by
spending money on this expressway, when what  we could have had was a better local
solution for the people of Kāpiti.
One of the things that this bill does is it removes the local voice from communities
when transport solutions are being offered by this Government. This is absolutely a
trend of this Government’s and that is very, very sad.
I want to just go back to the K āpiti Expressway because it was a funny twist of
events. When the National Government came into power, the member up in K āpiti, the
member for Ōtaki, Nathan Guy, was absolutely cool  with Labour’s plan. He wanted the
Western Link Road. He said he was working hard with the local mayor to get this
project started because the funding had been allocated and the community wanted this
road. Unfortunately, Steven Joyce and the National Party’s plan  to keep building
monstrosity roads rolled Mr Guy, and th e Western Link Road turned into the K āpiti
Expressway. It is another example that this Government is blindly building motorways.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: I rise to take the last call on this bill, the Land Transport
Management Amendment Bill, for the Greens. We will be opposing this bill because, as
the House has heard from my colleague Julie A nne Genter, it is completely flawed. It is
weighted towards roads, roads, and more ro ads as the only transport option. It allows
this Government to borrow to fund infrastruc ture that may not stack up economically. It
allows for public-private partnerships and ro ad tolling, so it privatises more of the
public purse. Worst of all, this bill once more strips decision making away from
Auckland.
4 Jun 2013 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 10709
What is it about this Government? Why doe s it hate Auckland so much? One of the
first things this Government did when it came into power was to remove Auckland’s
regional fuel tax. It was being collected to invest in public transport—things like the
electric trains—and was an opportunity for Auckland to save up for the central rail link,
which has been on the agenda for years. In the Auckland Council’s submission to the
Transport and Industrial Relati ons Committee it specifically asked to retain the ability
for the council to gather regional fuel taxes because, as the council said in its
submission: “It is important to not pre-em pt the outcome of Auckland’s investigation
and consultation process in relation to a lternative transport funding mechanisms, by
removing one of these mechanisms. Auckla nd Council considers that the removal of
regional fuel tax as a potential funding opti on could be inconsistent with consultation
principles established in case law.”
This bill not only undermines the council’s abili ty to raise mone y for transport
options, but it also says that whatever deci sions the council makes about the spending
priorities it may have, they have to be consistent with the Government’s policy
statement. As noted in the verbal subm ission from the Auckland Council, this
provision—what the Government is trying to do here—cuts across section 15 of the
Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009, which states that the governing body
of Auckland Council is responsible and demo cratically accountable for setting transport
objectives in Auckland.
The ratepayers in Auckland contribute about $400 million a year to Auckland
Transport for transport infrastr ucture. I remind the House that it is not just roads. It is
actually public transport, walki ng, and cycling options. It is not just the roads that the
Minister may have chosen, for dodgy, uneconomic reasons. I spoke with the chair of the
Auckland Transport board today,  councillor Mike Lee, who sa ys that this Government
has deliberately singled out Auckland in this piece of legislation and has at least been
consistent in its approach to dismantling any type of democracy for the region.
The super-city legislation was the first go the Government had. The legislation for
the forced amalgamation also created the council-controlled orga nisation, Auckland
Transport, which is now, with this legi slation, fast becoming a Government-taking-
control organisation. We have seen since then that the Government has sought to
undermine Auckland Council in every way—in the Resource Management Act changes,
in the decision-making process around the unitary plan, in the changes to the Local
Government Act, and, more recently, with the housing bill that will force Auckland into
more urban spread, when Aucklanders want a compact city.
The Auckland Council submission points out th e potential for conflict, when it says
in its submission that “The provisions relating to the Auckland Regional Land Transport
Plan need to take into acc ount the different governance arrangements in Auckland and
the existence of the Auckland (Spatial) Plan.”, which was required of it by this
Government when it set up the super-city. This  Government has inte rfered so much in
Auckland that it is fast becoming the worst nanny State Government in history.
We will not be voting for this bill. It cedes  power to the Government, so that it can
give more power to its vested interests. The Skycity deal is a classic example of that.
With this interference there is less contro l for ordinary citizens over their environment,
and indeed over their lives. We will not be voting for it.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): I thought we were actually discussing
the Land Transport Management Amendment B ill. I am not quite sure what was going
on there. You see, the key to land transport is ultimately about  integration. That is what
this bill does.
10710 Land Transport Management Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
They always say that a journey starts from  A and moves to B. Well, here we are at
the third reading. We have moved from A thro ugh to B, so I commend this bill to the
House.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Land Transport Management
Amendment Bill be now read a third time.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I move, That the Employment
Relations Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee to consider the Employment Relations Amendment Bill.
This bill implements the Government’s policies aimed at a flexible and fair employment
relations framework for both employees and employers. The bill c ontinues our strong,
unrelenting focus on reducing complian ce costs and unnecessarily burdensome
regulation. We want to ensure that empl oyers have the confidence to compete and
expand, while key protections fo r employees are maintained. There are matters in this
bill in which I am anticipating keen interest, such as the amendments to Part 6A of the
Employment Relations Act. On that part icular issue, for example, I encourage
submissions. I will watch the select committ ee process with interest, and I am open to
considering changes that may be recommended.
This Government is committed to main taining the framework for collective
bargaining, but we wish to ensu re that there is adequate fl exibility and choice within
that framework. The Government is also keen that ineffective and unnecessarily
protracted bargaining that has productivity and other social  impacts is avoided, and that
the fairness and balance of  bargaining requirements ar e appropriate. To prevent
unnecessary and protracted collective bargai ning, the bill will return to the original
position of the duty of good faith in the Employment Relations Act, whereby a
concluded collective agreement is not requir ed. Additionally, to provide certainty for
parties that collective bargai ning is concluded, they will  be able to apply for a
declaration to that effect from the Employment Relations Authority.
The Government is proposing several other improvements to the collective
bargaining framework. These improvements will offer workplaces greater flexibility
and will remove unnecessary requirements. The proposals include employers being able
to opt out of being a party to bargaining fo r multi-employer collective agreements. This
recognises that employers should not have to enter negotiations with other employers
that may be their competitors. Another proposal is to remove the 30-day rule for new
employees who are not union members. Employ ers will now be able to offer the terms
and conditions they want to offer to new employees who are not union members,
instead of being required to offer the term s and conditions in the relevant collective
agreement for the first 30 days of employme nt. Unions and employers will now be able
to initiate collective bargaining at the same time. A collective agreement will now
continue in force for up to 12 months afte r it expires, whether it is the union or the
employer that initiated bargaining, resulting in a level playing field.
4 Jun 2013 Employment Relations Amendment Bill 10711
The bill provides that in response to a partial strike , employers will have the
additional choice of either reducing an employee’s pay by a proportionate amount or
deducting a fixed percentage of wages. Curr ently, employers are restricted in their
response to a partial strike. They can susp end employees, lock them out, or simply
accept the partial performance of work by em ployees. This proposal provides for more
proportionate responses. More certainty is n eeded in the bargaining environment, in
relation to industrial action. Employers and employees need to know what action the
other is undertaking and the nature  of that action before it begins. The bill will improve
the current lack of certainty by requiring advance written notice of any proposed strikes
and lockouts. This is similar to the current regime for strikes and lockouts in essential
services. Any withdrawal of that notice wi ll also need to be in writing. Failure to
provide the required notice of a strike or lockout will m ean that the action will be
unlawful.
This Government also considers that employees and employers should be able to
agree on flexible work practices that suit both parties. To this end, following a statutory
review of the flexible working arrange ments provisions under the Act in 2012, the
Government is proposing a number of changes that acknowledge that the workplace
needs to better reflect modern lifestyles.  These proposed changes include extending the
right to request flexible working arrangeme nts to all employees, removing the 6-month
period before an employee can request flexible work, removing the limit on the number
of requests an employee may make for flex ible work over a 12-month period, and
reducing the time frame for employers to consider requests for flexible working
arrangements. Flexible working arrangements not only provide employees with work-
life balance but improve productivity. Th is provides a win-wi n for New Zealand
employers and employees.
The bill addresses issues arising from a case considered in the Employment Court
involving restructuring at Massey University. The cas e highlighted conflicting
obligations for employers regarding the disc losure of personal information under the
Employment Relations Act, the Privacy Act, and the Official Information Act. This has
created uncertainly for New Zealand employe rs. The bill will therefore amend the duty
of good faith to clarify that it does not require employers to provide an employee with
access to confidential personal information about  another person or to evaluate material
about the employee concerned wh ere an employer is proposing to make a decision that
will or is likely to affect an employee’s continued employment.
Last year the Government completed a re view of the continuity of employment
provisions in Part 6A of the Act. The review found that there were significant
operational issues for businesses. These issues centred on transferring employees’
entitlements and information to a new employer.  The proposals in the bill will provide
more certainty and clarity for employers, while retaining key benefits for affected
employees. Also, the Government has been es pecially concerned about the impact of
Part 6A on small to medium sized businesses.  The bill will exempt small to medium
sized businesses from certain parts of Part 6A, which will remove significant
compliance costs for small to medium size d enterprises. The associated persons
limitation in the bill is designed to disc ourage large employers from gaming the
exemption by setting up smaller businesses. I am , as I have said, especially keen to hear
what affected parties have to say on the Part 6A proposals in the bill—in particular, the
associated persons limitation—and how they think it will work in practice. I will
carefully consider their submissions and the recommendations of the select committee.
This bill will also speed up Employment Re lations Authority processes with regard
to determinations. This should be welcomed  by employers and employees alike. The
authority currently has a best -practice target of 6 weeks to issue a determination.
10712 Employment Relations Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013
However, this has not been achieved in recent times, and I consider that a statutory time
frame is necessary. The bill will require that at the end of an investigation meeting the
authority will have to provide either an oral determinati on followed by a written record
of that determination within 3 months or an  oral indication of pr eliminary findings to
the parties, subject to additional informati on being received. Again, a 3-month deadline
for a final decision would appl y from when the additional information is received. This
change supports the authority ’s objective of delivering sp eedy, informal, and practical
justice. Additionally, the proposal for an imme diate oral determination will provide the
parties with an opportunity to  consider their re spective positions and whether they may
wish to settle their dispute between themse lves, without waiting for the authority to
issue the final written record. The bill proposes to—

OBITUARIES 
Hon Dame Margaret Kerslake Shields 
Mr SPEAKER: Honourable members, I regret to inform the House of the death on 
29 May 2013 of the Hon Dame Margaret Kerslake Shields DNZM, QSO, who 
represented the Kapiti el ectorate from 1981 to 1990. From 1984 to 1990 she held a 
number of portfolios, includi ng Minister of Customs, Mini ster of Consumer Affairs, 
Minister of Statistics, and Minister of Women’s Affairs. I desire on behalf of this House 
to express our sense of the loss we have su stained and our sympat hy with the relatives 
of the late former member. I now ask members to stand with me and observe a period of 
silence as a mark of respect for her memory. 
Honourable members stood as a mark of respect. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Prime Minister—Decision Making and Constitutional Safeguards 
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by all his statements regarding Government policy? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does he stand by his statement that the Auditor-General’s 
report into the Skycity deal vindicates his Government, given that the Auditor-General’s 
response to his claim was not to agree with  him, but rather to state: “we have 
established deficiencies on the part of both officials and Ministers.”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Absolutely, and the reason for that, as the member will be 
aware, is that the Auditor-General’s report was divided into three parts. The first part of 
it was focused on my involvement, and I was totally and utterly cl eared and vindicated 
in that. That was my only involvement. 
Dr Russel Norman : I seek leave to ta ble a legal opinion by constitutional lawyer 
Stephen Franks, principal at Fr anks and Ogilvie, outlining se rious legal deficiencies in 
the Government’s Skycity deal. The opinion is dated 16 May 2013. 
Mr SPEAKER: Leave is sought to table that le gal opinion. Is there any objection? 
There appears to be none. It can be tabled. 
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does he agree with Mr Franks’ view that the agreement with 
Skycity is “arguably unlawful ” and “skirts important constitutional safeguards”; if he 
does not understand this constitutional princi ple, will he read the central case on the 
issue, the case of Fitzgerald v Muldoon? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No, but I am sure what Mr Franks would find unlawful is 
someone coming in and telling the Ne w Zealand public that they have 100,000 
signatures— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Dr Russel Norman : Does he agree with Mr Franks ’ view that “The ability to 
‘purchase’ a dispensation from regulation sits uncomfortably with the rule of law.”? 
10626 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No, and no more than Labour would agree with that, given it 
did exactly the same deal back in 2001. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does he agree with Mr Franks that “Case law discourages 
anything … to fetter Parliament’s … power to legislate on future matters,”; if so, will he 
reconsider the aspects of the Skycity deal that do exactly this, such as the 35-year 
clause? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No. 
Dr Russel Norman : Is this backroom deal with  Skycity—along with the cancelling 
of democracy in Canterbury, taking away the ri ghts of carers to have  their day in court, 
giving Bathurst Resources the keys to our conservation estate, stopping free speech at 
sea, granting the Government Communications Security Bureau the power to spy on us, 
and failing to act in good faith to reform MMP—not indicative of a Government that 
will not let our democracy stand in the wa y of special favours for its friends and 
donors? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: If the Government was doing that  I might be inclined to agree 
with him, but it is ac tually not correct. If one looks at, for instance, the changes to 
people’s ability to protest at sea, the ability is very much there. There is a safety area 
that actually makes sense to all partie s. When it comes to the Government 
Communications Security Bureau, the member  sits on the Intelligence and Security 
Committee and is well and truly aware that, in fact, the Government Communications 
Security Bureau has been carrying out activ ities under an agency relationship for a long 
period of time. In fact, all we are doing is clarifying the law, so there is no change in 
position there. There is no backroom deal with  Skycity; it has been totally transparent. 
And even though the member does not like to hear it, my role in that was totally cleared 
by the Auditor-General. 
Dr Russel Norman: Yeah, right! 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Would the member just ask his supplementary question. 
Dr Russel Norman : Will he listen to Otago University law professor Andrew 
Geddis, Canterbury University law professo r Philip Joseph, former Prime Minister and 
Law Commission head Sir Geoffrey Palmer, cu rrent New Zealander of the Year Anne 
Salmond—[Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I am having trouble hearing the question. Would the member 
please start the question again. 
Dr Russel Norman : Will he listen to Otago University law professor Andrew 
Geddis, Canterbury University law professo r Philip Joseph, former Prime Minister and 
Law Commission head Sir Geoffrey Palmer, cu rrent New Zealander of the Year Anne 
Salmond, and many, many other New Zealanders, who have raised concerns about the 
Government riding roughshod over New Zeala nders’ democratic rights and over our 
constitution? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I would not agree with the point that they are making. I would 
have to look at all the different contexts. They may not be in exactly the same place. But 
the bottom line is th at the Government was elected  under a mandate it took to the 
people. It has absolutely stuck to that mandate. When it comes to these issues, the 
Government has presented them to the pe ople of New Zeala nd. The people who are 
riding roughshod over the rest of New Zeal and are the Greens, who have played 
economic sabotage with the country and do not seem to care about that. 
Dr Russel Norman : Given that answer, can the Prime Minister point to exactly 
where in his election platform he promised th at he would remove from family carers of 
disabled people the right to go to court to  challenge the lawful ness of Government 
actions? 
4 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 10627 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I would have to go back and look at al l of the particular 
details, but, from memory, the Government made it clear we would look at the matter. 
Let us understand exactly what the Government did in that legislation, which is that it 
said, rightfully so, that it would address the issues raised in the Atkinson case. It also 
gave the right to pay family caregivers when they were looking after an adult disabled 
child. But the Government also said that there has been a very longstanding position—a 
very longstanding position—where there was,  arguably, a line dr awn about where the 
State’s responsibilities start and finish and where family responsibilities start and finish. 
This Government is actually moving the country to a place that only two other countries 
in the world are in, and we happen to be doing something that Labour never did in 
office. 
Income Gap, Parity with Australia—Minimum Wage 
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
David Shearer : Does he stand by his statement that his Government has a “100 
percent record” on the minimum wage; if s o, how does he explain the now $6-plus an 
hour gap between Australia and New Zealand, after Australia raised its minimum wage 
to NZ$19.80 an hour? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes. The Government has been raising the minimum wage 
within the bounds of what we think is possible to  ensure that we preserve people’s 
work. If we look at the minimum wage in New Zealand, it is $13.75. That is half the 
average adult working wage. Th at puts us at the highest av erage in the OECD. We also 
have the significant payments, which we have maintained throughout the difficult times, 
of Working for Families. As I pointed out in the House last week, if somebody earns 
$40,000— 
Dr David Clark: The widest gap between rich and poor ever. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, you may not want to hear it, but if you want to let me 
give the answer, I am more than happy to do so. OK, so if you go and have a look at 
someone who earned the minimum wage of  $13.75 an hour for 40 hours per week and 
who was bringing up three children, that person would earn just a touch under $29,000 a 
year. They would pay $4,500 in tax, and by the time they got their Working for Families 
payments and accommodation supplements, they would receive over another $20,000-
odd in the hand. That makes New Zealand, in the relative scheme of  things, reasonably 
generous for at-risk and low-income New Zealanders. 
David Shearer : Why does he think a minimum wage worker deserves $3 in 
Australia for every $2 they would earn in  New Zealand for doing exactly the same 
work? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Firstly, there are different i ssues in each country. There are 
different costs—the inflation rates being si gnificantly higher in Australia. For a period 
of time, they have had higher levels of inte rest rates. But one of the most important 
points is that there is a balancing act here between making sure that people get pay rises 
and making sure that people do not lose their jobs. If the member be lieves there is no 
correlation between the two, he  is not only demonstrating that he does not understand 
economics but he is equally free to go and tell New Zealanders on the campaign trail 
that he wants to put them in the dole queue, because that is the simple message you will 
be sending them. 
David Shearer: Is he aware that Australia’s unemployment rate is lower than New 
Zealand’s, despite a higher minimum wage; if  so, does not that confirm the Department 
10628 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013 
of Labour’s finding in 2004 of “positive em ployment responses” to minimum wage 
increases under the last Government? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Yes. I am surprised that the member is spending so much time 
wanting to quote Australia, because if one look s at a few things that have happened in 
Australia recently—let us just look at thos e. Firstly, its unemployment rate is on the 
way up. Our unemployment rate has been on a track lower. This Government is going to 
get New Zealand back into surplus by 2014-15;  the Australian Government is likely to 
get back into surplus by onl y 2016-17. The BNZ believes that  this country will grow 
faster than Australia in the next few years. And I notice that the member does not get on 
his feet any more and ask about people leavi ng for Australia, and the reason is that they 
are not leaving in droves any more; they ar e responding to New Zealand. In fact, maybe 
the member should— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! That is a sufficiently long answer.  
David Shearer: Given that he said in 2008 of Ne w Zealanders leaving for Australia 
that it was a vote of no c onfidence in Helen Clark’s Gove rnment, what does he say to 
people now, given that the number is 43 percent higher today? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, yes, some people have left for Australia—a lot more— 
Hon Members: Oh! 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, I am glad they are cheer ing, because a lot more of them 
left under a Labour Gove rnment numerically. [ Interruption] Yes, they did—yes, they 
did. By the way, if it is such a bad place to live—[Interruption] Well, if it is such a— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! That is a very unsatisfactory interjection coming from over 
on that side. 
David Shearer: Supplementary question. 
Mr SPEAKER: Supplementary— 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No, I have not fini shed—no, I have not fini shed. And if it is 
such a bad place to live, under such a bad Government, then maybe someone with 
Australian citizenship will want to go back to Australia, rather than live under this 
Government in New Zealand. 
David Shearer : Is he aware that McDonald’s, KFC, Starbucks, Pizza Hut, The 
Warehouse, Farmers, Kmart, Bunnings, and Countdown are not implementing his youth 
minimum wage rates; if so, does that mean that major corporates actually care more 
about New Zealanders’ cost of living than the Government does? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes, I am aware of that. I think the important point to note 
here is that this is the minimum wage. You are not actually required to pay that wage, 
and the vast bulk of New Zealand workers are paid well and trul y above the minimum 
wage. But here is a very si mple point: if you are 16 or 17,  under this Government, the 
message is that an employer may give you a chance to get a job. You see, these people 
on the other side of the House, they do not want to give employers any incentives— 
David Shearer: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The Prime Minister answered 
the question in the first sentence. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER : Order! If the member is happy with the answer, then we will 
proceed to further supplementary questions. 
Hon David Parker: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We have got into the habit 
of having long speeches from Ministers in an swers, and it always requires a point of 
order from us to bring the answer to an end— 
Mr SPEAKER: No. [Interruption] Order! That is not right, and if the member wants 
to have another look at the recording earli er, he will see that I brought the Prime 
Minister to heel only about two questions ago, when I felt the an swer was quite long 
enough. 
4 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 10629 
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus, Reduction in Debt, and 
Superannuation 
3. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What progress is 
the Government making in reaching its fiscal targets of returning to surplus in 2014/15 
and reducing net government debt to 20 percent of GDP by 2020? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : The Government is on track to 
meeting both of those targets. Budget for ecasts show a surplus of $75 million in 2014-
15 and net debt peaking at 28.7 percent of GDP  in the same year before falling to 17.6 
percent of GDP in 2021. Taking on more de bt over the past few years has been 
appropriate to support our future economic gr owth and to cushion New Zealanders and 
their families from the worst effects of recessi on. But, at the same time as taking on the 
debt, the Government has laid out a path back  to surplus and, furthermore, a path back 
to reducing Government debt to levels that we believe are prudent. 
Paul Goldsmith: Why is it important that the Gove rnment gets back to surplus and 
starts repaying debt? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Although the level of Government debt is well below that of 
many other Governments that we compare ourse lves with, it is important that we keep 
Government debt low in order to offset very  high household debt and to ensure that we 
can manage through another r ecession. Net Government debt  is still rising today by 
around $130 million a week and will reach $70 billion in 2016-17, up from around $10 
billion just 5 years ago. Th at is the equivalent of around $15,000 for each and every 
New Zealander. We simply believe that it w ould be prudent to return Government debt 
to lower levels so that we are better able to reduce the pressure on interest rates rising 
sooner than they otherwise would, and reduce pressure on an exchange rate that is 
already higher than is comfortable for us. 
Paul Goldsmith : What recent reports has the Minister received on Government 
finances? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Treasury today issued the Government Financial Statements 
for the 10 months to 30 April. They show that a stronger economy and the tax reforms 
of 2010 are underpinning more tax revenue.  Combined with the Government’s 
responsible control over expenditure, this has restricted the deficit to less than $4 billion 
for the 10 months, which is $600 million less th an was forecast in the Budget just a few 
weeks ago. Tax revenue is around $3.1 billion higher than the corresponding period last 
year. This is one of a number of indicators that New Zealanders have some well-earned 
confidence and optimism about the future. 
Paul Goldsmith : What are some of the risks to the Government’s improving 
finances and the brighter outlook for the economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: There are some risks in the global economy. Europe still has 
deep-seated and long-term debt problems and productivity problems. The US economy 
looks to be recovering, but it is unclear just how robust that is. China faces risks of both 
lower growth and problems with excessive cr edit. In Australia there seems to be a 
sharper than expected downturn in mining investment, which could lead to Australia 
having lower growth rates over the next couple of years th an in New Zealand. So there 
are global risks and also dom estic risks if the Government does not stay on track with 
this moderate, consistent, and long-term economic policy. 
Hon David Parker : Does he agree that his claims  to fiscal responsibility are 
undermined by his refusal to address the superannuation entitleme nt age well in 
advance, so that people have time to prep are, given that costs of superannuation have 
increased by $3 billion, from $7 billion to $10 billion per annum, in the last 5 years, and 
that in just 2 years’ time the cost of New Zealand superannuation to the taxpayer will be 
more than the entire cost of preschool, primary, intermediate, and secondary education? 
10630 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Jun 2013 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : No, I do not agree.  Of course, no one is proposing changes 
in the age of eligibility in a way that w ould affect the costs of superannuation over the 
next 2 years. The Government has been so busy dealing with the large and rising costs 
of law and order and welfare, which got out of control under the previous Government. 
Fortunately, we are having some success in  bringing those long- term costs under 
control.

Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister responsible for Novopay) : Today was the day 
the Report of the Ministerial Inqu iry into the Novopay Project  was released. Unlike 
what the Greens have just said in that last speech, where they seek to blame the 
Ministers, the point of  the report, I th ink, is clearly that there is blame to go around for 
all parties, and, sadly, nobody has acquitted themselves with great distinction in the 
introduction of this project. There is a bigge r question, actually, because this is not the 
first information and communica tions technology project that has had issues. In fact, it 
is not the first information and communicati ons technology projec t with the education 
payroll that has had issu es. In fact, you can go back to the mid-1990s and the 
introduction of a payroll unde r another company’s name where there was again an 
inquiry, this time by the head of the Ministry  of Education, about concerns in the way 
that that particular programme was intr oduced. The net result wa s that a number of 
changes were made, and it was thought that  these things would not happen again. So 
rather than just leaping to the political conclusion that the Greens seek to leap to, and no

least read a few pages of the report and ask yourself what actually went wrong here. 
 Sadly, what went wrong was that in a number of ways the people whom the public 
should be able to rely on—som e of the staff, some of th e suppliers—in this instance 
were not able to or did not fully perform their role well. The problems with Novopay, as 
the report notes, have affected public trust a nd confidence in the Ministry of Education, 
and, of course, also in the wider public s ector. The report iden tifies weaknesses in 
project governance and project leadership th at allowed the system to go live, with a 
number of significant risks that the ministry  and its vendors, including Talent2, were, in 
the words of the inquiry, “over-confident of managing.” These risks, as we now know, 
resulted in service issues that the minist ry and Talent2 were unprepared for and they 
were overwhelmed by their nature and scale.  
The report goes into the history of what happened in the whole saga, and it goes back 
many years, right the way to 2005 and ear lier. It makes the observation that New 
Zealand’s school payroll is very  complex. It compares it with  the health sector payroll. 
But it is also very complex, with some very unique elements to it. As a result there was 
extensive customisation of the Novopay software. The ministry notes there was a failure 
by the ministry to involve the users of the Novopay system in the schools and appreciate 
their requirements. So those two things alone indicate some of the difficulties that you 
can see happen in these situations when the project that was set up did not first seek to 
simplify its business processes, and did not stay close enough to the users of the system.  
Probably one of the biggest issues was th e lack of accountability for independent 
quality assurance. Ministers were entitled to expect that the quality assurance processes 
that the State sector has would have applie d in this case, and, unfortunately, despite 
assurances that they did, this was not the case. The result is that Ministers were not well 
served by the information they were given on the project. The report notes that reporting 
to Ministers was “inconsisten t, … unduly optimistic and so metimes misrepresented the 
situation.” I think it would be important to quote, in light of what Ms Turei has just said,

overrepresented project readiness and its chan ce of success.” That was the paper that
