the Budget debate on the issue of housing, which is indeed an issue that has dominated 
much of the coverage and deba te of this year’s Budget. I guess, to start on a positive 
note, the Government does deserve to be c ongratulated—in the sense that it has finally 
cottoned on to the fact that we do have an affordable housing crisis in New Zealand. I 
must say it took it long enough. As we know, this affordable housing crisis is absolutely 
the worst in Auckland, where the average hou se price last year  was $735,000. That is 
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10663 
the average price to buy a new home in Auck land and that increase d 12 percent in the 
last calendar year alone. So any time you hear the Minist er of Housing crowing about 
low interest rates and how affordable housing is I would just remind you of that figure. 
Not only that, but in Auckland it takes a staggering 71 percent of the average take-home 
pay to service the mortga ge on a house that is priced in the first qua rtile. That is, this 
house is one of the cheapest quarter of houses in Auckland and it takes 71 percent of the 
average income to service the mortgage on that house. When we talk about housing 
affordability, anything over 30 percent of your income spent on housing is considered to 
put you in housing stress, and for that house to be severely unaffordable. We have a 
situation in Auckland where it takes 71 percen t of the average take-home pay to service 
the mortgage on one of the cheapest houses in th e market. So that is your crisis for you, 
and it is a pretty severe one.  
Well, the problem is supply and demand, ri ght? We know that in Auckland we need 
about 13,000 new dwellings to be consented each year. We have been averaging only 
about 3,000 so it is no surpri se that we have a severe hous ing crisis in Auckland. It is 
worst in Auckland but it is actually bad ev erywhere. That equivalent figure for the 
national average in New Zealand is that it  takes 49 percent of the average take-home 
income to service a mortgage on a lower-qua rtile house. So, again, remembering that 
anything over 30 percent is  severely unaffordable and puts a household in housing 
stress, we have got a problem across the whol e of the country. In places like the Central 
Otago lakes, Nelson and Marlborough, We llington, and Waikato that problem is 
elevated above the national average, so we have a major problem.  
What we have seen from the Government in terms of solutions is the Housing 
Accords and Special Housing Areas Bill, whic h I look forward to beginning to hear the

Unfortunately, the legislation does not deal wi th the issue just in Auckland, it actually

not consulted on the drafting of  the legislation, once it sa w it actually f ound that there 
were inconsistencies between the legislation and the accord that it thought it had signed 
up to with the Government.  
But there are serious problems with the m odels that are proposed in the Housing 
Accords and Special Housing Areas Bill. First of all, it is based on the idea that the 
development at Hobsonville Point is the answer to affordable housing in Auckland. 
Given that the so-called affordable houses at  Hobsonville Point cost  either just over 
$400,000 or $485,000, which is not affordable for most people, that is not a great model 
to base it on. There is also  no guaranteed percentage of affordable homes in the new 
special housing areas that are going to be created, and they  override local democracy. 
Those other regions that I mentioned, where housing affordability is also a problem, had 
better watch out because the Government is coming to create special housing areas in 
their region whether they like it  or not. All the power is with  the Minister, and, if they 
cannot negotiate an accord with the Minister, he can just put a special housing area in 
place, regardless of whether the local c ouncil actually agrees , overriding both the 
Resource Management Act and the local democracy for that area. And remember, at the

Zealanders who are in severe  housing stress at the moment. So congratulations to the 
10664 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013 
Government on identifying a problem—it is a shame that none of the measures do

Hon MARYAN STREET (Labour) : As we discuss the Budget that this 
Government has handed down I think it is important to consider  the Government’s 
progress through its agenda to exploit all of New Zealand’s natural resources. In that 
context, it is necessary to look at the im portance that the Government places on its 
environment budget. I have taken a look at Vote Environment and I find it absolutely 
remarkable that there has not been one single policy initiative in the environment 
budget—not one new idea, not one new progr amme, not one new policy initiative to 
protect, maintain, and enhance our environment.  
The Minister for the Environment has done things, but they are not reflected in this 
Budget. Let me give the House some exampl es. The budget for Vote Environment is to 
be set against our claims—our diminishing clai ms, and our claims that are consistently 
under criticism—of being 100 percent pure. We  have poor and declining water quality. 
We have erosion of our protections for our  environment, proposed in the Minister’s 
second tranche of Resource Management Ac t amendments, and we have some self-
interest reflected in the water recommendati ons and proposals that the Minister put out 
earlier this year. I would real ly like to know whether the Minister even put in a bid for 
her environment vote, because it is not apparent from this Budget.  
I will just list some of the things that ar e contained in the Vote Environment part of 
the Budget—let us have a look at them. E nvironmental management obligations and 
programmes—there is no change, absolu tely no change. Improving resource 
management—there is a drop of $2.4 million from the previous year, so improving 
resource management, as a Budget line, gets a cut. This needs to be explained. If the 
members opposite wish to give the Minister a heads-up, that will be asked in the 
estimates questions when she appears before the select committee.  
I will tell the House where one area of increase has happened, and it is in the funding 
to service the Minister. Funding to service the Minister has gone up by $313,000, and 
the note attached to that in the vote is that  the ministry expects that there will be an 
increase in ministerials as a result of  the Resource Management Act and water 
management reforms. Clearly, the Minister is aware that the Resource Management Act 
reforms and the water management reforms are go ing to be controversial, so in order to 
bolster her own ability to answer the quest ions that are going to flood in and the 
challenges that are going to be taken agai nst her, she has increased the funding to 
service her office by $313,000. That does not enhance the environment one iota.  
Advice on environmental hazards and waste— there is no change; no change there. 
The waste levy administration and assessm ent of projects for funding by the levy—
there is a drop of $600,000; $610,000, actually. But it is a $600,000 drop in the waste 
levy administration and assessments of project s that are funded by that levy to see how 
various industries can minimise their waste production. So th ere is not any vision about 
next year or the year after, and whet her or not our waste production and our 
minimisation of that is going to improve. There are no new targets. There are no new 
ideas. In fact, there is a cut of $600,000 in  that area. The Contaminated Sites 
Remediation Fund—there is no change there. There is no change in the Contaminated 
Sites Remediation Fund. How is the Minister intending to deal with new contaminated 
sites as they emerge?  
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10667 
She has only to look in her backyard at the Ōwaka Pit in her electorate, which has 
had medium-density fibreboard combusting sp ontaneously and releasing toxins into the 
air. This has been happening for months. The fi re has gone out only just in the last 2 or 
3 weeks. The Minister clearly does not bothe r about that, even t hough it is in her 
electorate, because the prevai ling wind makes those toxic fumes blow over the people 
who live in the electorate of  my colleague Megan Woods. The Minister is not so 
concerned about the people in that electorate that she thinks there is anything that needs

some discomfort. So even for the Minister’s  own backyard she ha s not appropriated or,

Ōwaka Pit is now in a state that needs re mediation. The fire is out; now the ground has 
to be recovered.  
The Contestable Waste Minimisation F und—no change. This fund has a certain 
allocation per year. Sometimes the funds are not spent in 1 year and they are moved into 
future years, but there is no change. Where there has been an increase—and here we go 
again—is to the Envi ronmental Protection Authority, which gets an increase of $1.9

functions under our exclusive economic zone  legislation and the Exclusive Economic

There is no change to the Fresh Star t for Fresh Water Clean-up Fund for New

overall change. Lake Ōkareka in Rotorua is suffocating from hornwort. It is a hugely

of our natural resources. It does not matter whether we have the legal right to do it or 
not, this Government will proceed to expl oit our environment in order to produce 
dollars, and usually for its friends. So Skycity was sold the gambling laws, Warner Bros

laws. Thank you. 
MAGGIE BARRY (National—North Shore) : Budget 2013 is Bill English’s fifth 
Budget and it is, indeed, buildi ng momentum. It confirms that  New Zealand is back on 
track, with more economic growth, more jobs, rising wages, and a return to surplus by 
2014-15. That is all great news for New Zealand, and very bad news for the Opposition, 
which is bereft, as we have heard this afte rnoon, of any fresh ideas or policies. Both 
Labour and the Greens are, of course—and ha ve proven it time a nd again—anti-growth 
parties. They are opposed to a ny and all initiative s that would create jobs and boost the 
economy. The Opposition’s policies of borrowi ng more and spending more would take 
10668 Budget Debate 4 Jun 2013 
our economy backwards at a great rate. A nd when no one would lend us any more 
money, what is its solution? It is to print more, of course. That is the sort of madness 
that the unholy alliance of no ideas would deli ver. It is the tired old tried and failed 
policies of Labour and the “Watermelon Gr eens”—those individuals who are green on 
the outside and socialist red at heart, and who think they are doing so well.  
This Budget 2013 is a defining document from a Government that is spending 
prudently, not spending up large, which is  all Opposition member s can come up with. 
So I am not going to waste any more time th is afternoon on them. Instead, I intend to 
focus on the very positive measures that we re introduced in the Budget in the vitally 
important areas of health, housing, and welfar e. As our very competent and successful 
health Minister, Tony Ryall, outlined at the start of today’s Budget debate, this John 
Key - led Government is investing more in  health than ever before. The Minister 
outlined the number of green prescriptions and the strong focus on investing in 
preventative care. To recap, we are making a $1.6 billion investment available over 4 
years. That has boosted the total health spending to a record level of $14.7 billion.  
Let us look specifically at where that is be ing targeted. As our population is healthier 
and we are living longer, it is projected, as the Minister indicated, that by 2045 or 2050 
there are going to be 150,000 New Zealande rs with dementia. As I and many New 
Zealand families know only too well, the painfu l reality of living with dementia is a 
terrible struggle for the sufferers and for their families, who have to watch as the people 
they love gradually decline and need mo re and more high-level support. My late 
mother’s 10-year decline with multi-infarct dementia was not untypical. It was very sad 
to see a once independent, successful businesswoman and vibrant personality struggling 
to do the simple things like making tea a nd toast, and desperately wanting to stay 
independent and in her own home for as l ong as possible. To help people in these 
difficult situations, we are investing an extra $70 million in aged care and dementia 
services. That money is being very carefully targeted into the areas where it will help 
most.  
As my mother, Agnes, lost her ability to recognise people and places, it became even 
more important to her to stay in her own home, because it was a safe place and it was a 
place where she was familiar with all he r surroundings and her garden. She was a 
happier and calmer person there. But, as that eventually took its toll on her, Mum 
needed more and more support to stay at home. Although I was able to pay privately for 
much of the assistance that she needed, it is a very difficult thing to manage long term. I 
know that the $20 million that has been allocated in this year’s Budget targeted 
specifically to be invested in home support se rvices will be invaluable. Some things are 
priceless. It will provide practical help so that people can stay in the familiar 
environment of their own home for as long as  possible. With an ageing population, we 
need to ensure the best possible quality of life for dementia sufferers and for their 
families. It is very clear to me that it is important to detect dementia as early as possible. 
I know of many families who were in denial  for a long time, and who were just not 
aware of the onset of dementia  and its early signs. So they  experienced, I am afraid to 
say, heart-breaking misunderstandings and fami ly rifts, actually, un til they understood 
what was happening.  
Overall, as a society, we need to have  a much better and earlier awareness of 
dementia and its inevitable pathway. When  the time does come for more expert 
intervention and residential care options, we need a workforce that is equipped with the 
right level of training. There is no questi on in my mind that caregivers need to be 
compassionate, and they need that quality in abundance. I believe it is basically a 
vocational guidance—it is a cal ling, really, to look after people who are losing their 
minds to dementia. There is also the need  for better training and more specifically 
4 Jun 2013 Budget Debate 10669 
skilled people to meet th at growing demand. To meet that, we have allowed $3.2 
million towards training for health professionals and towards awareness programmes, 
and also for early detection assistance for th e clinical teams. These kinds of conditions 
require that high level of skill as well as that high level of compassion. Believe me, I 
and people who have experienced it think that  is money well spent. It will make a huge 
difference to the quality of life for the pe rson suffering from dementia and for their 
families. With the best will in the world it is very difficult, once the condition has 
reached a certain stage, for most New Zeala nd families to look after dementia sufferers 
at home. That is why the $12 million increase in funding for bed subsidies and the vital 
encouragement for further investment in demen tia beds are essential. So over the next 4 
years we are also funding, through the district health boards, an additional $33.2 million 
on aged residential care subsidies.  
In the vital area of housing, the Minister Dr Nick Smith is as determined through his 
portfolio as the health Minister, Tony Ryall, is  with health, to help the vulnerable in our 
society. We know that crowded, cold, and damp  conditions contribute to dismal health 
outcomes. So making homes warmer, drier, and healthier is one of his priorities. It is the 
right thing to do. And, unlike the waffle a nd the weasel words of the Opposition, Dr 
Smith is not leaving that to chance. An extra $100 million investment in the highly 
successful home insulation programme is goi ng to boost the number of homes insulated 
to 230,000 by September this year. That is a clear and measurable thing. So all State 
houses that are capable of being insulated will be. It is a measure of the standard of our 
State housing stock. He is developing and tr ialling a Housing Warrant of Fitness to 
apply to all 69,000 Housing New Zealand Corpor ation properties, so that over the next 
3 years this Government is making a record investment of $2.9 billion in State housing. 
It is also making very bold changes to the way that we deliver housing assistance, and it 
is targeting it to the people who really need it.  
The shift from State dominated housing to community housing has been very 
successful in Europe, in North America, and in Australia. So in Budget 2013 our 
Government has announced that we are al so going to extend in come-related rent 
subsidies to community housing providers. Churches, charities, and other NGOs often 
integrate housing with other wraparound services  to people with disabilities, to people 
with mental health issues, and to people with drug and alcohol problems. These sorts of 
wraparound services can often do, let us face it , a better job of m eeting their clients’ 
complex needs. This Government is determined  to create the right environment to grow 
the community housing sector.  
Quality affordable housing is good for the economy and it is also very good for 
communities. High housing costs ultimately rais e debt and increases demand for social 
assistance. Under this Government, the Ki wi dream of owning your own home will 
again become a reality and within reach of low and middle income New Zealanders. We 
have announced a raft of measures to make housing more affordable. We are looking at 
increasing land supply, we are streamlini ng consent and compliance costs, we are 
looking at better delivery of core infrastruc ture to support that new housing, and we are 
also getting on top of the costs around build ing materials and cons truction. We are not 
just sitting back and leaving it to chance;  we are doing somethi ng about it. We have 
concrete, measurable things.  
As my colleague Jonathan Young said in hi s earlier call, we ar e not just aiding 
people, we are enabling people. That is why I come to our welfare reforms. They are 
increasing, and under Budget 2013 low-income families will be receiving greater 
support. It is really a combination of what we have been doing—extending proven 
programmes and also introducing new initia tives, targeting res ources and targeting 
support. This is complemented by the G overnment’s $139.3 million investment through

the Social Housing Fund, which others ha ve detailed. Helping people to help 
themselves is what is at th e heart of this Government’s Budget. This is a Government 
and this is a Budget with real heart and m easurable outcomes th at will really help

This Government has put another $1.5 million to support budgeting services, as well, 
for people who have not ever really been ta ught how to grasp the reality of budgeting, 
and making sure their cheque books work a nd making sure they are not overspending. 
Those are lessons that perhaps the Labour colleagues across the way could well benefit

To end, I will say that the people in my No rth Shore electorate have given me very

were some of the things that they have b een looking for. They wanted to have some 
better provisions there, and what we are doing there with  the reduction in the levies has

EDUCATION AMENDMENT BILL 
Third Reading 
Hon HEKIA PARATA (Minister of Education) : I move, That the Education 
Amendment Bill be now read a third time . The Education Amendment Bill amends the 
Education Act 1989. It will play a key role in supporting the Government’s objective of 
how we get five out of five  students achieving educational success. This Government is 
absolutely focused on that. We do not want educational success for a few—for some—
but for all, so we have focused on a full range of measures that will deliver that 
possibility to all New Zealand school students  and learners. This bi ll helps deal with a 
number of things, in fact. It creates th e legal framework by which we will establish 
partnership schools or kura hourua. It also looks at the provision for how school staff 
may exercise search and surrender provisions, in order to ensure that schools are safe 
and secure places while protecting the rights of students. It also  makes provision for a 
number of other areas that will allow greater flexibility in the delivery of education in 
New Zealand.  
Starting with the two significant or substa ntial provisions in te rms of creating the 
legal framework for partnership schools or kura hourua, we know that it will help us 
deliver a third option for educ ational provision in New Zeal and. It will enable us to 
have a legal framework that allows for pa rtnership between the community sectors, 
business, and education, because this Government recognises that there is not a 
monopoly on how quality education can be delivered. In fact, it can be delivered 
through a number of ways, and we are interested in exploring all of those ways, because 
we will leave no option uncons idered in how we ensure that we raise educational 
achievement for five out of five kids.  
We know that our education system in Ne w Zealand is world class but not world 
leading. We know that it is top performing as  an education jurisdic tion. It performs for 
the vast majority but not for all. We know  that those who have been traditionally 
underserved by our education system are the same groups of people year in and year 
out. So there is a system response that we need to make. We want those parts of our 
education system that are performing well for the majority of our students to continue to 
perform well and, indeed, to perform better, bu t we also want to address those parts of 
the system that are not performing as well. That means working with all of the schools 
4 Jun 2013 Education Amendment Bill 10673 
that we have—and we have over 2,500. T hose 2,500 schools already canvass a range of 
options. We have single-sex and coed; we ha ve total immersion in English and total 
immersion in Māori, and bilingual units; we have faith-based and secular-based schools; 
we have small, medium, and large schools; an d, of course, they ar e spread the length 
and breadth of our country.  
What partnership schools do is offer us another optio n—another option that is 
focused on results, on transparency, on ensuri ng that the sponsors who propose and go 
through a very thorough approval process are focused on how they will deliver 
educational results for the students whose parents choose that they should go there. 
There will be no compulsion in  this. Partnership schools pr ovide another option, but it 
will be transparent in terms of what is exp ected. It will be transparent in terms of the 
conduct of its business. It will be transparent in that the disciplinary provisions of the 
Ombudsmen Act will apply. It will be transparen t in that all of the requirements will be 
specified in a contract between the Ministry  of Education, on behalf of the Crown, and 
the successful sponsor, and all the reporting th at will be expected in respect of that, 
whether financial, operational,  or educational, will be reported to the Ministry of 
Education, which, of course, will ensure that it is captured by the Official Information 
Act.  
 The bill provides that the sponsors may recommend that a proportion of their staff 
may not be registered as teachers, but that  is not to be confused with not having 
qualifications and not having skills. Indeed, kura kaupapa had the same kind of difficult 
birth that the Opposition w ould try to attend partnershi ps schools with. There was a 
belief that kura were so different from the re st of the mainstream system that they could 
not possibly be good, when the facts, which have been incontrovertible since they 
started, are that children and young people who go to kura by and large, on average, do 
better—Māori kids—than they do in the mainstream system. The kura will tell us that 
much of that success is due  to experts in te reo me ōna tikanga, who may not be 
registered teachers but nevertheless deliver learning in ways that ensure educational 
success. We envisage the same sort of track  record occurring here with partnership 
schools. So what this legislation does is put around it a lega l framework that makes this 
option clear, stable, transparent, and focuse d on getting five out of five kids being 
educationally successful.  
As I have said, there will be no compulsion for a parent to send their child here, as 
there is no compulsion for a pare nt to send their child to any particular type of school. 
And, as I have said many times before too, it is not the type of school; it is the quality of 
performance. We will be holding these school s to the highest standards. We will be 
expecting that they will be able to deliver successfully to these kids, and if not, the 
ultimate sanction will apply, and that is that they can, and will, be closed.  
A second part of this legislation focuses on ensuring that we are very clear about 
what the rights are of not only teachers and pr incipals but also othe r authorised staff to 
ensure a safe and secure environment wher ein learning can break out, potential can be 
realised, and educational success can be within  reach of every one of our students. But 
we are realistic. We know that schools are also microcosms of society and that there can 
be dangers and unsafe instruments or behaviours that are brought into schools. We want 
to ensure that our teachers and other authorised  staff have the ability to exercise search 
and surrender responsib ilities that ensure th at where staff suspect that a student may 
indeed be harbouring inappropr iate equipment or anything th at might present a danger 
to other students, staff have the ability to require these young people to disclose those.  
The Education and Science Committee members have worked really hard together, 
and with the sector, to strike a very good balance between ensuri ng the safety of all 
students and protecting the rights of the dignity  and privacy of other students. This has 
10674 Education Amendment Bill 4 Jun 2013 
been a very challenging balance to strike, an d I think that this le gislation does that. It 
will be reinforced by the establishment of guidelines, which will be formulated under 
the Secretary for Education’s auspices, but also through involving a working group 
from the sector. After all, principals and teachers are the ones who every day face these 
challenges and want to know that they ar e going to have sensible and practicable 
provisions by which they can exercise these cautions.  
The final part of this legisl ation deals with a range of ot her provisions, all of which 
are dedicated to this Government’s commitment to raising educational achievement for 
all kids. One of the things it starts off with is a recogniti on that boards of trustees are 
Crown entities but, unlike every other Crown entity, they have no purpose articulated at 
law. This legislation remedies that omissi on by making it very clea r that the role and 
purpose of boards in everything they do is to focus on ensu ring that every student has 
the opportunity to do well educationally. So, wh ether it is the management of property, 
financial responsibilities to be discharged, the kind of curriculum programme that is to 
be taught, or the kinds of skills that are to  be employed at the school, the board is doing 
all of that with one clear focus, and that is to raise the achievement of all.  
Allied to that is a provision for making timetabling flexible. We learnt from 
Christchurch that by enabling schools to have flexibility in their timetables, they could 
cater for a whole range of students, but in pa rticular for that very  permeable interface, 
which this Government has made more perm eable, in the secondary -tertiary transition, 
where young people go off to trades academies fo r 2 or 3 days a week, or take up other 
options such as internships, practicums,  and so forth. We do not want a hidebound 
structure within schools that precludes that possibility. We want educational success to 
not only be in reach but also be achieved by five out of five students, and this legislation 
puts that within their grasp.

The bill has three main components. Firs t, it simplifies the Act’s planning and 
funding framework. Second, it streamlines  the Act’s tolling and public-private 
partnership provisions, and, third, it implements a new public transport operating model.  
Key changes made by the bill are, first, to planning and funding. The bill amends the 
Act’s planning and funding framework by making it simpler, more streamlined, and less 
prescriptive. To achieve this, the bill fo cuses decision making on three key criteria: 
effectiveness, efficiency, and safety. It al so combines the former five national and 
regional transport planning documents into three main documents. The bill simplifies 
the Act’s consultation provisi ons and enables regions to tailor their engagement 
processes to specific situations. The bill also allows the New Zealand Transport Agency 
to borrow against National Land Transport Fu nd revenue to finance projects with the 
approval of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport, should circumstances 
suggest there is a good case for borrowing and it is prudent to do so.  
The bill also amends the Act’s tolling a nd public-private partnership provisions. The 
bill simplifies and streamlines the Act’s fr amework for assessing tolling schemes and 
processes for improving public-private partnerships. These changes will reduce 
potential barriers to the use of the Ac t’s tolling and public-private partnership 
provisions while maintaining r obust approval processes. In re spect of regional fuel tax, 
the inefficient and impractical regional fuel tax put in place in 2008 is repealed.  
Finally, the bill establishes the public transport operating model in legislation. This 
model provides a new framework for building long-term partnerships between regional 
councils and public transport operators to de liver public transport services. The model 
will deliver more competitive public transpor t services that are less reliant on public 
subsidy. Over time, public transport users will  see better integration of services and 
better-quality services with more focus on customer needs.  
The Land Transport Management Amendment Bill is an important bill and I am 
confident that it will only improve land tran sport planning and decision making, as well 
as ensuring that central and local governme nt get better value for money from their 
investment in public transport. It will also support all of our effo rts to cut unnecessary 
red tape to create better, more effective legislation. I commend this bill to the House.

EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AMENDMENT BILL 
First Reading 
Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Minister of Labour) : I move, That the Employment 
Relations Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Transport and 
Industrial Relations Committee to consider the Employment Relations Amendment Bill. 
This bill implements the Government’s policies aimed at a flexible and fair employment 
relations framework for both employees and employers. The bill c ontinues our strong, 
unrelenting focus on reducing complian ce costs and unnecessarily burdensome 
regulation. We want to ensure that empl oyers have the confidence to compete and 
expand, while key protections fo r employees are maintained. There are matters in this 
bill in which I am anticipating keen interest, such as the amendments to Part 6A of the 
Employment Relations Act. On that part icular issue, for example, I encourage 
submissions. I will watch the select committ ee process with interest, and I am open to 
considering changes that may be recommended.  
This Government is committed to main taining the framework for collective 
bargaining, but we wish to ensu re that there is adequate fl exibility and choice within 
that framework. The Government is also keen that ineffective and unnecessarily 
protracted bargaining that has productivity and other social  impacts is avoided, and that 
the fairness and balance of  bargaining requirements ar e appropriate. To prevent 
unnecessary and protracted collective bargai ning, the bill will return to the original 
position of the duty of good faith in the Employment Relations Act, whereby a 
concluded collective agreement is not requir ed. Additionally, to provide certainty for 
parties that collective bargai ning is concluded, they will  be able to apply for a 
declaration to that effect from the Employment Relations Authority.  
The Government is proposing several other improvements to the collective 
bargaining framework. These improvements will offer workplaces greater flexibility 
and will remove unnecessary requirements. The proposals include employers being able 
to opt out of being a party to bargaining fo r multi-employer collective agreements. This 
recognises that employers should not have to enter negotiations with other employers 
that may be their competitors. Another proposal is to remove the 30-day rule for new 
employees who are not union members. Employ ers will now be able to offer the terms 
and conditions they want to offer to new employees who are not union members, 
instead of being required to offer the term s and conditions in the relevant collective 
agreement for the first 30 days of employme nt. Unions and employers will now be able 
to initiate collective bargaining at the same time. A collective agreement will now 
continue in force for up to 12 months afte r it expires, whether it is the union or the 
employer that initiated bargaining, resulting in a level playing field.  
4 Jun 2013 Employment Relations Amendment Bill 10711 
The bill provides that in response to a partial strike , employers will have the 
additional choice of either reducing an employee’s pay by a proportionate amount or 
deducting a fixed percentage of wages. Curr ently, employers are restricted in their 
response to a partial strike. They can susp end employees, lock them out, or simply 
accept the partial performance of work by em ployees. This proposal provides for more 
proportionate responses. More certainty is n eeded in the bargaining environment, in 
relation to industrial action. Employers and employees need to know what action the 
other is undertaking and the nature  of that action before it begins. The bill will improve 
the current lack of certainty by requiring advance written notice of any proposed strikes 
and lockouts. This is similar to the current regime for strikes and lockouts in essential 
services. Any withdrawal of that notice wi ll also need to be in writing. Failure to 
provide the required notice of a strike or lockout will m ean that the action will be 
unlawful.  
This Government also considers that employees and employers should be able to 
agree on flexible work practices that suit both parties. To this end, following a statutory 
review of the flexible working arrange ments provisions under the Act in 2012, the 
Government is proposing a number of changes that acknowledge that the workplace 
needs to better reflect modern lifestyles.  These proposed changes include extending the 
right to request flexible working arrangeme nts to all employees, removing the 6-month 
period before an employee can request flexible work, removing the limit on the number 
of requests an employee may make for flex ible work over a 12-month period, and 
reducing the time frame for employers to consider requests for flexible working 
arrangements. Flexible working arrangements not only provide employees with work-
life balance but improve productivity. Th is provides a win-wi n for New Zealand 
employers and employees.  
The bill addresses issues arising from a case considered in the Employment Court 
involving restructuring at Massey University. The cas e highlighted conflicting 
obligations for employers regarding the disc losure of personal information under the 
Employment Relations Act, the Privacy Act, and the Official Information Act. This has 
created uncertainly for New Zealand employe rs. The bill will therefore amend the duty 
of good faith to clarify that it does not require employers to provide an employee with 
access to confidential personal information about  another person or to evaluate material 
about the employee concerned wh ere an employer is proposing to make a decision that 
will or is likely to affect an employee’s continued employment.  
Last year the Government completed a re view of the continuity of employment 
provisions in Part 6A of the Act. The review found that there were significant 
operational issues for businesses. These issues centred on transferring employees’ 
entitlements and information to a new employer.  The proposals in the bill will provide 
more certainty and clarity for employers, while retaining key benefits for affected 
employees. Also, the Government has been es pecially concerned about the impact of 
Part 6A on small to medium sized businesses.  The bill will exempt small to medium 
sized businesses from certain parts of Part 6A, which will remove significant 
compliance costs for small to medium size d enterprises. The associated persons 
limitation in the bill is designed to disc ourage large employers from gaming the 
exemption by setting up smaller businesses. I am , as I have said, especially keen to hear 
what affected parties have to say on the Part 6A proposals in the bill—in particular, the 
associated persons limitation—and how they think it will work in practice. I will 
carefully consider their submissions and the recommendations of the select committee.  
This bill will also speed up Employment Re lations Authority processes with regard 
to determinations. This should be welcomed  by employers and employees alike. The 
authority currently has a best -practice target of 6 weeks to issue a determination.
